q: Match List I with List II: List I (Drug) — A. Nicotine, B. Morphine, C. Heroin, D. Cocaine. List II (Effect) — I. Causes sense of euphoria and increased energy, II. Stimulates adrenal gland to release catecholamines into blood circulation, III. Effective sedative and painkiller, IV. A depressant; slows down body function.
e: Nicotine stimulates adrenal gland release of catecholamines (II); Morphine is an effective sedative/painkiller (III); Heroin is a depressant slowing body function (IV); Cocaine causes euphoria and increased energy (I). A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

t: Matching biomolecule to type of bond
q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Protein, (b) Unsaturated fatty acid, (c) Nucleic acid, (d) Polysaccharide with (i) C=C double bonds, (ii) Phosphodiester bonds, (iii) Glycosidic bonds, (iv) Peptide bonds.
e: Protein has peptide bonds (iv); unsaturated fatty acid has C=C double bonds (i); nucleic acid has phosphodiester bonds (ii); polysaccharide has glycosidic bonds (iii). (a)-(iv),(b)-(i),(c)-(ii),(d)-(iii).

q: It is said that the elemental composition of living organisms and that of inanimate objects (like earth's crust) are similar, if all the elements present are analysed. However, a closer look shows that
o: living organisms have more gold in them than inanimate objects.
living organisms have more water in their body than inanimate objects.
living organisms have more carbon, oxygen and hydrogen per unit mass than inanimate objects.
living organisms have more calcium in them than inanimate objects.
e: Although living and non-living matter share the same basic elements, living organisms contain a much higher proportion of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen per unit mass (mainly as part of organic biomolecules) compared to inanimate matter like earth's crust.

q: Many elements are found in living organisms, either free or in the form of compounds. Which of the following is not found in living organisms?
e: Silicon, while abundant in the earth's crust, is not a characteristic or significant component of living tissues, unlike magnesium, iron, and sodium, which play well-known biological roles.

q: An amino acid, under certain conditions, has both positive and negative charges simultaneously in the same molecule. Such a form of an amino acid is called
e: The zwitterionic form of an amino acid carries both a positively charged amino group and a negatively charged carboxyl group simultaneously, giving the molecule an overall neutral charge.

q: A homopolymer has only one type of building block (monomer) repeated several times. Proteins are heteropolymers usually made of
e: Proteins are heteropolymers constructed from approximately 20 different types of amino acid monomers, linked by peptide bonds.

q: Proteins perform many physiological functions, apart from cellular structural organisation. Which of the following represents an additional function that some proteins discharge?
e: Besides structural roles, some proteins function as hormones (e.g., insulin, glucagon) that regulate physiological processes — a key additional function performed by proteins.

t: Sources of narcotic drugs from plants
q: Which part of poppy plant is used to obtain the drug 'Smack'?
e: Smack (heroin, derived from morphine) is obtained from the latex of the poppy plant (Papaver somniferum), extracted from the unripe seed capsules.

q: The protein produced by Bacillus thuringiensis that is toxic to certain insects is encoded by which gene?
e: The cry genes (crystallin genes) in Bacillus thuringiensis encode Cry proteins (crystal proteins), which are toxic to specific insect larvae. These genes are used to develop insect-resistant Bt crops.

q: Golden Rice is a genetically modified variety enriched with which nutrient?
e: Golden Rice has been genetically engineered to produce beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A, in the endosperm of rice grains. It was developed to address Vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

q: Bt toxin produced by Bacillus thuringiensis is encoded by which gene?
e: Bt toxin is encoded by the 'cry' gene (crystal protein gene) in Bacillus thuringiensis. Different cry genes (e.g., cryIAc, cryIIAb) produce proteins toxic to specific insects. The nif gene is for nitrogen fixation, bar gene confers herbicide resistance, and rol gene affects plant morphology.

q: Bt cotton was developed to provide resistance against which of the following pests?
e: Bt cotton expresses the Bt toxin (cry genes like cryIAc and cryIIAb) that specifically targets bollworms (Helicoverpa armigera), which are major cotton pests. Aphids, whiteflies, and thrips are sucking pests and are not effectively controlled by Bt toxin.

q: GEAC stands for
e: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) is the Indian regulatory body responsible for approving genetically modified organisms and products for research and commercial use.

q: ADA is an enzyme that is deficient in the genetic disorder SCID. What is the full form of ADA?
e: ADA stands for adenosine deaminase, an enzyme crucial for normal immune function; its deficiency causes Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), historically treated via gene therapy.

t: Biotechnology Applications - Bt Crops and Gene Therapy
q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) α-1 antitrypsin (B) Cry IAb (C) Cry IAc (D) Enzyme replacement therapy
List II: (I) Cotton bollworm (II) ADA deficiency (III) Emphysema (IV) Corn borer
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: α-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema (A-III). Cry IAb protein confers resistance against corn borer (B-IV). Cry IAc protein confers resistance against cotton bollworm (C-I). ADA deficiency is treated with enzyme replacement therapy/gene therapy (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is correct.

q:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I: (a) Protoplast fusion, (b) Plant tissue culture, (c) Meristem culture, (d) Micropropagation
List-II: (i) Totipotency, (ii) Pomato, (iii) Somaclones, (iv) Virus free plants
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
(1) a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i
(2) a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i
(3) a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii
(4) a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii
e: Protoplast fusion = Pomato (hybrid of potato and tomato); Plant tissue culture = Totipotency (the underlying principle); Meristem culture = Virus free plants; Micropropagation = Somaclones. So a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.

q: Now a days it is possible to detect the mutated gene causing cancer by allowing radioactive probe to hybridise its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by its detection using autoradiography because:
o: Mutated gene does not appear on photographic film as the probe has complementarity with it.
Mutated gene partially appears on a photographic film.
Mutated gene completely and clearly appears on a photographic film.
Mutated gene does not appear on a photographic film as the probe has no complementarity with it.
e: The radioactive probe is designed to be complementary to the normal (non-mutated) gene sequence. Since it cannot hybridize with the mutated gene (no complementarity), the mutated gene does not appear (no signal) on the autoradiograph/photographic film.

q: In gene therapy of Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, the patient requires periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes because:
o: Retroviral vector is introduced into these lymphocytes.
Gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at embryonic stages
Lymphocytes from patient's blood are grown in culture, outside the body.
Genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal cells.
e: Since the genetically engineered lymphocytes used in ADA gene therapy are not immortal cells, they eventually die out, requiring periodic infusion of the engineered cells to sustain therapeutic effect.

q: Statements related to human Insulin are given below. Which statement(s) is/are correct about genetically engineered Insulin? (a) Pro-hormone insulin contain extra stretch of C-peptide (b) A-peptide and B-peptide chains of insulin were produced separately in E.coli, extracted and combined by creating disulphide bond between them. (c) Insulin used for treating Diabetes was extracted from Cattles and Pigs. (d) Pro-hormone Insulin needs to be processed for converting into a mature and functional hormone. (e) Some patients develop allergic reactions to the foreign insulin. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
e: In genetically engineered (recombinant) human insulin production, the A and B peptide chains are produced separately using two different strains of E. coli, then extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds, exactly as described in statement (b) only - this is specific to Eli Lilly's Humulin process and distinguishes it from the natural pro-hormone processing pathway.

q: Match the following columns and select the correct option: (a) Bt cotton, (b) Adenosine deaminase deficiency, (c) RNAi, (d) PCR with (i) Gene therapy, (ii) Cellular defence, (iii) Detection of HIV infection, (iv) Bacillus thuringiensis
e: Bt cotton involves the toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis (iv), Adenosine deaminase deficiency is treated via gene therapy (i), RNAi is used as a cellular defence mechanism against invading viruses/transposons (ii), and PCR is used for detection of HIV infection (iii). This matches a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.

q: In ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay), which of the following pairs correctly describes the principle used?
o: Antigen-antigen interaction detected by radioactive labelling
Antibody-antigen interaction detected by enzyme-conjugated antibody producing a colour change
DNA hybridization detected by antibody-conjugated reporter molecule
PCR amplification of pathogen DNA detected by fluorescent dye
e: ELISA is based on antigen-antibody interactions. An enzyme-conjugated antibody binds to the antigen of interest. When the substrate is added, the enzyme converts it, producing a measurable colour change. This allows detection and quantification of antigens (or antibodies) in a sample.

q: Rosie, the transgenic cow, produced milk with human alpha-lactalbumin. What was the primary reason this milk was considered nutritionally superior for human infants compared to normal cow milk?
o: It had higher fat content similar to human milk
It lacked lactose, making it suitable for lactose-intolerant infants
It had a more balanced protein profile, closely resembling human breast milk
It contained antibodies for passive immunity in newborns
e: Rosie was the first transgenic cow producing human alpha-lactalbumin in her milk (2.4 g/L). This protein made the milk nutritionally richer and more balanced in protein composition, resembling human breast milk more closely, making it more suitable for human infants than normal cow's milk.

q: Which of the following best defines 'biopiracy' in the context of biotechnology?
o: Illegal smuggling of genetically modified organisms across international borders
Unauthorized use of biological resources and associated traditional knowledge of local communities by corporations without compensation
Theft of laboratory organisms used in biotechnology research by rival companies
Patent infringement of genetically engineered products between multinational companies
e: Biopiracy refers to the unauthorized and uncompensated exploitation of biological resources (plants, microbes, etc.) and associated traditional knowledge of indigenous/local communities by multinational corporations or researchers for commercial purposes. Examples include attempts to patent uses of turmeric and basmati rice.

q: Which of the following statements about recombinant human insulin production is INCORRECT?
o: Pro-insulin is an inactive precursor that needs processing to become active insulin
A and B chains of insulin are produced separately and combined in vitro by disulfide bonds
The C-peptide connecting A and B chains is retained in the final recombinant insulin product
Recombinant insulin eliminates the risk of immune reactions associated with animal-derived insulin
e: This statement is incorrect. In recombinant insulin production, the A and B chains are produced separately in E. coli. They are then extracted and combined in vitro, with disulfide bonds forming between them. The C-peptide (connecting peptide of proinsulin) is NOT present in the final active insulin product — it is removed during processing, just as it is in natural insulin maturation.

q: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl suffering from ADA deficiency. Which of the following statements about this therapy is INCORRECT?
o: ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) deficiency is caused by deletion of the gene for ADA enzyme
Lymphocytes from the patient's blood were grown in culture and a functional ADA gene was introduced using a retroviral vector
The genetically engineered lymphocytes were returned to the patient and provided a permanent cure for the disease
ADA deficiency leads to compromised immune function
e: The gene therapy for ADA deficiency was NOT a permanent cure. The introduced lymphocytes had a limited lifespan in the body. Since the cells were not introduced into the bone marrow stem cells, the patient required periodic infusions of genetically engineered lymphocytes. A permanent cure would require introduction of the functional gene into early embryonic cells or bone marrow stem cells. All other statements are correct.

q: Which of the following best describes 'biopiracy' in the context of biotechnology?
o: Illegal smuggling of genetically modified seeds across international borders
Unauthorized use of bio-resources and traditional knowledge from developing nations by developed nations without proper compensation
Piracy of proprietary biotechnological processes and patented molecular techniques
Theft of biological samples from research laboratories for commercial use
e: Biopiracy refers to the exploitation of biological resources and associated traditional/indigenous knowledge from biodiversity-rich developing countries by multinational companies and research organizations from developed countries, without proper authorization or sharing of benefits with the source country or communities. Classic examples include patents on Basmati rice (RiceTec Inc.) and turmeric's wound-healing properties, which were later challenged by India. It does not simply refer to smuggling seeds or stealing from labs.

q: Golden Rice is a genetically engineered variety that produces beta-carotene in its endosperm. Which of the following genes were introduced to achieve this?
o: Genes encoding phytoene synthase from daffodil and lycopene beta-cyclase from bacteria
Genes encoding phytoene synthase from daffodil and phytoene desaturase from Erwinia uredovora
Genes encoding carotenoid synthase from maize and phytoene desaturase from bacteria
Genes encoding lycopene cyclase from tomato and carotenoid isomerase from daffodil
e: The original Golden Rice (developed by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer) was created by introducing two genes: phytoene synthase (psy) from daffodil (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) and phytoene desaturase (crtI) from the bacterium Erwinia uredovora. These two enzymes together convert geranylgeranyl diphosphate into beta-carotene in the rice endosperm. The later Golden Rice 2 used the maize psy gene for higher production, but the original version used daffodil and bacterial genes.

q: Streptokinase produced by bacterium Streptococcus is used for
e: Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering, is used as a 'clot buster' for removing clots from the blood vessels of patients who have undergone myocardial infarction leading to heart attack.

q: Which of the following genetically engineered organisms was used by Eli Lilly to prepare human insulin?
e: Eli Lilly (an American company) produced the two DNA chains of human insulin (A and B chains) and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli bacterium to produce human insulin.

q:
Neoplastic characteristics of cells refer to:
(A) A mass of proliferating cell
(B) Rapid growth of cells
(C) Invasion and damage to the surrounding tissue
(D) Those confined to original location
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Neoplastic characteristics (11th NCERT Page No. 141): uncontrolled, excessive, abnormal cell division leads to a mass of proliferating cells forming a tumor (A); very fast, undifferentiated cell division (B); malignant neoplastic cells damage surrounding tissue by invasion and neovascularization (C). Confinement to original location (D) is benign, not neoplastic/malignant. So A, B, C only.

q: Silencing of specific mRNA is possible via RNAi because of -
e: RNA interference (RNAi) involves complementary RNA molecules that bind to and neutralize/silence the specific mRNA, forming double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) that is then degraded by the cell. Class 12th NCERT Page - 180.

q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Bt toxins are insect group specific and coded by a gene cry IAc.
Statement II: Bt toxin exists as inactive protoxin in B. thuringiensis. However, after ingestion by the insect the inactive protoxin gets converted into active form due to acidic pH of the insect gut.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
e: Statement I is true - Bt toxins are indeed insect group specific and coded by cry genes like cry IAc. Statement II is false - the Bt protoxin gets converted to its active form due to the ALKALINE pH of the insect gut, not acidic pH. 12th NCERT Page No. 179-180.

q: The inactive form of Bt toxin is converted to the active form in the insect gut_______
e: Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis as an inactive protoxin. In the insect gut, the alkaline pH environment solubilizes and helps convert the inactive protoxin into its active, toxic form, which then binds to the gut epithelium and causes cell lysis.

q: Which kind of therapy was given in 1990 to a four-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency?
e: In 1990, the first gene therapy was administered to a four-year-old girl with ADA deficiency, a landmark case in gene therapy history.

q: Stirred-tank bioreactors have been designed for:
o: Ensuring anaerobic conditions in the culture vessel
Addition of preservatives to the product
Availability of oxygen throughout the process
e: Stirred-tank bioreactors have a stirrer and oxygen-delivery system to ensure adequate mixing and oxygen availability throughout the culture, maintaining aerobic conditions and homogeneity.

q: When gene targeting involving gene amplification is attempted in an individual's tissue to treat disease, it is known as:
e: Gene therapy involves correction of a gene defect by delivering a normal gene into an individual's cells/tissue to treat disease, as was done for ADA deficiency.

q: Which of the following is true for golden rice?
o: It is drought tolerant, developed using Agrobacterium vector.
It has yellow grains, because of a gene introduced from a primitive variety of rice.
It is vitamin A enriched, with a gene from daffodil.
It is pest resistant, with a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis.
e: Golden rice is vitamin A (beta-carotene) enriched, developed by introducing genes from daffodil (and other sources) into the rice genome, giving the grains a golden-yellow color.

q: What triggers activation of protoxin to active bt toxin of Bacillus thuringiensis in boll worm?
e: The alkaline pH of the insect gut triggers the solubilization and activation of the Bt protoxin into its active toxin form, which then binds to the midgut epithelium causing cell lysis.

q: Which of the following is a commercial blood cholesterol lowering agent?
e: Statins are commercially used as blood cholesterol lowering agents, produced using the fungus Monascus purpureus.

q: If a geneticist uses the blind approach for sequencing the whole genome of an organism, followed by assignment of function to different segments, the methodology adopted by him is called as:
e: Sequence annotation is the process of identifying genes and assigning functions to different segments of a genome after it has been sequenced using a 'blind' (shotgun-type) sequencing approach, as was done in the Human Genome Project.

q: Identify the microorganism which is responsible for the production of an immunosuppressive molecule cyclosporin A:
e: Cyclosporin A, an immunosuppressive drug widely used in organ transplant patients to prevent rejection, is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum.

t: Regulatory bodies for genetically modified organisms in India
q: In India, the organisation responsible for assessing the safety of introducing genetically modified organisms for public use is
o: Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
e: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC), functioning under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, is the apex regulatory body responsible for assessing the safety of releasing genetically modified organisms and products for public use in India.

q: Use of bioresources by multinational companies and organisations without authorisation from the concerned country and its people is called
e: Biopiracy refers to the unauthorised use/exploitation of a country's bioresources (and associated traditional knowledge) by other nations or multinational companies without fair compensation or permission.

t: Intellectual property rights disputes (Basmati rice case)
q: A 'new' variety of rice was patented by a foreign company, though such varieties have been present in India for a long time. This is related to
e: This refers to the well-known controversy over the patenting of Basmati rice by a foreign (US) company, despite Basmati varieties having existed and been cultivated in India for a long time.

q: By which method was a new breed 'Hisardale' of sheep formed by using Bikaneri ewes and Marino rams?
e: Hisardale, a new sheep breed, was developed by cross-breeding Bikaneri ewes with Marino rams, combining desirable traits from both breeds.

q: Bt cotton variety that was developed by the introduction of toxin gene of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is resistant to:
e: Bt cotton expresses the Cry toxin protein from Bacillus thuringiensis, which is toxic specifically to certain insect pests (like the cotton bollworm), making the plant resistant to these insect pests.

t: Sequence of steps in somatic hybridisation
q: Arrange the following steps of somatic hybridisation in a correct sequence: A. Digestion of cell walls. B. Isolation of naked protoplasts. C. Fusion of protoplasts to get hybrid protoplast. D. Isolation of single cells from two different varieties of plants. E. Growing hybrid protoplast to form a new plant.
e: Sequence: isolate single cells (D) → digest cell walls (A) → isolate naked protoplasts (B) → fuse protoplasts (C) → grow into new plant (E): D, A, B, C, E.

t: Reason for large holes in Swiss cheese
q: What is the reason behind production of large holes in 'Swiss Cheese'?
o: The production of large amount of CO2 and H2 by Trichoderma polysporum
The production of large amount of CO2 and H2 by lactic acid bacteria called Lactobacillus
The production of large amount of CO2 by Propionibacterium sharmanii
The production of large amount of CO2 by Clostridium butylicum
e: Swiss cheese's characteristic large holes are produced by CO2 released by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii (shermanii) during fermentation.

t: Bt toxin genes controlling cotton bollworm and corn borer
q: The toxin proteins isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis, coded by which of the following genes would control cotton bollworm and corn borer, respectively?
e: cryIAc controls cotton bollworm and cryIAb controls corn borer.

t: Use of alpha-1-antitrypsin from transgenic animals
q: The human protein named α-1-antitrypsin, obtained from transgenic animals, is used for the treatment of ___________.
e: Human alpha-1-antitrypsin produced by transgenic animals is used to treat emphysema.

t: Term for gene amplification therapy in tissues
q: When gene targetting involving gene amplification is attempted in an individual's tissue to treat disease, it is known as:
e: Gene therapy involves correcting a genetic defect by introducing a normal gene or modifying gene expression in target tissues.

t: Matching plant biotechnology term to application
q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Protoplast fusion, (b) Plant tissue culture, (c) Meristem culture, (d) Micropropagation with (i) Totipotency, (ii) Pomato, (iii) Somaclones, (iv) Virus free plants.
e: Protoplast fusion gives hybrids like Pomato (ii); Plant tissue culture is based on totipotency (i); Meristem culture gives virus-free plants (iv); Micropropagation produces somaclones (iii). (a)-(ii),(b)-(i),(c)-(iv),(d)-(iii).

t: Term for DNA sequences used in DNA fingerprinting
q: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions in DNA sequence, called as:
e: DNA fingerprinting relies on highly variable repetitive DNA sequences, known as repetitive DNA (specifically VNTRs within satellite DNA regions) — per key, repetitive DNA.

q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Aspergillus niger, (b) Acetobacter aceti, (c) Clostridium butylicum, (d) Lactobacillus with (i) Acetic Acid, (ii) Lactic Acid, (iii) Citric Acid, (iv) Butyric Acid.
e: Aspergillus niger produces citric acid (iii); Acetobacter aceti produces acetic acid (i); Clostridium butylicum produces butyric acid (iv); Lactobacillus produces lactic acid (ii). (a)-(iii),(b)-(i),(c)-(iv),(d)-(ii).

q: Which of the following is not an objective of Biofortification in crops?
e: Biofortification targets nutritional improvement (protein, vitamins, micronutrients), not disease resistance, so improving disease resistance is not its objective.

q: The first recombinant DNA pharmaceutical product approved for human use was:
e: Recombinant human insulin (Humulin) was the first recombinant DNA-derived pharmaceutical product approved for human therapeutic use. It was produced using E. coli by Eli Lilly in 1982, replacing insulin extracted from pig or cow pancreas.

q: RNA interference (RNAi) technology was used to develop nematode-resistant tobacco plants. Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism?
o: Sense RNA introduced silences the parasite's gene by methylation
Double-stranded RNA specific to the parasite gene is introduced, which silences the gene via RISC complex
Antisense RNA binds to the host mRNA to prevent nematode attachment
siRNA introduced into the plant causes hypersensitive response against nematodes
e: In RNAi, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) complementary to a specific parasite gene is introduced into the host plant. This dsRNA activates the RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex), which degrades the corresponding mRNA in the nematode, silencing the gene and preventing parasitism.

q: The Bt toxin is a protoxin in bacteria but becomes active in the insect gut. What condition in the insect midgut activates the toxin?
o: Presence of digestive enzymes at low temperature
e: The Bt protoxin is solubilized and activated in the highly alkaline pH of the insect midgut. The activated toxin then binds to the epithelial cells lining the gut, creating pores that cause cell swelling, lysis, and death of the insect. Mammals have acidic stomachs, so the toxin is not activated in them.

q: The first clinical gene therapy trial was performed in 1990 on a 4-year-old girl suffering from which disease?
e: The first clinical gene therapy was conducted in 1990 on a girl with ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) deficiency, a form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). Functional ADA-encoding gene was introduced into her lymphocytes, which were then reinfused. However, this therapy was not permanent as the lymphocytes had a limited life span.

q: RNA interference (RNAi) technology was used to develop nematode-resistant tobacco plants. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which RNAi silences the nematode gene?
o: Double-stranded RNA complementary to nematode mRNA is introduced, leading to its degradation by the host cell's RISC complex
Single-stranded antisense RNA binds to nematode DNA and prevents its transcription
siRNA produced by the plant integrates into the nematode genome and disrupts gene expression
The plant produces ribozymes that specifically cleave nematode ribosomal RNA
e: RNAi involves the introduction of dsRNA that is complementary to the target nematode gene (e.g., msp gene). This dsRNA is processed into siRNA by Dicer enzyme and incorporated into RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex), which then degrades the complementary mRNA of the nematode, silencing the gene. The nematode feeding on this plant ingests the dsRNA and its essential gene is silenced.

q: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is used as a diagnostic tool. The principle of ELISA is based on:
o: Antigen-antibody interaction detected by an enzyme-linked colour reaction
Amplification of pathogenic DNA using specific primers
Separation of proteins by molecular weight using gel electrophoresis
Hybridization of labelled probes with complementary pathogen nucleic acid
e: ELISA is based on the specific antigen-antibody interaction. A secondary antibody conjugated to an enzyme (e.g., alkaline phosphatase or horseradish peroxidase) binds to the antigen-antibody complex. The enzyme converts a substrate into a coloured product, whose intensity indicates the presence and amount of antigen. PCR uses primers for DNA amplification, gel electrophoresis separates proteins by size, and Southern/Northern blotting uses labelled probes.

q: Rosie, the first transgenic cow, produced human protein-enriched milk. Which human protein was present in her milk?
e: Rosie was the first transgenic cow produced in 1997, and she expressed the human alpha-lactalbumin gene. Her milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin, making it nutritionally more balanced (richer in the essential amino acid) for human babies compared to normal cow's milk. Human insulin is produced by transgenic E. coli, human growth hormone by transgenic organisms like bacteria, and Factor IX by transgenic sheep (Tracy).

t: Role of C-peptide in Insulin Maturation
q: The C-peptide of human insulin is
o: a part of the mature insulin molecule.
responsible for the formation of disulphide bridges.
removed during the maturation of pro-insulin to insulin.
e: Pro-insulin contains an extra connecting (C) peptide linking the A and B chains; this C-peptide is enzymatically removed during the maturation process, leaving the mature, biologically active insulin molecule.

q: α-1 antitrypsin is
e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin, produced using biotechnology, is used to treat emphysema, a lung condition that can result from a hereditary deficiency of this protein.

q: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies DNA following the equation.
e: PCR amplifies DNA exponentially in geometric progression — the DNA doubles with each cycle, following 2ⁿ where n is the number of cycles.

t: DNA Isolation - Role of Chilled Ethanol
q: During the purification process for recombinant DNA technology, addition of chilled ethanol precipitates out:
e: Addition of chilled ethanol causes DNA to precipitate out of the aqueous solution, which is a standard step in DNA isolation/purification for recombinant DNA technology.

q: In gene gun method used to introduce alien DNA into host cells, microparticles of _____ metal are used.
e: In the gene gun (biolistic) method, microparticles of tungsten or gold coated with DNA are bombarded into host cells to introduce alien DNA.

q: Upon exposure to UV radiation, DNA stained with ethidium bromide will show:
e: DNA stained with ethidium bromide fluoresces with a bright orange colour when exposed to UV radiation, allowing visualization of DNA bands on a gel.

q: Which of the following is not a cloning vector?
e: A probe is a labelled single-stranded DNA/RNA fragment used to detect a specific DNA sequence, not a cloning vector. YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome), pBR322 (a plasmid), and BAC (Bacterial Artificial Chromosome) are all cloning vectors.

q: During PCR, primers bind to the DNA strands in the______step.
e: PCR has three main steps: denaturation (DNA strands separate at high temperature), annealing (primers bind/anneal to the complementary single-stranded DNA template), and extension (DNA polymerase extends the primers to synthesize new DNA strands). Primers bind during the annealing step.

q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Plasmids are autonomously replicating DNA.
Statement II: Plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
e: Plasmids are circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that exist independently of the bacterial chromosome and are capable of autonomous (independent) replication -- Statement I is correct. They are indeed extrachromosomal, i.e., separate from the main bacterial chromosome -- Statement II is correct. Both statements are correct.

q: A foreign DNA and plasmid cut by the same restriction endonuclease can be joined to form a recombinant plasmid using:
e: DNA ligase joins the cut ends of foreign DNA and plasmid vector (both cut by the same restriction enzyme) to form a recombinant plasmid.

q: A specific recognition sequence identified by endonucleases to make cuts at specific positions within the DNA is:
e: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific palindromic nucleotide sequences in DNA and cut at those specific positions.

q: Which one of the following equipments is essentially required for growing microbes on a large scale, for industrial production of enzymes?
e: A bioreactor is essentially required for growing microbes on a large scale for industrial production of enzymes and other biotechnology products.

q: The process of separation and purification of expressed protein before marketing is called:
e: Downstream processing refers to the series of steps (separation, purification, formulation, and preservation) applied to a biotechnologically produced product before it is marketed.

q: The DNA fragments separated on an agarose gel can be visualised after staining with:
e: Ethidium bromide intercalates into DNA and fluoresces under UV light, allowing DNA fragments separated on an agarose gel to be visualised.

q: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sequences called:
e: Restriction endonucleases recognize and cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences — sequences that read the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction. These are called recognition or palindromic sequences.

q: Which of the following is NOT a desirable property of a cloning vector?
e: A cloning vector should have an ori (to replicate independently), selectable markers (to identify transformants), and cloning sites. High molecular weight is not desirable; vectors should ideally be small to allow easy manipulation and efficient transformation.

q: Which enzyme is used to join two DNA fragments (insert and vector) after they have been cut by restriction enzymes?
e: DNA ligase is the enzyme that forms phosphodiester bonds between the cut ends of DNA fragments, effectively sealing the nicks and joining the insert to the vector to form recombinant DNA.

q: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sequences called palindromic sequences. Which of the following best describes a palindromic sequence in double-stranded DNA?
o: A sequence that reads the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction
A sequence that codes for a specific amino acid on only one strand
A sequence present only at the ends of linear DNA molecules
A sequence that is methylated and protected from restriction enzyme activity
e: Palindromic sequences in dsDNA read the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction. For example, 5'-GAATTC-3' on one strand pairs with 3'-CTTAAG-5' on the other, which when read 5'→3' is also GAATTC. This symmetry allows restriction enzymes to recognize and cut these sites.

q: Which of the following features is NOT a required characteristic of a cloning vector?
o: Ability to integrate into the host chromosome permanently
e: A cloning vector must have an origin of replication (to replicate independently), a selectable marker (to identify transformed cells), and a cloning site (to insert foreign DNA). Permanent chromosomal integration is not a requirement; most vectors replicate as extrachromosomal elements (plasmids).

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, which statement correctly describes the movement of DNA fragments?
o: Larger fragments move faster and travel farther from the well
Smaller fragments move faster toward the positive electrode
All fragments move at the same speed regardless of size
Fragments move toward the negative electrode due to their positive charge
e: DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode (anode) under an electric field. Smaller fragments experience less resistance in the gel matrix and therefore migrate faster, traveling farther from the well compared to larger fragments.

q: Restriction endonucleases are also called 'molecular scissors'. Which of the following statements about them is CORRECT?
o: They cut DNA at random positions throughout the genome
They recognize specific palindromic nucleotide sequences and cut DNA at those sites
They join two DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds
They are found only in eukaryotic cells as a defense mechanism
e: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific palindromic sequences (sequences that read the same on both strands in 5'→3' direction) and cut double-stranded DNA at or near these sites. They are naturally found in bacteria (prokaryotes) as a defense against foreign DNA, not in eukaryotes.

q: In Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), which enzyme is used and why is it preferred over a regular DNA polymerase?
o: RNA polymerase; because it does not require a primer
Taq polymerase; because it is thermostable and active at high temperatures
DNA ligase; because it joins Okazaki fragments efficiently
Reverse transcriptase; because it synthesizes DNA from RNA template
e: PCR uses Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus. Since PCR involves repeated cycles of high-temperature denaturation (~94°C), a thermostable DNA polymerase is essential. Regular DNA polymerases would denature at such temperatures, requiring fresh enzyme to be added each cycle.

q: The correct sequence of steps in one cycle of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is:
e: Each cycle of PCR consists of three steps in order: (1) Denaturation – the double-stranded DNA template is heated to ~94°C to separate the two strands; (2) Annealing – the temperature is lowered (~50–65°C) to allow primers to bind to complementary sequences on each strand; (3) Extension – the temperature is raised to ~72°C (optimum for Taq polymerase) and the polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands. This cycle is repeated 30–40 times, exponentially amplifying the target sequence.

q: The rising of dough (used in making bread) is due to
o: hydrolysis of wheat flour starch into sugars.
e: Yeast added to dough ferments the sugars present, releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped within the dough and causes it to rise.

q: Who among the following was awarded the Nobel Prize for the development of the PCR technique?
e: Kary Mullis was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993 for developing the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) technique.

t: Fate of Foreign DNA Transferred into Alien Organism
q:
What is the fate of a piece of DNA carrying only gene of interest which is transferred into an alien organism?
A. The piece of DNA would be able to multiply itself independently in the progeny cells of the organism.
B. It may get integrated into the genome of the recipient.
C. It may multiply and be inherited along with the host DNA.
D. The alien piece of DNA is not an integral part of chromosome.
E. It shows ability to replicate.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: A foreign DNA piece (gene of interest alone, without an origin of replication) cannot multiply independently - it needs to either integrate into the host genome (B) or be part of a vector that replicates along with host DNA (C) to be inherited. So B and C only. 12th NCERT Page No. 164.

q: Plasmid pBR322 has PstI restriction enzyme site within gene ampR that confers ampicillin resistance. If this enzyme is used for inserting a gene for β-galactoside production and the recombinant plasmid is inserted in an E.coli strain:
o: It will be able to produce a novel protein with dual ability.
It will not be able to confer ampicillin resistance to the host cell.
The transformed cells will have the ability to resist ampicillin as well as produce β-galactoside.
It will lead to lysis of host cell.
e: Inserting the foreign gene at the PstI site within the ampR gene causes insertional inactivation of the ampicillin resistance gene, so the recombinant plasmid will NOT confer ampicillin resistance to the host cell.

q: With regard to insulin choose correct options, (a) C-peptide is not present in mature insulin. (b) The insulin produced by rDNA technology has C-peptide. (c) The pro-insulin has C-peptide. (d) A-peptide and B-peptide of insulin are interconnected by disulphide bridges. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Mature insulin lacks the C-peptide (it is removed during processing). Pro-insulin contains the C-peptide. The A and B peptide chains of mature insulin are held together by disulphide bridges. Insulin produced by rDNA technology (recombinant) does not have the C-peptide since only A and B chains are synthesized separately and joined.

q: Match the following: (a) Inhibitor of catalytic activity, (b) Possess peptide bonds, (c) Cell wall material in fungi, (d) Secondary metabolite with (i) Ricin, (ii) Malonate, (iii) Chitin, (iv) Collagen
e: Malonate is an inhibitor of catalytic activity (succinate dehydrogenase) (ii), Collagen possesses peptide bonds (iv), Chitin is the cell wall material in fungi (iii), and Ricin is a secondary metabolite (toxic protein) (i). This matches a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.

q: Match the organism with its use in biotechnology: (a) Bacillus thuringiensis, (b) Thermus aquaticus, (c) Agrobacterium tumefaciens, (d) Salmonella typhimurium with (i) Cloning vector, (ii) Construction of first rDNA molecule, (iii) DNA polymerase, (iv) Cry proteins
e: Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Cry proteins (iv), Thermus aquaticus is the source of heat-stable Taq DNA polymerase (iii), Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used as a cloning vector (i) in plant transformation, and Salmonella typhimurium was used in the construction of the first rDNA molecule (ii). This matches a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.

q: In the pBR322 plasmid, if a foreign DNA is inserted into the BamHI site within the tetracycline resistance gene (tetR), which of the following outcomes is expected for transformants grown on ampicillin and tetracycline plates respectively?
o: Grow on both ampicillin and tetracycline plates
Die on ampicillin plate, grow on tetracycline plate
Grow on ampicillin plate, die on tetracycline plate
Die on both ampicillin and tetracycline plates
e: Insertion of foreign DNA into the BamHI site disrupts the tetR gene (insertional inactivation), so recombinants lose tetracycline resistance. However, the ampR gene remains intact. Therefore, recombinants grow on ampicillin (intact ampR) but die on tetracycline (disrupted tetR), allowing identification of recombinants.

q: After the biosynthetic stage in a bioreactor, the product must be subjected to downstream processing. Which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of downstream processing steps?
e: Downstream processing follows a defined sequence: first Separation (of the desired product from the culture medium/cells), then Purification (to remove contaminants), followed by Formulation (making it suitable for the intended use), and finally Quality control (testing for safety and efficacy) before release.

q: Micro-injection as a method of recombinant DNA delivery into animal cells involves:
o: Using electric pulses to create temporary pores in the cell membrane
Directly injecting recombinant DNA into the nucleus of the host cell using a fine needle
Coating DNA onto gold particles and bombarding cells
Using liposomes to encapsulate and deliver DNA across the cell membrane
e: Micro-injection involves directly injecting the recombinant DNA solution into the nucleus of an animal cell using a very fine glass needle (micropipette). This method bypasses cellular barriers and is used especially in animal transgenics. Electroporation uses electric pulses, biolistics uses gold particles, and liposome-mediated transfer uses lipid vesicles.

q: After biosynthesis of a recombinant therapeutic protein in a bioreactor, several downstream processing steps are required before it can be used as a drug. Which of the following represents the CORRECT order of major downstream processing stages?
e: Downstream processing follows the sequence: (1) Separation of the product from the culture broth/cells, (2) Purification using techniques like chromatography to remove contaminants, (3) Formulation into the final dosage form (with excipients, stabilizers, etc.), and (4) Clinical trials/quality control for therapeutic use. This order ensures safety and efficacy of the final product.

q: When constructing a genomic library vs. a cDNA library, a researcher studying the expression of a mammalian gene in bacteria would prefer a cDNA library. What is the most critical reason for this preference?
o: cDNA is double-stranded and can be directly inserted into bacterial vectors, whereas genomic DNA is always single-stranded
Mammalian genomic DNA contains introns that bacteria cannot splice out, whereas cDNA lacks introns
cDNA libraries contain regulatory promoter sequences that function better in bacterial systems
Genomic DNA degrades rapidly in bacteria, making cDNA a more stable alternative
e: Mammalian genes contain introns (non-coding sequences) that must be spliced out of pre-mRNA to produce functional mRNA. Bacteria lack the spliceosomal machinery to process introns. cDNA is synthesized from mature mRNA (already spliced) using reverse transcriptase, so it lacks introns. When expressed in bacteria, cDNA yields the correct functional protein, unlike genomic DNA which would produce non-functional protein due to intron inclusion.

q: Blue-white screening is used to identify recombinant colonies when cloning into the lacZ gene of a vector. A researcher plates transformed bacteria on medium containing X-gal and IPTG. Which observation correctly identifies cells carrying a recombinant plasmid with the insert?
o: Blue colonies, because the insert restores lacZ function and produces β-galactosidase
White colonies, because insertion into lacZ disrupts β-galactosidase production
Blue colonies, because IPTG induces a different gene that metabolizes X-gal
White colonies, because the insert provides a repressor that blocks lacZ transcription
e: In blue-white screening, the foreign DNA insert is ligated into the multiple cloning site within the lacZ gene. This insertional inactivation disrupts the lacZ gene, preventing synthesis of functional β-galactosidase. Without β-galactosidase, the colorless substrate X-gal cannot be cleaved into its blue product. Therefore, recombinant colonies appear WHITE, while non-recombinant colonies (intact lacZ) appear BLUE.

q: EcoRI restriction enzyme cuts the sequence 5'-GAATTC-3'. After cutting with EcoRI, which type of ends are generated and what enzyme is required to join such fragments?
o: Blunt ends; DNA ligase joins them without any additional requirement
Sticky (cohesive) ends with 5' overhangs; DNA ligase joins complementary sticky ends
Sticky ends with 3' overhangs; reverse transcriptase joins complementary sticky ends
Blunt ends with phosphate groups; polynucleotide kinase joins them
e: EcoRI cuts between G and AATTC on both strands, generating sticky ends with 5' overhangs (5'-AATT-3' single-stranded tails). These cohesive/sticky ends can hydrogen-bond with complementary sticky ends of other EcoRI-cut fragments. DNA ligase then seals the nick by forming phosphodiester bonds, joining the fragments permanently.

q: To make competent E. coli cells for uptake of recombinant DNA, which treatment is used and what is the underlying principle?
o: Treatment with lysozyme to digest the cell wall, allowing direct DNA entry
Treatment with divalent cations (e.g., CaCl₂) followed by heat shock to increase cell membrane permeability for DNA uptake
Treatment with protease enzymes to remove membrane proteins that block DNA entry
UV irradiation to create pores in the outer membrane for passive DNA diffusion
e: E. coli cells do not naturally take up foreign DNA. To make them 'competent' (capable of uptake), they are treated with divalent cations like Ca²⁺ (CaCl₂), which neutralizes the negative charges on both the DNA and the cell membrane. A brief heat shock (42°C) then creates a temporary increase in membrane permeability, allowing DNA to enter the cell. This process is called chemical transformation.

q: A scientist wants to clone a human insulin gene in bacteria. Instead of using the genomic DNA directly, cDNA is preferred. What is the most important reason for this?
o: cDNA is smaller in size so it fits more easily into the plasmid vector
Bacteria lack the machinery (spliceosomes) to remove introns, so cDNA (made from mRNA, lacking introns) ensures proper protein expression
cDNA carries its own promoter sequences that are recognized by bacterial RNA polymerase
Genomic DNA cannot be cut by restriction enzymes, so cDNA must be used
e: Eukaryotic genes like human insulin contain non-coding sequences called introns. Bacteria lack the splicing machinery (spliceosomes) needed to remove introns from pre-mRNA. If genomic DNA were cloned, the mRNA produced would not be properly processed, resulting in a non-functional protein. cDNA is synthesized from mature mRNA (which has already been spliced) using reverse transcriptase, so it lacks introns and can be directly expressed in bacterial cells to produce functional insulin protein.

q: In the represented plasmid (pBR322-like, with BamH1, Tet R, Ori, EcoR1, β-Galactosidase, and amp marked) an alien piece of DNA is inserted at EcoRI site. Which of the following strategies will be chosen to select the recombinant colonies?
o: Using ampicillin & tetracyclin containing medium plate.
Blue color colonies will be selected.
White color colonies will be selected.
Blue color colonies grown on ampicillin plates can be selected.
e: Insertion of the alien DNA at the EcoRI site (within the β-galactosidase gene) causes insertional inactivation of β-galactosidase, so recombinant colonies appear white (no blue colour due to no enzyme activity on X-gal), while non-recombinant colonies remain blue. So white colonies are selected.

t: Gel Electrophoresis and Recombinant DNA Construction
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The DNA fragments extracted from gel electrophoresis can be used in construction of recombinant DNA.
Statement II: Smaller size DNA fragments are observed near anode while larger fragments are found near the wells in an agarose gel.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both statement I and statement II are correct
Both statement I and statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct. DNA fragments eluted from gel electrophoresis are used to construct recombinant DNA. In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move towards the anode (positive electrode) based on size, with smaller fragments moving faster/farther (near anode) and larger fragments remaining closer to the wells. Class 12th NCERT Page - 168.

t: Enzymes NOT Essential for Gene Cloning
q:
Which of the following enzyme(s) are NOT essential for gene cloning?
A. Restriction enzymes
B. DNA ligase
C. DNA mutase
D. DNA recombinase
E. DNA polymerase
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Restriction enzymes (A), DNA ligase (B) and DNA polymerase (E) are essential tools for gene cloning. DNA mutase (C) is not a standard enzyme term used in molecular biology, and DNA recombinase (D) helps in crossing over during meiosis-I and is not associated with gene cloning. So C and D only are NOT essential.

q:
The blue and white selectable markers have been developed which differentiate recombinant colonies from non-recombinant colonies on the basis of their ability to produce colour in the presence of a chromogenic substrate.
Given below are two statements about this method:
Statement I: The blue coloured colonies have DNA insert in the plasmid and they are identified as recombinant colonies.
Statement II: The colonies without blue colour have DNA insert in the plasmid and are identified as recombinant colonies.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both statement I and statement II are correct
Both statement I and statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
e: Insertion of DNA into the lacZ gene region disrupts (inactivates) the gene, so recombinant colonies (with the DNA insert) cannot produce the enzyme that acts on the chromogenic substrate, and appear WHITE (colourless), not blue. Non-recombinant colonies (without insert) retain a functional lacZ gene and appear blue. So Statement I is incorrect, Statement II (colonies without blue colour = recombinant) is correct. 12th NCERT Page - 170 (Insertional inactivation).

q: Hind II always cuts DNA molecules at a particular point called recognition sequence and it consists of:
e: Hind II recognizes a specific six base-pair sequence in the DNA and always cuts at the same point within that recognition sequence, so the recognition sequence consists of 6 bp.

q: The "Ti plasmid" of Agrobacterium tumefaciens stands for:
e: The Ti (Tumor inducing) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally causes crown gall disease in plants and has been modified by scientists into a vector for delivering genes of interest into plant cells.

q: Which of the following statements in incorrect.
o: Bio-reactors are used to produce small scale bacterial cultures.
Bio-reactors have an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system and foam control system.
A bio-reactor provides optimal growth conditions for achieving the desired product
Most commonly used bio-reactors are of stirring type.
e: Bio-reactors are actually used to produce large scale (not small scale) cultures of cells/microbes for producing biotechnological products, making this statement incorrect. The other statements correctly describe bioreactor features and function.

q: Main steps in the formation of Recombinant DNA are given below. Arrange these steps in a correct sequence. (A) Insertion of recombinant DNA into the host cell. (B) Cutting of DNA at specific location by restriction enzyme. (C) Isolation of desired DNA fragment. (D) Amplification of gene of interest using PCR. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: The correct sequence is: first cut the DNA at specific locations using restriction enzymes (B), then isolate the desired DNA fragment (C), amplify the gene of interest using PCR (D), and finally insert the recombinant DNA into the host cell (A). So the order is B, C, D, A.

t: Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology - Cloning Vector Features
q:
Match List-I with List-II
List-I: A. Transformation, B. Cloning site, C. Selection, D. Ori
List-II: I. Restriction enzyme, II. Transfer DNA to host bacteria, III. Replication, IV. Antibiotic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
e: Transformation refers to the process of transferring (recombinant) DNA into host bacteria (II). The cloning site is where restriction enzymes cut to insert foreign DNA (I). Selection of transformants is typically done using antibiotic resistance markers (IV). Ori (origin of replication) is responsible for autonomous replication of the vector DNA (III). So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

q: Which of the following is not a component of downstream processing?
e: Expression occurs during the upstream process (gene expression in host), while separation, purification, and preservation are all parts of downstream processing.

q: Which of the following restriction enzymes produces blunt ends?
e: EcoRV is a restriction enzyme that cuts DNA to produce blunt ends, while Hind III, Sal I, and Xho I produce sticky/cohesive ends.

q: DNA strands on a gel stained with ethidium bromide when viewed under UV radiation, appear as:
e: DNA fragments stained with ethidium bromide, when exposed to UV light, fluoresce and appear as bright orange bands on the gel.

q: Which of the following is NOT an application of PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)?
e: PCR amplifies DNA segments and is used for gene mutation detection, molecular diagnosis, and gene amplification — but it does not purify proteins, which is unrelated to its function.

q: Which of the following is a correct sequence of steps in a PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)?
e: PCR steps proceed in the order: Denaturation (separating DNA strands at high temp) → Annealing (primers bind) → Extension (DNA polymerase extends new strand).

q: During the process of gene amplification using PCR, if very high temperature is not maintained in the beginning, then which of the following steps of PCR will be affected first?
e: Denaturation is the first step of PCR, requiring very high temperature (~94-96°C) to separate the double-stranded DNA into single strands. If high temperature isn't maintained initially, denaturation fails first.

q: DNA precipitation of a mixture of biomolecules can be achieved by treatment with
e: DNA is precipitated from a mixture of biomolecules by adding chilled ethanol, which causes the DNA to come out of solution as fine threads.

q: Following statements describe the characteristics of the enzyme, Restriction Endonuclease. Identify the incorrect statement.
o: The enzyme cuts the sugar-phosphate backbone at specific sites on each strand.
The enzyme recognizes a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence in the DNA.
The enzyme cuts DNA molecule at identified position within the DNA.
The enzyme binds DNA at specific sites and cuts only one of the two strands.
e: Restriction endonucleases cut BOTH strands of the DNA at specific sites (not just one strand), making statement 4 incorrect.

q: Which one of the following statement is not true regarding gel electrophoresis technique?
o: The process of extraction of separated DNA strands from gel is called elution.
The separated DNA fragments are stained by using ethidium bromide.
The presence of chromogenic substrate gives blue coloured DNA bands on the gel.
Bright orange coloured bands of DNA can be observed in the gel when exposed to UV light.
e: Chromogenic substrates are used in techniques like blue-white screening for selecting recombinant colonies, not in gel electrophoresis for visualizing DNA bands. DNA bands in gel electrophoresis are visualized using ethidium bromide staining and UV light (giving orange fluorescence), making statement 3 incorrect.

q: Transposons can be used during which one of the following?
e: Transposons (mobile genetic elements) can be used as tools for gene silencing by inserting into genes and disrupting their function, among other molecular biology applications.

q: In the following palindromic base sequences of DNA, which one can be cut easily by particular restriction enzyme? (1) 5'GATACT3'; 3'CTATGA5' (2) 5'GAATTC3'; 3'CTTAAG5' (3) 5'CTCAGT3'; 3'GAGTCA5' (4) 5'GTATTC3'; 3'CATAAG5'
e: A true palindromic sequence reads the same 5' to 3' on both strands. GAATTC/CTTAAG (reading the complementary strand 5' to 3' as GAATTC) is a true palindrome and is the recognition sequence for the restriction enzyme EcoRI, making it easily cut.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Restriction endonucleases recognise specific sequence to cut DNA known as palindromic nucleotide sequence. Statement II: Restriction endonucleases cut the DNA strand a little away from the centre of the palindromic site. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct: restriction endonucleases recognize palindromic sequences, and they typically cut the DNA at specific points slightly away from the exact center of the palindromic recognition site, generating sticky or blunt ends.

q: Which of the following is not a desirable feature of a cloning vector?
o: Presence of single restriction enzyme site
Presence of two or more recognition sites
e: A good cloning vector should have only a single recognition site for a given restriction enzyme; having two or more recognition sites for the same enzyme would fragment the vector upon digestion, which is undesirable.

q: DNA fragments are:
o: Either positively or negatively charged depending on their size
e: DNA fragments carry an overall negative charge due to the phosphate groups in their backbone, which is why they migrate towards the positive electrode (anode) during gel electrophoresis.

q: What is the criterion for DNA fragments movement on agarose gel during gel electrophoresis?
o: The smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves
Positively charged fragments move to farther end
Negatively charged fragments do not move
The larger the fragment size, the farther it moves
e: During gel electrophoresis, smaller DNA fragments move faster and farther through the gel matrix towards the positive electrode than larger fragments, which are retarded more by the gel matrix.

q: A gene whose expression helps to identify transformed cell is known as:
e: A selectable marker gene, when expressed, allows identification and selection of transformed cells (those that have successfully taken up the foreign DNA) from non-transformed ones, often via antibiotic resistance.

t: Sources of pollen preservation and fossilisation
q: Which of the following has proved helpful in preserving pollen as fossils?
e: Sporopollenin, present in the exine (outer wall) of pollen grains, is one of the most resistant organic materials known, allowing pollen grains to be preserved as fossils over long periods.

q: Which of the following is commonly used as a vector for introducing a DNA fragment in human lymphocytes?
e: Retroviral vectors are commonly used for introducing DNA fragments into human lymphocytes and other mammalian cells, as retroviruses can efficiently infect and integrate into the host genome.

t: Visualization of DNA in gel electrophoresis
q: In gel electrophoresis, separated DNA fragments can be visualized with the help of:
e: DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis are stained with ethidium bromide, which intercalates into the DNA and fluoresces under UV radiation, allowing the bands to be visualised.

q: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Restriction Enzymes.
o: Each restriction enzyme functions by inspecting the length of a DNA sequence.
They cut the strand of DNA at palindromic sites.
They are useful in genetic engineering.
Sticky ends can be joined by using DNA ligases.
e: Restriction enzymes function by recognising and binding to specific palindromic nucleotide sequences (not by inspecting length), and cutting the DNA at or near those sites; describing their function as inspecting the length of a DNA sequence is incorrect.

q: Choose the correct pair from the following:
o: Ligases - Join the two DNA molecules
Polymerases - Break the DNA into fragments
Nucleases - Separate the two strands of DNA
Exonucleases - Make cuts at specific positions within DNA
e: DNA ligases catalyse the joining of two DNA fragments/molecules together, correctly matching 'Ligases' with 'Join the two DNA molecules'.

t: Copy number control in vectors (origin of replication)
q: The sequence that controls the copy number of the linked DNA in the vector, is termed:
e: The origin of replication (Ori site) is the sequence responsible for initiating replication and controlling the number of copies of the linked/foreign DNA within the host cell.

q: In Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), the step at approximately 94–98°C is meant to:
o: Allow primers to anneal to template DNA
Denature double-stranded DNA into single strands
e: In PCR, the denaturation step (~94–98°C) breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands of DNA, separating them into single strands. These single strands then serve as templates in subsequent steps.

q: Sticky ends produced by restriction enzymes are useful in biotechnology because they:
o: Prevent degradation of DNA by exonucleases
Facilitate joining of DNA fragments by hydrogen bonding before ligation
Allow DNA polymerase to initiate replication
Enable the vector to enter the host cell more easily
e: Sticky ends are short, single-stranded overhangs left after restriction enzyme cleavage. They are complementary to other sticky ends generated by the same enzyme, allowing two DNA fragments to join via hydrogen bonding. DNA ligase then seals the nicks, forming a stable recombinant molecule.

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate towards the positive electrode (anode) because:
o: DNA is positively charged due to its sugar-phosphate backbone
DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate groups
DNA is neutral but attracted by the electric field
Agarose gel has negative charges that repel DNA towards the anode
e: DNA is a negatively charged molecule due to the phosphate groups in its sugar-phosphate backbone. Under an electric field, negatively charged DNA moves towards the positive electrode (anode). Smaller fragments move faster and travel farther.

q: The most commonly used bioreactor for large-scale production of recombinant proteins is the stirred-tank reactor. The main function of the impeller (stirrer) in this reactor is to:
o: Maintain sterile conditions by creating a pressure gradient
Provide uniform mixing and adequate aeration for growing cells
Separate the product from the culture medium continuously
Control the pH by neutralizing acidic metabolites
e: In a stirred-tank bioreactor, the impeller (stirrer) ensures uniform mixing of nutrients and provides adequate oxygen supply (aeration) to the growing microorganisms or cells, creating optimal conditions for large-scale biosynthesis.

q: A recombinant plasmid is constructed by inserting a foreign gene into the tetracycline resistance gene (tetR) of pBR322, which also carries an ampicillin resistance gene (ampR). Which result correctly identifies transformants carrying the recombinant plasmid?
o: Grows on ampicillin medium and tetracycline medium
Does not grow on ampicillin medium but grows on tetracycline medium
Grows on ampicillin medium but not on tetracycline medium
Does not grow on either ampicillin or tetracycline medium
e: Inserting foreign DNA into the tetR gene disrupts it (insertional inactivation), so the recombinant plasmid loses tetracycline resistance but retains ampicillin resistance. Transformants with recombinant plasmid will grow on ampicillin plates but will NOT grow on tetracycline plates, distinguishing them from non-recombinant transformants.

q: In Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), the step of denaturation is typically carried out at approximately 94–98°C. What is the primary purpose of this step?
o: To allow primers to bind to complementary sequences on the template DNA
To activate Taq polymerase for DNA synthesis
To separate the two strands of double-stranded DNA by breaking hydrogen bonds
To degrade RNA contaminants present in the DNA sample
e: The denaturation step at high temperature (94–98°C) breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two complementary strands of dsDNA, separating them into single strands. These single strands then serve as templates in subsequent steps. Primer annealing occurs at a lower temperature during the annealing step.

q: Stirred tank bioreactors are commonly used in large-scale production of recombinant proteins. Which of the following is the primary function of the stirrer/impeller in such a bioreactor?
o: To sterilize the culture medium by mechanical agitation
To maintain uniform mixing of nutrients and oxygen throughout the culture
To separate the product from the culture broth continuously
To regulate the pH by neutralizing acidic byproducts
e: The stirrer or impeller in a stirred tank bioreactor ensures uniform mixing of nutrients, oxygen (aeration), temperature, and pH throughout the culture medium. This homogeneity is critical for optimal microbial/cell growth and consistent production of the desired recombinant product.

q: The enzyme DNA ligase is essential in recombinant DNA technology. Which of the following best describes its role?
o: It cuts DNA at specific palindromic sequences to generate sticky ends
It synthesizes a complementary DNA strand using RNA as a template
It joins the cut ends of vector and insert DNA by forming phosphodiester bonds
It methylates adenine residues to protect DNA from self-restriction
e: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH end of one DNA fragment and the 5'-phosphate end of another. In recombinant DNA technology, it seals the nicks between the vector and insert DNA after ligation, creating a covalently closed recombinant DNA molecule.

q: Which of the following features is NOT essential for a plasmid to function as a cloning vector?
e: A cloning vector must have: (1) an origin of replication (ori) for autonomous replication, (2) a selectable marker to identify transformed cells, and (3) restriction enzyme recognition sites (cloning sites). A centromere is a structural component of eukaryotic chromosomes needed for segregation during cell division — it is not a requirement for a plasmid vector.

q: When a foreign gene is inserted into the lacZ gene of pUC19 plasmid vector, the transformed bacterial colonies appear white on X-gal plates. This is because:
o: The insertion activates the lacZ gene, producing excess β-galactosidase that converts X-gal to a white compound
The insertion disrupts the lacZ gene, preventing β-galactosidase production, so X-gal remains unhydrolysed and colonies appear white
The foreign gene encodes a white pigment that masks the blue colour
X-gal is not hydrolysed in the presence of an antibiotic resistance gene
e: This is the principle of insertional inactivation used for blue-white selection. When foreign DNA is inserted into the lacZ gene, it disrupts the gene, preventing functional β-galactosidase production. Without β-galactosidase, X-gal (a chromogenic substrate) is not hydrolysed into the blue product (5-bromo-4-chloro-indole), so recombinant colonies appear white. Non-recombinant colonies produce functional β-galactosidase and appear blue.

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis used to separate DNA fragments, which of the following correctly describes the movement of DNA fragments?
o: Larger fragments migrate faster toward the positive electrode because they carry more charge
Smaller fragments migrate faster toward the positive electrode due to less resistance in the gel matrix
All fragments migrate at the same speed since DNA has uniform charge density
Fragments migrate toward the negative electrode as DNA is negatively charged
e: DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate backbone and therefore migrates toward the positive electrode (anode) during electrophoresis. Smaller fragments face less resistance while moving through the pores of the agarose gel matrix and hence migrate faster, covering greater distance. Larger fragments move slower and remain closer to the wells. This allows separation of fragments by size.

q: Which of the following is the PRIMARY advantage of using a stirred-tank bioreactor over a simple fermenter for large-scale biotechnological production?
o: It eliminates the need for a sterile environment
It provides optimum conditions (temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrient supply) with continuous monitoring and control
It allows direct contact of the product with the atmosphere to aid in protein folding
It does not require any downstream processing after fermentation
e: Bioreactors are designed to provide the best possible conditions for achieving a desired product. Stirred-tank bioreactors have a system of impellers for mixing, spargers for oxygen supply, sensors for pH and temperature monitoring, and inlet/outlet ports — all allowing continuous monitoring and maintenance of optimal conditions for large-scale production of recombinant proteins or other biotechnological products.

q: The transfer of genetic material from one bacterium to another through the mediation of a vector like a virus is termed
e: Transduction is the process by which a bacteriophage (virus) acts as a vector, transferring genetic material from one bacterium to another, distinct from conjugation (direct cell-to-cell transfer) or transformation (uptake of free DNA from the environment).

q: 'Restriction' in the term restriction enzyme refers to
o: the cleaving of the phosphodiester bond in DNA by the enzyme.
the cutting of DNA at a specific position only.
the prevention of the multiplication of a bacteriophage within bacteria.
e: Restriction enzymes get their name from their originally discovered role in restricting (limiting) the growth of bacteriophages by cleaving the viral DNA, thereby protecting the bacterial cell.

q: The number of action potentials generated by sino-arterial node (SAN) in a healthy human is ______ per minute.
e: The sino-atrial node (SAN), the natural pacemaker of the heart, generates action potentials at a rate of approximately 70-75 per minute in a healthy resting human, setting the normal resting heart rate.

q: The opening between the right atrium and the right ventricle is guarded by_________
e: The opening between the right atrium and right ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve (three cusps). The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle.

q: Name the blood cells, whose reduction in number can cause clotting disorder, leading to excessive loss of blood from the body.
e: Thrombocytes (platelets) are essential for blood clotting; their reduced number (thrombocytopenia) causes clotting disorders and excessive bleeding.

q: Which enzyme is responsible for the conversion of inactive fibrinogens to fibrins?
e: Thrombin converts inactive fibrinogen into fibrin threads, which form the clot mesh.

q: Which one of the following types of cells lacks a nucleus in humans?
e: Mature human erythrocytes (RBCs) lose their nucleus during development, unlike white blood cells (neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes), which retain their nucleus.

q:
Match List I with List II:
List I: (A) P wave (B) QRS complex (C) T wave (D) T-P gap
List II: (I) Heart muscles are electrically silent. (II) Depolarisation of ventricles. (III) Depolarisation of atria. (IV) Repolarisation of ventricles.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: P wave represents depolarisation of the atria (A-III). QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles (B-II). T wave represents repolarisation of the ventricles (C-IV). T-P gap is when the heart muscles are electrically silent (D-I). So A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I is correct.

q: Which one of the following statements is correct?
o: The atrio-ventricular node (AVN) generates an action potential to stimulate atrial contraction
The tricuspid and the bicuspid valves open due to the pressure exerted by the simultaneous contraction of the atria
Blood moves freely from atrium to the ventricle during joint diastole.
Increased ventricular pressure causes closing of the semilunar valves.
e: During joint diastole, both atria and ventricles are relaxed and the AV valves are open, allowing blood to move freely from the atria into the ventricles, which is the correct statement among the options.

q: Match the following columns and select the correct option: (a) Eosinophils, (b) Basophils, (c) Neutrophils, (d) Lymphocytes with (i) Immune response, (ii) Phagocytosis, (iii) Release histaminase, destructive enzymes, (iv) Release granules containing histamine
e: Eosinophils resist infections and release histaminase/destructive enzymes (iii), Basophils release granules containing histamine (iv), Neutrophils are phagocytic (ii), and Lymphocytes are responsible for the immune response (i). This matches a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.

q: SA node is called pacemaker of the heart because:
o: It generates impulses controlling heart rate
It is located between atria and ventricles
It is present in both chambers
e: SA node (Sinoatrial node) in the right atrium generates electrical impulses at 70-75 beats/min that spread across the heart setting the rhythm. Hence it is the natural pacemaker.

q: What is the name of the blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the heart in a frog?
e: Vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from body parts to the sinus venosus, which then passes this blood into the right atrium of the frog's heart.

q: Cardiac activities of the heart are regulated by : A. Nodal tissue, B. A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata, C. Adrenal medullary hormones, D. Adrenal cortical hormones. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
e: The heart is myogenic, auto-regulated by the nodal tissue (A). A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates cardiac function via the autonomic nervous system (B). Adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline) also increase cardiac output (C). Adrenal cortical hormones are not involved in direct cardiac regulation (D is false). So A, B and C only.

q:
Following are the stages of pathway of conduction of an action potential through the heart:
A. AV bundle B. Purkinje fibres C. AV node D. Bundle Branches E. SA node
Choose the correct sequence of pathway from the options given below:
e: The cardiac action potential pathway is: SA node (E) initiates the impulse → AV node (C) → AV bundle (A) → Bundle Branches (D) → Purkinje fibres (B), which spread the impulse through the ventricles. So the correct sequence is E-C-A-D-B.

q: Which of the following statements are correct? A. Basophils are most abundant cells of the total WBCs. B. Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin. C. Basophils are involved in inflammatory response. D. Basophils have kidney shaped nucleus. E. Basophils are agranulocytes. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Statement B is correct — basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin. Statement C is correct — basophils play a role in the inflammatory response. Statement A is incorrect — neutrophils (not basophils) are the most abundant WBCs. Statement D is incorrect — monocytes (not basophils) have a kidney-shaped nucleus.
