Statement E is incorrect — basophils are granulocytes, not agranulocytes.

q: Under normal physiological conditions in human being every 100ml of oxygenated blood can deliver _____ ml of O₂ to the tissues.
e: Under normal physiological conditions, every 100 ml of oxygenated blood delivers around 5 ml of O₂ to the tissues.

q: Serum differs from blood in:
e: Serum is blood plasma without clotting factors (like fibrinogen), which are consumed during the clotting process. Antibodies, globulins and albumins remain present in serum.

q: What would be the heart rate of a person if the cardiac output is 5 L, blood volume in the ventricles at the end of diastole is 100 mL and at the end of ventricular systole is 50 mL?
e: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV = 100 - 50 = 50 mL = 0.05 L. Cardiac output = Stroke volume x Heart rate. 5 = 0.05 x HR, so HR = 100 beats per minute.

q:
Match the column-I with Column-II:
Column-I: (a) P-wave (b) QRS complex (c) T-wave (d) reduction in the size of T-wave
Column-II: (i) Depolarisation of ventricles (ii) Repolarisation of ventricles (iii) coronary ischemia (iv) Depolarisation of atria (v) Repolarisation of atria
Select the correct options:
e: P-wave represents Depolarisation of atria (iv); QRS complex represents Depolarisation of ventricles (i); T-wave represents Repolarisation of ventricles (ii); reduction in size of T-wave indicates coronary ischemia (iii).

q: Under normal physiological conditions in human being every 100 ml of oxygenated blood can deliver ________ ml of O2 to the tissues.
e: Under normal physiological conditions, 100 ml of oxygenated blood delivers approximately 5 ml of O2 to the tissues.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The coagulum is formed of network of threads called thrombins. Statement II: Spleen is the graveyard of erythrocytes. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: The coagulum (blood clot) is formed of a network of threads called fibrin, not thrombin, making Statement I incorrect. The spleen is indeed called the graveyard of erythrocytes since it destroys old and damaged red blood cells, making Statement II correct.

q: A decrease in blood pressure/volume will not cause the release of:
e: Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) is released in response to increased (not decreased) blood pressure/volume, causing vasodilation to lower blood pressure. A decrease in blood pressure/volume instead triggers the release of renin, aldosterone, and ADH to help restore blood pressure.

q: Adult human RBCs are enucleate. Which of the following statement(s) is/are most appropriate explanation for this feature? (a) They do not need to reproduce (b) They are somatic cells (c) They do not metabolize (d) All their internal space is available for oxygen transport
e: The absence of a nucleus in mature mammalian RBCs frees up additional internal space, which is used to pack more haemoglobin, maximizing the cell's capacity for oxygen transport, making statement (d) the most appropriate explanation.

q: The hepatic portal vein drains blood to liver from:
e: The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from the intestine (and other digestive organs) to the liver for processing before it enters the general circulation.

q: Frog's heart when taken out of the body continues to beat for sometime. Select the best option from the following statements: (a) Frog is a poikilotherm. (b) Frog does not have any coronary circulation. (c) Heart is 'myogenic' in nature. (d) Heart is autoexcitable.
e: The frog's isolated heart continues to beat because cardiac muscle is myogenic in nature (the heartbeat originates within the heart itself via the nodal tissue) and the heart is autoexcitable, able to generate its own rhythmic contractions without external nervous stimulation, matching statements (c) and (d).

q: Which of the following gastric cells indirectly help in erythropoiesis?
e: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the ileum. Vitamin B12 is required for proper erythropoiesis (RBC formation), so parietal cells indirectly assist erythropoiesis.

q: Match the items given in Column I (a. Fibrinogen, b. Globulin, c. Albumin) with those in Column II (i. Osmotic balance, ii. Blood clotting, iii. Defence mechanism) and select the correct option given below.
e: Fibrinogen is involved in blood clotting, globulins provide defence (antibodies), and albumin maintains osmotic balance of blood. This matches a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

q: Match the items given in Column I (a. Tricuspid valve, b. Bicuspid valve, c. Semilunar valve) with those in Column II (i. Between left atrium and left ventricle, ii. Between right ventricle and pulmonary artery, iii. Between right atrium and right ventricle) and select the correct option given below.
e: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle (iii), the bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle (i), and the semilunar valves lie between the ventricles and the pulmonary artery/aorta (ii). This matches a-iii, b-i, c-ii.

q: Which one of these animals is not a homeotherm?
e: Chelone (a turtle) is a reptile, which is poikilothermic (cold-blooded, body temperature varies with environment), unlike Macropus (kangaroo), Psittacula (parrot) and Camelus (camel), which are all mammals/birds and homeothermic (warm-blooded).

q: The QRS complex in a standard ECG represents:
e: The QRS complex in an ECG represents the depolarisation of the ventricles, which triggers ventricular contraction.

q: Match List I with List II: List I — A. Molluscs, B. Reptiles, C. Adult amphibians, D. Amoeba. List II — I. Pulmonary respiration only, II. Branchial respiration, III. Cellular respiration, IV. Pulmonary and Cutaneous respiration.
e: Molluscs respire via gills — branchial respiration (II); reptiles use pulmonary respiration only (I); adult amphibians use pulmonary and cutaneous respiration (IV); Amoeba (unicellular) uses cellular/diffusion respiration (III). A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

q: The WBC count of a person's blood sample is 8000/cu.mm. How many eosinophils and lymphocytes would be in the same blood sample approximately?
e: Eosinophils are ~2-3% of total WBC (≈160-240/cu.mm) and lymphocytes are ~20-25% (≈1600-2000/cu.mm) of 8000/cu.mm.

q: Which of the following cells does not exhibit phagocytotic activity?
e: Basophils release histamine and heparin and are involved in inflammatory/allergic responses, but they do not perform phagocytosis, unlike monocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages.

q: One of the common symptoms observed in people infected with dengue fever is
o: a significant decrease in RBC count.
a significant decrease in WBC count.
a significant decrease in platelet count.
a significant increase in platelet count.
e: Dengue fever characteristically causes a significant drop in platelet count (thrombocytopenia), which can lead to bleeding complications.

q: Which among the following is correct during each cardiac cycle?
o: The volume of blood pumped out by the right and left ventricles is the same.
The volume of blood pumped out by the right and left ventricles is different.
The volume of blood received by each atrium is different.
The volume of blood received by the aorta and pulmonary artery is different.
e: Since the pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series, the right and left ventricles must pump out equal volumes of blood per cardiac cycle to maintain circulatory balance.

q: Cardiac activity could be moderated by the autonomic nervous system. Tick the correct answer.
o: The parasympathetic system stimulates heart rate and stroke volume.
The sympathetic system stimulates heart rate and stroke volume.
The parasympathetic system decreases heart rate but increases stroke volume.
The sympathetic system decreases heart rate but increases stroke volume.
e: The sympathetic nervous system increases both heart rate and stroke volume (as in the fight-or-flight response), while the parasympathetic system (via the vagus nerve) decreases heart rate.

q: Mark the pair of substances among the following which is essential for coagulation of blood.
e: Calcium ions and platelet factors are both essential components of the blood clotting cascade, whereas heparin, oxalates, and citrates are anticoagulants that prevent clotting.

q: Which one of the following blood cells is involved in antibody production?
e: B-lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that produce and secrete antibodies as part of humoral immunity.

q: The cardiac impulse is initiated and conducted further up to the ventricle. The correct sequence of conduction of the impulse is
o: SA Node, AV Node, Purkinje fibre, AV Bundle
SA Node, Purkinje fibre, AV Node, AV Bundle
SA Node, AV Node, AV Bundle, Purkinje fibre
SA Node, Purkinje fibre, AV Bundle, AV Node
e: The cardiac electrical impulse travels in the sequence: SA node (pacemaker) → AV node → AV bundle (Bundle of His) → Purkinje fibres, which spread the impulse throughout the ventricular muscle.

q: What would be the cardiac output of a person having 72 heartbeats per minute and a stroke volume of 50 mL?
e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 72 × 50 = 3600 mL per minute.

q: Partial pressure of O2 in alveoli is approximately:
e: Alveolar pO2 ≈ 104 mmHg; Deoxygenated blood pO2 ≈ 40 mmHg. O2 moves from alveoli to blood down concentration gradient. CO2 moves opposite direction (45→40 mmHg).

q: Which of the following is an occupational respiratory disorder?
e: Silicosis is caused by chronic inhalation of silica dust, typically affecting workers in mining, stone-cutting and related industries, making it a classic occupational respiratory disorder.

q: Which of the following correctly describes the order of air passage during inhalation?
o: Nasal cavity → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli
Nasal cavity → Larynx → Pharynx → Trachea → Bronchioles → Bronchi → Alveoli
Nasal cavity → Trachea → Pharynx → Larynx → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli
Nasal cavity → Pharynx → Trachea → Larynx → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli
e: Air flows in the order: Nasal cavity → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli. The pharynx is a common passage for air and food, followed by the larynx (voice box), and then the trachea, which branches into bronchi and further into bronchioles ending in alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

q: In breathing movements, air volume can be estimated by
e: A spirometer is the instrument used to measure the various lung volumes and capacities involved in breathing.

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Expiratory Capacity (B) Functional residual capacity (C) Vital capacity (D) Inspiratory capacity
List II: (I) Expiratory reserve volume + Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve Volume (II) Tidal volume + Expiratory reserve volume (III) Tidal volume + Inspiratory reserve volume (IV) Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Expiratory capacity = Tidal volume + Expiratory reserve volume (A-II). Functional residual capacity = Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume (B-IV). Vital capacity = Expiratory reserve volume + Tidal volume + Inspiratory reserve volume (C-I). Inspiratory capacity = Tidal volume + Inspiratory reserve volume (D-III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III is correct.

q: Which of the following statements about the respiratory rhythm centre is CORRECT?
o: It is located in the pons region of the brain and directly senses oxygen levels in blood.
It is located in the medulla oblongata and can be activated by the pneumotaxic centre to increase respiratory rate.
It is located in the medulla oblongata, and the pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate its function to reduce the duration of inspiration.
It is located in the cerebellum and responds primarily to changes in blood pH.
e: The respiratory rhythm centre is located in the medulla oblongata and controls the basic rhythm of breathing. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the function of this rhythm centre—it signals to reduce the duration of inspiration, thereby altering respiratory rate and rhythm. The chemosensitive area near the rhythm centre responds to CO₂, H⁺ levels (not O₂ directly) and signals the rhythm centre accordingly.

q: A person suffers a puncture in the chest cavity in an accident, without any direct damage to the lungs. Its effect could be
o: a rapid increase in breathing rate.
e: A puncture in the chest wall destroys the negative intrapleural pressure that keeps the lung inflated, causing the lung to collapse (pneumothorax) and effectively halting normal breathing on the affected side.

q: Mark the incorrect statement in the context of O2 binding to Hb.
e: Lower pH (higher H+ concentration) actually decreases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, favouring O2 release rather than binding (the Bohr effect) — so it does not favour O2 binding, unlike lower temperature, lower pCO2, and higher pO2, all of which do favour binding.

q: The respiratory process is regulated by certain specialised centres in the brain. One of the following centres can reduce the inspiratory duration upon stimulation.
e: The pneumotaxic centre, located in the pons, can moderate the function of the medullary inspiratory centre and reduce the duration of inspiration when stimulated.

q: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve will show a right shift in case of
e: A high pCO2 (as in actively respiring tissues) lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right and promoting O2 release to the tissues.

q: Which of the following factors are favourable for the formation of oxyhaemoglobin in alveoli?
o: Low pCO2 and High H+ concentration
High pO2 and Lesser H+ concentration
e: Oxyhaemoglobin formation is favoured by high pO2, low pCO2, lesser H+ concentration, and lower temperature — conditions present in the alveoli. These factors shift the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to favor oxygen binding.

t: Lung Volumes and Capacities - Vital Capacity
q: Vital capacity of lung is ____________.
e: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a maximal inspiration, and is calculated as IRV (Inspiratory Reserve Volume) + ERV (Expiratory Reserve Volume) + TV (Tidal Volume).

t: Functions of Conducting Part of Respiratory System
q: Which of the following is not the function of conduction part of respiratory system?
o: Temperature of inhaled air is brought to body temperature
Provides surface for diffusion of O₂ and CO₂
It clears inhaled air from foreign particles
e: The conducting part (nose to terminal bronchioles) humidifies, warms, and filters inhaled air, but does not provide surface for gaseous exchange — that is the function of the respiratory/exchange part (alveoli).

q: The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli of the lungs is:
o: Less than that of carbon dioxide
Equal to that in the blood
More than that in the blood
Less than that in the blood
e: The partial pressure of O2 in alveolar air (~104 mm Hg) is higher than in deoxygenated blood (~40 mm Hg) arriving at the lungs, which drives diffusion of oxygen from alveoli into blood.

q: Lungs do not collapse between breaths and some air always remains in the lungs which can never be expelled because:
o: Pressure in the lungs is higher than the atmospheric pressure
There is a negative pressure in the lungs
There is a negative intrapleural pressure pulling at the lung walls
There is a positive intrapleural pressure
e: The negative (sub-atmospheric) intrapleural pressure keeps the lungs pulled against the thoracic wall, preventing total collapse and keeping residual air in the lungs at all times.

q: Select the favourable conditions required for the formation of oxyhaemoglobin at the alveoli.
o: Low pO2, low pCO2, more H+, higher temperature
High pO2, low pCO2, less H+, lower temperature
Low pO2, high pCO2, more H+, higher temperature
High pO2, high pCO2, less H+, higher temperature
e: Oxyhaemoglobin formation at alveoli is favoured by high pO2, low pCO2, less H+ concentration, and lower temperature — opposite conditions favour oxygen release at tissues (Bohr effect).

q: The partial pressures (in mm Hg) of oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) at alveoli (the site of diffusion) are:
e: At the alveoli, the partial pressure of O2 is about 104 mm Hg and partial pressure of CO2 is about 40 mm Hg.

q:
Assertion (A): A person goes to high altitude and experiences 'altitude sickness' with symptoms like breathing difficulty and heart palpitations.
Reason (R): Due to low atmospheric pressure at hight altitude, the body does not get sufficient oxygyen. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
e: Altitude sickness occurs because at high altitude, atmospheric pressure is low, resulting in insufficient oxygen availability to the body, causing breathing difficulty and heart palpitations. Both statements are true and R correctly explains A.

q: Tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume of an athlete is 500 mL and 1000 mL respectively. What will be his expiratory capacity if the residual volume is 1200 mL?
e: Expiratory capacity = Tidal Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume = 500 + 1000 = 1500 mL. Residual volume is not part of expiratory capacity.

q: Which of the following is not the function of conducting part of respiratory system?
o: It clears inhaled air from foreign particles
Temperature of inhaled air is brought to body temperature
Provides surface for diffusion of O2 and CO2
e: The conducting part (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) only transports, cleans, humidifies and warms air. Gas diffusion occurs in the respiratory part (alveoli), not the conducting part.

q: Match List-I with List-II: List-I: (a) Bronchioles (b) Goblet Cell (c) Tendons (d) Adipose Tissue. List-II: (i) Dense Regular Connective Tissue (ii) Loose Connective Tissue (iii) Glandular Tissue (iv) Ciliated Epithelium. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Bronchioles are lined with ciliated epithelium, goblet cells are glandular (secretory) tissue, tendons are made of dense regular connective tissue, and adipose tissue is a type of loose connective tissue, matching (a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).

q: Lungs are made up of air-filled sacs, the alveoli. They do not collapse even after forceful expiration, because of:
e: Residual Volume (RV) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs even after the most forceful expiration, preventing the alveoli from completely collapsing.

q: Which of the following options correctly represents the lung conditions in asthma and emphysema, respectively?
o: Inflammation of bronchioles; Decreased respiratory surface
Decreased respiratory surface; Inflammation of bronchioles
Increased respiratory surface; Inflammation of bronchioles
Increased number of bronchioles; Increased respiratory surface
e: Asthma involves inflammation of the bronchioles causing difficulty in breathing, while emphysema involves damage to the alveolar walls, leading to a decreased respiratory surface area for gas exchange.

q: Match the items given in Column I (a. Tidal volume, b. Inspiratory Reserve volume, c. Expiratory Reserve volume, d. Residual volume) with those in Column II (i. 2500-3000 mL, ii. 1100-1200 mL, iii. 500-550 mL, iv. 1000-1100 mL) and select the correct option given below.
e: Tidal volume is about 500 mL (iii), Inspiratory Reserve Volume is about 2500-3000 mL (i), Expiratory Reserve Volume is about 1000-1100 mL... per the official answer key the correct match is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

q: Stomatal movement is not affected by
e: Stomatal opening and closing is primarily regulated by light, CO2 concentration and temperature, but not significantly by O2 concentration.

q: Select the correct events that occur during inspiration. (a) Contraction of diaphragm. (b) Contraction of external inter-costal muscles. (c) Pulmonary volume decreases. (d) Intra pulmonary pressure increases.
e: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles contract to lift the ribcage, both increasing thoracic volume (not decreasing pulmonary volume) and decreasing (not increasing) intrapulmonary pressure. So (a) and (b) are the correct events.

t: Transport of oxygen and factors affecting it
q: Identify the wrong statement with reference to transport of oxygen.
o: Binding of oxygen with haemoglobin is mainly related to partial pressure of O2.
Partial pressure of CO2 can interfere with O2 binding with haemoglobin.
Higher H+ conc. in alveoli favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin.
Low pCO2 in alveoli favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin.
e: Higher H+ concentration (lower pH) actually decreases the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (Bohr effect), favouring the release (not formation) of oxyhaemoglobin, making this statement incorrect.

t: Correct sequence of steps in human respiration
q: In humans, respiration occurs in the following steps. Arrange these steps in the correct order: A. Diffusion of O2 and CO2 between blood and tissues. B. Diffusion of O2 across alveolar membrane. C. Pulmonary ventilation by which atmospheric air is drawn in and CO2 rich alveolar air is released out. D. Cellular respiration. E. Transport of gases by the blood.
e: Sequence: pulmonary ventilation (C) → diffusion of gases across alveolar membrane (B) → transport of gases by blood (E) → diffusion between blood and tissues (A) → cellular respiration (D): C, B, E, A, D.

q: Match List I with List II: List I (Respiratory Volume) — A. ERV (Expiratory Reserve Volume), B. RV (Residual Volume), C. IRV (Inspiratory Reserve Volume), D. TV (Tidal Volume). List II (Capacity in mL) — I. 2500-3000 mL, II. 500 mL, III. 1000-1100 mL, IV. 1100-1200 mL.
e: ERV is about 1000-1100 mL (III); RV is about 1100-1200 mL (IV); IRV is about 2500-3000 mL (I); TV is about 500 mL (II). A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

q: Following are the statements about prostomium of earthworm. (a) It serves as a covering for mouth. (b) It helps to open cracks in the soil into which it can crawl. (c) It is one of the sensory structures. (d) It is the first body segment. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: The prostomium covers the mouth (a), helps open soil cracks for crawling (b), and acts as a sensory structure (c), but it is a lobe, not a true body segment (d is false). (a), (b) and (c) are correct.

q: Approximately what percentage of CO₂ is transported in blood as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in plasma?
e: About 70–75% of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) dissolved in plasma. This occurs due to the chloride shift: CO₂ enters RBCs, reacts with water (catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ then moves into plasma. About 20–25% is carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and ~7% is dissolved directly in plasma.

q: A healthy adult male has a tidal volume of 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume of 2500 mL, and expiratory reserve volume of 1000 mL. What is his Vital Capacity?
e: Vital Capacity (VC) = Tidal Volume (TV) + Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) + Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV). VC = 500 + 2500 + 1000 = 4000 mL. Vital capacity represents the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation. It does not include the residual volume (~1100–1200 mL), which cannot be expelled even after forceful expiration.

q: Respiration in insects is called direct because
o: the cells exchange O2/CO2 directly with the air in the tracheal tubes.
the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the coelomic fluid.
the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the air outside through the body surface.
tracheal tubes exchange O2/CO2 directly with the haemocoel, which then exchanges with tissues.
e: In insects, the tracheal system delivers air directly to individual cells/tissues through branching tracheal tubes, bypassing the circulatory system entirely — making gas exchange 'direct'.

q: It is known that exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful to animals because
e: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin with a much higher affinity than oxygen, displacing oxygen and drastically reducing the blood's capacity to transport O2.

q: Mark the true statement among the following with reference to normal breathing.
o: Inspiration is a passive process whereas expiration is active.
Inspiration is an active process whereas expiration is passive.
Inspiration and expiration are both active processes.
Inspiration and expiration are both passive processes.
e: During normal quiet breathing, inspiration is an active process requiring contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, while expiration is passive, resulting from relaxation of these muscles and elastic recoil of the lungs.

q: A person breathes in some volume of air by forced inspiration after having a forced expiration. This quantity of air taken in is the
e: The maximum volume of air that can be forcibly inspired after a forced (maximal) expiration represents the vital capacity, which excludes the residual volume remaining in the lungs.

q: CO2 dissociates from carbaminohaemoglobin when
o: pCO2 is high and pO2 is low.
pO2 is high and pCO2 is low.
e: In the alveoli, where pO2 is high and pCO2 is low, CO2 is released (dissociates) from carbaminohaemoglobin and exhaled, opposite to conditions in the tissues where CO2 binds to haemoglobin.

q: Crossing over occurs during which stage of meiosis?
e: Crossing over (exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes) occurs during Pachytene stage of Prophase I of meiosis. This is a key source of genetic variation.

q: What is the main function of the spindle fibers during mitosis?
e: At the onset of anaphase, each chromosome splits and the daughter chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) migrate towards opposite poles with the help of spindle fibers. Class 11th NCERT Page No.123.

q: Spindle fibers attach to kinetochore of chromosomes during:
e: During metaphase, chromosomes align at the equatorial plate and spindle fibers from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of the chromosomes, preparing them for separation in anaphase.

q: Among eukaryotes, replication of DNA takes place in:
e: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase in the eukaryotic cell cycle.

q: The correct sequence of adult cell cycle phases is ________.
e: The cell cycle proceeds in the order: G1 (Gap 1) → S (Synthesis, DNA replication) → G2 (Gap 2) → M (Mitosis).

q: During cell growth, DNA synthesis takes place in:
e: DNA synthesis (replication) occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle.

q: Cells in G0 phase:
e: Cells in G0 phase (quiescent phase) exit the active cell cycle and remain in a metabolically active but non-dividing state.

q: The correct sequence of phases of cell cycle is:
e: The correct sequence of cell cycle phases is G1 (Gap 1) -> S (Synthesis) -> G2 (Gap 2) -> M (Mitosis).

q: The concept of "Omnis cellula-e cellula" regarding cell division was first proposed by:
e: Rudolf Virchow proposed the concept 'Omnis cellula-e cellula' (all cells arise from pre-existing cells), modifying the cell theory.

q: Meiosis occurs in organisms during
e: Meiosis occurs specifically during gametogenesis in sexual reproduction, to produce haploid gametes; vegetative (asexual) reproduction does not involve meiosis.

q: Mitosis is characterised by
e: Mitosis is an equational division in which the daughter cells receive the same chromosome number as the parent cell, unlike meiosis, which is a reduction division.

t: Meiosis - Prophase I Substages and Anaphase
q: Select the correct statements: (A) Tetrad formation is seen during Leptotene. (B) During Anaphase, the centromeres split and chromatids separate. (C) Terminalization takes place during Pachytene. (D) Nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER are reformed during Telophase. (E) Crossing over takes place between sister chromatids of homologous chromosome. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Statement B is correct — during anaphase, centromeres split and sister chromatids separate towards opposite poles. Statement D is correct — the nucleolus, Golgi complex, and ER are reformed during telophase. Statement A is incorrect — tetrad formation occurs during zygotene (pairing of homologous chromosomes), not leptotene. Statement C is incorrect — terminalization occurs during diplotene/diakinesis, not pachytene. Statement E is incorrect — crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids.

q: When cell has stalled DNA replication fork, which checkpoint should be predominantly activated?
e: A stalled DNA replication fork primarily activates the intra-S-phase checkpoint, closely linked with the G1/S checkpoint, which prevents cells with incompletely replicated or damaged DNA from proceeding.

q:
Match the stages of meiosis in Column-I to their characteristic features in Column-II and select the correct option using the codes given below:
Column-I: a. Pachytene, b. Metaphase I, c. Diakinesis, d. Zygotene
Column-II: (i) Pairing of homologous chromosomes, (ii) Terminalization of chiasmata, (iii) Crossing-over takes place, (iv) Chromosomes align at equatorial plate
Codes:
(1) a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i
(2) a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i
(3) a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii
(4) a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i
e: Pachytene = crossing-over takes place; Metaphase I = chromosomes align at equatorial plate; Diakinesis = terminalization of chiasmata; Zygotene = pairing of homologous chromosomes. So a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.

q:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I: (a) S phase, (b) G2 phase, (c) Quiescent stage, (d) G1 phase
List-II: (i) Proteins are synthesized, (ii) Inactive phase, (iii) Interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication, (iv) DNA replication
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
(1) a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i
(2) a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv
(3) a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i
(4) a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii
e: S phase = DNA replication; G2 phase = proteins synthesized (preparation for mitosis); Quiescent stage (G0) = inactive phase; G1 phase = interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication. So a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.

q: Anaphase Promoting Complex (APC) is a protein degradation machinery necessary for proper mitosis of animal cells. If APC is defective in a human cell, which of the following is expected to occur?
o: Recombination of chromosome arms will occur
e: APC is required to degrade securin, which releases separase to cleave cohesin holding sister chromatids together. If APC is defective, sister chromatids cannot separate, so chromosomes will not segregate during anaphase.

q: At which stage of meiosis is the genetic constitution of gametes finally decided?
e: Although crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (anaphase I) shuffle genetic material, the final genetic makeup of each gamete is fixed only at anaphase II, when sister chromatids (which may carry recombined segments) separate.

q: A bivalent of meiosis I consists of
e: A bivalent (tetrad) is formed by pairing of two homologous chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids — giving a total of four chromatids and two centromeres (one per homologous chromosome).

t: Meiotic Prophase I - Leptotene and Diplotene Stages
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Chromosomes become gradually visible under light microscope during leptotene stage.
Statement-II: The beginning of diplotene stage is recognized by dissolution of synaptonemal complex.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are true.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are false.
e: Both statements are correct - during leptotene, chromosomes gradually condense and become visible under a light microscope; the beginning of diplotene is marked by dissolution of the synaptonemal complex and separation of homologous chromosomes except at chiasmata. 11th NCERT Page No. 126.

q:
Following are the stages of cell division:
A. Gap 2 phase B. Cytokinesis C. Synthesis phase D. Karyokinesis E. Gap 1 phase
Choose the correct sequence of stages from the options given below:
e: The cell cycle proceeds as: Gap 1 phase (E) → Synthesis phase (C) → Gap 2 phase (A) → Karyokinesis/Mitosis (D) → Cytokinesis (B). So the correct sequence is E-C-A-D-B.

q: Which of the following stages of meiosis involves division of centromere?
e: In Anaphase II of meiosis, the centromeres split and sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, similar to mitotic anaphase. In meiosis I, centromeres do not divide.

q: The process of appearance of recombination nodules occurs at which sub stage of prophase I in meiosis?
e: Recombination nodules, the sites of crossing over, appear during the pachytene substage of prophase I in meiosis.

q: Match List I with List II: List I: A. M Phase, B. G2 Phase, C. Quiescent stage, D. G1 Phase. List II: I. Proteins are synthesized, II. Inactive phase, III. Interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication, IV. Equational division. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: M Phase involves mitosis, which is an equational division (A-IV). G2 Phase is when proteins are synthesized in preparation for mitosis (B-I). Quiescent stage (G0) is the inactive phase where cells do not divide further (C-II). G1 Phase is the interval between the end of mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication (D-III). So the correct match is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

t: Cell Cycle - G0 Phase and Centrosome Duplication
q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: During G0 phase of cell cycle the cell is metabolically inactive. Statement II: The centrosome undergoes duplication during S phase of interphase. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
e: Statement I is incorrect — during the G0 (quiescent) phase, the cell is metabolically ACTIVE but does not proliferate/divide (it is not metabolically inactive). Statement II is correct — the centrosome duplicates during the S phase of interphase, along with DNA replication.

t: Meiosis I - Prophase I and Comparison with Mitosis
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Chromosomes are fully condensed at the end of prophase I.
Statement II: Meiosis I resembles mitosis.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is false
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
e: By the end of prophase I (diakinesis stage), chromosomes are fully condensed -- Statement I is correct. Meiosis I is a reductional division involving pairing of homologous chromosomes, crossing over, and separation of homologs, which is fundamentally different from mitosis (where sister chromatids separate and chromosome number is maintained) -- so Statement II is false.

q: The fruit fly has 8 chromosomes (2n) in each cell. During interphase of Mitosis if the number of chromosomes at G1 phase is 8, what would be the number of chromosomes after S phase?
e: DNA replication during S phase doubles the DNA content (each chromosome now has two sister chromatids), but the number of CHROMOSOMES remains 8 — it is the DNA content/chromatid number that doubles, not the chromosome count.

q: Which stage of meiotic prophase shows terminalisation of chiasmata as its distinctive feature?
e: Diakinesis is characterized by terminalisation of chiasmata, where chiasmata move towards the ends of the chromosomes before metaphase I.

q: Which one of the following never occurs during mitotic cell division?
o: Spindle fibres attach to kinetochores of chromosomes
Movement of centrioles towards opposite poles
Coiling and condensation of the chromatids
e: Pairing of homologous chromosomes (synapsis) occurs only during meiosis (prophase I), not during mitosis. Spindle fiber attachment, centriole movement, and chromatid condensation all occur during mitosis.

t: Types of Chromosomes Based on Centromere Position
q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Metacentric chromosome (b) Acrocentric chromosome (c) Submetacentric (d) Telocentric chromosome -- List-II: (i) Centromere situated close to the end forming one extremely short and one very long arms (ii) Centromere at the terminal end (iii) Centromere in the middle forming two equal arms of chromosomes (iv) Centromere slightly away from the middle forming one shorter arm and one longer arm. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Metacentric chromosome has centromere in the middle forming equal arms (iii). Acrocentric has centromere close to the end forming one very short and one very long arm (i). Submetacentric has centromere slightly away from the middle, forming one shorter and one longer arm (iv). Telocentric has centromere at the terminal end (ii). So a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.

q: Regarding Meiosis, which of the statements is incorrect?
o: There are two stages in Meiosis, Meiosis-I and II
DNA replication occurs in S phase of Meiosis-II
Pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination occurs in Meiosis-I
Four haploid cells are formed at the end of Meiosis-II
e: DNA replication occurs only once, during the S phase before Meiosis-I begins (interphase I), not during Meiosis-II. Meiosis-II proceeds without further DNA replication, making statement 2 incorrect.

q: Select the incorrect statement with reference to mitosis:
o: All the chromosomes lie at the equator at metaphase
Spindle fibres attach to centromere of chromosomes
Splitting of centromere occurs at anaphase
e: Precisely, spindle fibres attach to the kinetochore located at the centromere region, not directly to the centromere itself, so stating that spindle fibres attach to the 'centromere' is the incorrect statement in the standard NCERT framework.

q: Which of the following options gives the correct sequence of events during mitosis?
o: condensation -> nuclear membrane disassembly -> arrangement at equator -> centromere division -> segregation -> telophase
condensation -> crossing over -> nuclear membrane disassembly -> segregation -> telophase
condensation -> arrangement at equator -> centromere division -> segregation -> telophase
condensation -> nuclear membrane disassembly -> crossing over -> segregation -> telophase
e: The correct sequence of mitotic events is chromosome condensation (prophase), nuclear membrane disassembly (prometaphase), arrangement of chromosomes at the equator (metaphase), centromere division (anaphase onset), chromatid segregation (anaphase), and telophase. Crossing over does not occur in mitosis.

t: Quiescent stage of the cell cycle
q: Some dividing cells exit the cell cycle and enter vegetative inactive stage. This is called quiescent stage (G0). This process occurs at the end of:
e: Cells that exit the cell cycle to enter the quiescent (G0) stage typically do so at the end of the G1 phase, before committing to DNA replication (S phase).

q: Identify the correct statement with regard to the G1 phase (Gap 1) of interphase.
o: DNA synthesis or replication takes place.
Reorganisation of all cell components takes place.
Cell is metabolically active, grows but does not replicate its DNA.
e: During G1 phase, the cell is metabolically highly active and grows in size, synthesising proteins and RNA needed for DNA replication, but DNA replication itself (which occurs in S phase) has not yet begun.

t: Matching cell cycle phase to activity
q: Match List I with List II: List I (Phase of cell cycle) — A. G1 phase, B. S phase, C. G2 phase, D. M phase. List II (Activity) — I. Actual cell division occurs, II. Cell is metabolically active and continuously grows but does not replicate its DNA, III. Synthesis of DNA occurs and the amount of DNA per cell doubles, IV. Proteins are synthesised while cell growth continues.
e: G1: cell grows, metabolically active, no DNA replication (II); S phase: DNA synthesis/doubling (III); G2: protein synthesis continues, cell prepares for division (IV); M phase: actual division (I). A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

t: Characteristic not seen in elongation phase of plant cells
q: Which one of the following is not a characteristic of plant cells in the phase of elongation?
e: In the phase of elongation (not meristematic/division phase), cells enlarge, vacuolate, but do not show large conspicuous nuclei (characteristic of actively dividing meristematic cells, not elongating cells).

q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) S phase, (b) G2 phase, (c) Quiescent stage, (d) G1 phase with (i) Proteins are synthesized, (ii) Inactive phase, (iii) Interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication, (iv) DNA replication.
e: S phase involves DNA replication (iv); G2 phase involves protein synthesis (i); Quiescent stage (G0) is an inactive phase (ii); G1 phase is the interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication (iii). (a)-(iv),(b)-(i),(c)-(ii),(d)-(iii).

q: The centriole undergoes duplication during:
e: Centriole duplication occurs during the S-phase (synthesis phase) of interphase, along with DNA replication.

q: Meiosis in diploid organisms results in
o: reduction in the number of chromosomes.
e: Meiosis produces haploid gametes, halves the chromosome number (diploid to haploid), and introduces genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment — all three occur together.

q: During anaphase I of meiosis
e: In anaphase I, the paired homologous chromosomes of each bivalent separate and move to opposite poles, while sister chromatids remain joined until anaphase II.

q: Cells which are not dividing are likely to be at
e: Cells that exit the active cell cycle and are not dividing enter a quiescent state called the G0 phase.

q: Which of the events listed below is not observed during mitosis?
o: Movement of centrioles to opposite poles
Appearance of chromosomes with two chromatids joined together at the centromere
e: Crossing over (exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes) is a hallmark of meiosis (occurring during prophase I) and is not observed during mitosis.

q: Identify the wrong statement about meiosis.
o: At the end of meiosis, the number of chromosomes is reduced to half.
Two cycles of DNA replication occur.
e: Meiosis involves only a single round of DNA replication, followed by two successive divisions (meiosis I and meiosis II), not two cycles of DNA replication — making this statement wrong.

q: Select the correct statement about the G1 phase.
o: DNA in the cell does not replicate.
It is not a phase of synthesis of macromolecules.
e: G1 (Gap 1) phase is a period of active metabolic activity, cell growth, and macromolecule synthesis in preparation for DNA replication, but the DNA itself does not replicate until the subsequent S phase.

q: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
e: Mitochondria produce ATP via cellular respiration. They have double membranes and their own DNA. Mitchondria are sites of aerobic respiration and produce most of the cell's ATP supply.

q: The protein portion of an enzyme is called:
e: The protein part of an enzyme is called apoenzyme, while the non-protein part is called a cofactor. Class 11th NCERT Page No.118.

q: The cofactor of the enzyme carboxypeptidase is:
e: Zinc is the cofactor (metal ion) required for the activity of the enzyme carboxypeptidase. 11th NCERT Page No. 118.

q: Which of the following functions is carried out by cytoskeleton in a cell?
e: The cytoskeleton, made up of microfilaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, is responsible for mechanical support, motility, and maintenance of cell shape.

q: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum _________
o: is the major site for the synthesis of lipids
is actively involved in protein synthesis
is a site for the synthesis of carbohydrates
has ribosomes attached to its surface
e: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) lacks ribosomes on its surface and is the major site for the synthesis of lipids (including steroid hormones) in the cell. Protein synthesis and ribosome attachment are characteristic of rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER).

q: Cell theory was formulated by _______.
e: The cell theory was formulated by Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann (1838-39), later expanded by Rudolf Virchow who proposed that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

q: Endomembrane system includes ________.
o: endoplasmic reticulum, chloroplast, peroxisomes and vacuole
Golgi complex, chloroplast, peroxisomes and vacuole
endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuole
e: The endomembrane system consists of organelles that function together through direct connection or vesicular transport: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, and vacuoles. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are NOT part of the endomembrane system since they are semi-autonomous, double-membraned organelles with their own genetic material.

q: The plastid that stores xanthophyll is known as _______.
e: Chromoplasts are the plastids that store carotenoid pigments, including xanthophylls (yellow pigments) and carotenes, giving fruits and flowers their yellow, orange, or red colours.

q: Mitochondrial inner membrane encloses __________.
e: The inner mitochondrial membrane encloses the matrix, a semi-fluid substance containing enzymes of the Krebs cycle, mitochondrial DNA, ribosomes, and other components.

q: A cell organelle containing hydrolytic enzymes is:
e: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes used for intracellular digestion.

q: The organelles that are included in the endomembrane system are:
o: Golgi complex, Endoplasmic reticulum, Mitochondria and Lysosomes
Endoplasmic reticulum, Mitochondria, Ribosomes and Lysosomes
Endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, Lysosomes and Vacuoles
Golgi complex, Mitochondria, Ribosomes and Lysosmsomes
e: The endomembrane system includes endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria and ribosomes are not part of the endomembrane system as they function independently.

q: Which of the following cell organelles is responsible for extracting energy from carbohydrates to form ATP?
e: The mitochondrion is the site of cellular respiration, where energy stored in carbohydrates (and other food molecules) is extracted and converted into ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.

t: Non-membrane bound cell organelles in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes
q: Non-membrane bound cell organelles found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells are ___________.
e: Ribosomes are non-membrane bound organelles present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

q: Dobson units are used to measure thickness of:
e: Dobson units measure the thickness (total column) of atmospheric ozone.

q: Which of the following is a feature found in prokaryotic cells but NOT in eukaryotic cells?
e: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their genetic material is present in an undefined region called the nucleoid. Ribosomes, cell membrane, and DNA are present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

q: The primary cell wall of plants is composed mainly of which polysaccharide?
e: The primary cell wall of plant cells is composed mainly of cellulose, a polysaccharide made of glucose units linked by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls; lignin is deposited in the secondary cell wall; glycogen is an animal storage polysaccharide.

q: Select the statement that is not true for ribosomes.
o: Have no role in protein synthesis.
e: Ribosomes are the primary site of protein synthesis in the cell (translating mRNA into polypeptides), so the statement that they have no role in protein synthesis is false.

q: Who proposed the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
e: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane in 1972, describing proteins as a mosaic embedded within a fluid lipid bilayer.

q: Which scientist is credited with coining the term 'cell' after observing cork under a microscope?
e: Robert Hooke in 1665 observed thin slices of cork under a primitive microscope and coined the term 'cell' to describe the small, box-like compartments he saw. Leeuwenhoek observed living microorganisms, Brown discovered the nucleus, and Schleiden proposed the cell theory for plants.

q: Which of the following features is present in prokaryotic cells but absent in eukaryotic cells?
e: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; instead, their genetic material is present in a region called the nucleoid. Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells possess ribosomes, a cell membrane, and DNA — though the ribosome size differs (70S vs 80S).

q: Which of the following organelles is found in plant cells but NOT in typical animal cells?
e: Plastids (including chloroplasts, chromoplasts, and leucoplasts) are organelles found exclusively in plant cells (and some algae). They are absent in animal cells. Mitochondria, ribosomes, and endoplasmic reticulum are present in both plant and animal cells.

q: Which of the following statements correctly describes an addition made to the cell theory by Rudolf Virchow in 1855?
o: All cells have a nucleus that controls cellular activities
New cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula)
Cells are the structural and functional units of all living organisms
All organisms are composed of one or more cells
e: Rudolf Virchow modified and expanded the cell theory by stating 'Omnis cellula-e cellula', meaning new cells arise only from pre-existing cells. The original cell theory was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann; Virchow's contribution completed it by explaining cell origin.

q:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I: (a) Cristae, (b) Thylakoids, (c) Centromere, (d) Cisternae
List-II: (i) Primary constriction in chromosome, (ii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus, (iii) Infoldings in mitochondria, (iv) Flattened membranous sacs in stroma of plastids
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
(1) a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i
(2) a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i
(3) a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii
(4) a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii
e: Cristae = infoldings in mitochondria; Thylakoids = flattened membranous sacs in stroma of plastids; Centromere = primary constriction in chromosome; Cisternae = disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus. So a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

q: Chloroplasts, chromoplasts, and leucoplasts are interconvertible forms of plastids. Which statement best describes chromoplasts?
o: They contain chlorophyll and are involved in photosynthesis
They are colorless and store starch, fats, or proteins
They contain carotenoid pigments and impart color to flowers and fruits
They are found only in the root cells of plants
e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoid pigments (carotenes and xanthophylls) that impart yellow, orange, and red colors to flowers, fruits, and some leaves, aiding in pollination and seed dispersal. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll; leucoplasts are colorless storage plastids.

q: According to the Fluid Mosaic Model proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the cell membrane?
o: Phospholipids form a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing outward
Proteins are embedded in the lipid bilayer and can move laterally
The membrane is a rigid, static structure that maintains a fixed protein arrangement
Cholesterol is intercalated among phospholipids in animal cell membranes
e: The Fluid Mosaic Model describes the membrane as a dynamic, fluid structure where both lipids and proteins can move laterally. The model explicitly rejects the idea of a rigid, static membrane. Options A, B, and D are all correct features of the Fluid Mosaic Model.

q: Ribosomes in prokaryotic cells are 70S, composed of 50S and 30S subunits. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S. However, which eukaryotic organelles contain 70S ribosomes, supporting the endosymbiotic theory?
e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain 70S ribosomes (similar to prokaryotic ribosomes), which is one of the key pieces of evidence for the endosymbiotic theory — suggesting these organelles evolved from ancient prokaryotic ancestors engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells.

q: In a cell, the nuclear pores regulate communication between the nucleus and cytoplasm. Which of the following most accurately describes their function?
o: They passively allow all molecules below 1 Da to enter the nucleus freely
They selectively transport macromolecules such as mRNA out and proteins in, in an energy-dependent manner
They allow free bidirectional flow of all ions and proteins without any selectivity
They exclusively export newly synthesized ribosomes and prevent any import
e: Nuclear pores are large protein complexes that regulate nucleo-cytoplasmic transport. They allow passive diffusion of small molecules but actively and selectively transport large macromolecules. mRNA and ribosomal subunits are exported while transcription factors and other proteins are imported — both processes are often energy-dependent (GTP-driven).

q: According to the Fluid Mosaic Model proposed by Singer and Nicolson, the plasma membrane is described as fluid because:
o: Proteins are embedded in a rigid, static lipid bilayer
Phospholipid molecules can move laterally within the bilayer, giving it flexibility
The membrane dissolves in water as it is composed of hydrophilic molecules
Carbohydrates on the membrane surface allow it to flow around the cell
e: The 'fluid' aspect of the Fluid Mosaic Model refers to the ability of phospholipid molecules to move laterally (and to some extent flip-flop) within the bilayer, giving the membrane its flexible, dynamic nature. The 'mosaic' aspect refers to proteins embedded in or on the bilayer. This was proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972.

q: In a prokaryotic cell, the 70S ribosome dissociates into two subunits. Which combination correctly identifies these subunits and a molecule associated with only the larger subunit?
o: 40S and 60S subunits; 5S rRNA is found only in the 60S subunit
30S and 50S subunits; 23S rRNA is found only in the 50S subunit
30S and 50S subunits; 16S rRNA is found only in the 50S subunit
20S and 60S subunits; 5.8S rRNA is found only in the 60S subunit
e: The prokaryotic 70S ribosome is composed of a 30S (small) and 50S (large) subunit. The 30S subunit contains 16S rRNA and ~21 proteins, while the 50S subunit contains 23S rRNA, 5S rRNA, and ~31 proteins. The 40S+60S combination belongs to eukaryotic ribosomes (80S). Option C is incorrect because 16S rRNA is in the 30S subunit, not 50S.

q: The inner membrane of mitochondria is highly folded into structures called cristae. What is the primary functional significance of these folds?
o: They increase the surface area for the Krebs cycle reactions that occur on the inner membrane
They increase the surface area for the F₀-F₁ ATP synthase complexes involved in oxidative phosphorylation
They provide structural rigidity to the mitochondrial matrix
They house ribosomes responsible for mitochondrial protein synthesis
e: The cristae increase the surface area of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is the site of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase (F₀-F₁ particles). This greatly enhances the capacity for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production. The Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix, not on the inner membrane.

q: During interphase, chromatin exists in two distinct forms. Heterochromatin, as compared to euchromatin, is best characterized by which of the following?
o: It is loosely packed, gene-rich, and transcriptionally active
It is densely packed, stains darkly, and is largely transcriptionally inactive
It is loosely packed, stains lightly, and contains repetitive non-coding sequences only
It is densely packed, stains darkly, and is always found near the center of the nucleus
e: Heterochromatin is the densely packed, darkly staining form of chromatin that is largely transcriptionally inactive. It is typically located near the nuclear envelope. Euchromatin, in contrast, is loosely packed, lightly staining, and transcriptionally active. Both forms can contain coding and non-coding sequences.

q: Fluid mosaic model of cell membrane was proposed by:
e: Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed the fluid mosaic model describing the cell membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded (mosaic pattern). This is the current accepted model.

q: From the statements given below choose the correct option : A. The eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S and prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S. B. Each ribosome has two sub-units. C. The two sub-units of 80S ribosome are 60S and 40S while that of 70S are 50S and 30S. D. The two sub-units of 80S ribosome are 60S and 20S and that of 70S are 50S and 20S. E. The two sub-units of 80S are 60S and 30S and that of 70S are 50S and 30S.
e: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (subunits 60S and 40S), prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (subunits 50S and 30S). Each ribosome has two subunits. So statements A, B, and C are true.

q: Match List - I with List - II. List – I: A. Centromere, B. Cilium, C. Cristae, D. Cell membrane. List – II: I. Mitochondrion, II. Cell division, III. Cell movement, IV. Phospholipid Bilayer. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
e: Centromere is involved in cell division (chromosome segregation) (II). Cilium helps in cell movement (III). Cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane (I). Cell membrane is composed of a phospholipid bilayer and proteins (IV). So A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

q: A specialised membranous structure in a prokaryotic cell which helps in cell wall formation, DNA replication and respiration is :
e: Mesosomes are formed by extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell (vesicles, tubules, lamellae). They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, and also in respiration and secretion processes.

q: Inhibition of Succinic dehydrogenase enzyme by malonate is a classical example of:
e: Malonate closely resembles the substrate succinate in structure and competes with it for the active site of succinic dehydrogenase, making this a classic example of competitive inhibition. 11th NCERT Page No. 117.

t: Cell Organelle Functions (Match List: Nucleolus, Centriole, Leucoplasts, Golgi)
q:
Match List-I with List-II
List-I: (A) Nucleolus (B) Centriole (C) Leucoplasts (D) Golgi apparatus
List-II: (I) Site of formation of glycolipids (II) Organization like the cartwheel (III) Site for active ribosomal RNA synthesis (IV) For storing nutrients
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Nucleolus is the site for active ribosomal RNA synthesis (III). Centriole has an organization like the cartwheel (II). Leucoplasts are used for storing nutrients (IV). Golgi apparatus is the site of formation of glycolipids (I). So A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I. 11th NCERT Page No. 95, 99, 100.

q: The DNA present in chloroplast is:
e: Chloroplasts, like mitochondria, are semi-autonomous organelles that contain their own circular, double-stranded DNA and ribosomes, enabling them to synthesize some of their own proteins.

q:
Match List I with List II:
List I: (A) Axoneme (B) Cartwheel pattern (C) Crista (D) Satellite
List II: (I) Centriole (II) Cilia and flagella (III) Chromosome (IV) Mitochondria
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Axoneme is the core structure of cilia and flagella (A-II). Cartwheel pattern describes the structural arrangement of centrioles (B-I). Crista are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane (C-IV). Satellite refers to a secondary constriction region associated with chromosomes (D-III). So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III is correct.

q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are both double membrane bound organelles.
Statement II: Inner membrane of mitochondria is relatively less permeable, as compared to chloroplast.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
e: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts are indeed double membrane bound organelles (Statement I correct). The inner mitochondrial membrane is relatively impermeable compared to the chloroplast membrane, which has specific proteins allowing selective permeability (Statement II correct).

q: Which of the following are NOT considered as part of endomembrane system? A. Mitochondria, B. Endoplasmic Reticulum, C. Chloroplasts, D. Golgi complex, E. Peroxisomes. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
e: The endomembrane system includes the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, and vacuoles, which are functionally and structurally related. Mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes are NOT part of the endomembrane system because their functions are not coordinated with the rest of the system (they have their own distinct origin and function).

q:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: A. Cristae, B. Cisternae, C. Thylakoids, D. Phospholipid
List-II: I. Flat membrane sacs in stroma of chloroplast, II. Infoldings in mitochondria, III. Cell membrane, IV. Disc shaped sacs in the Golgi apparatus
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane (II). Cisternae are the disc-shaped sacs stacked in the Golgi apparatus (IV). Thylakoids are flat membrane sacs within the stroma of the chloroplast (I). Phospholipids are the major structural component of the cell membrane (III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

q:
Which of the following is an incorrect statement?
(1) Nuclear pores act as passages for proteins and RNA molecules in both directions between nucleus and cytoplasm.
(2) Mature sieve tube elements possess a conspicuous nucleus and usual cytoplasmic organelles.
(3) Microbodies are present both in plant and animal cells.
(4) The perinuclear space forms a barrier between the materials present inside the nucleus and that of the cytoplasm.
e: Mature sieve tube elements LACK a nucleus (they are enucleate) and most cytoplasmic organelles at maturity, making statement 2 incorrect.

q: Identify the types of cell junctions that help to stop the leakage of the substances across a tissue and facilitation of communication with neighbouring cells via rapid transfer of ions molecules.
o: Adhering junctions and Gap junctions, respectively.
Gap junctions and Adhering junctions, respectively.
Tight junctions and Gap junctions, respectively.
Adhering junctions and Tight junctions respectively.
e: Tight junctions prevent leakage of substances across tissues by sealing adjacent cells. Gap junctions facilitate rapid communication between cells via transfer of ions and small molecules.

q: Which of the following pair of organelles does not contain DNA?
e: Lysosomes and vacuoles are membrane-bound organelles that do not contain DNA. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous organelles that DO contain their own DNA.

q: Which of the following statements regarding mitochondria is incorrect?
o: Inner membrane is convoluted with infoldings.
Mitochondrial matrix contains single circular DNA molecule and ribosomes.
Outer membrane is permeable to monomers of carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
Enzymes of electron transport are embedded in outer membrane.
e: Enzymes of the electron transport chain are embedded in the INNER mitochondrial membrane, not the outer membrane. This makes statement 4 incorrect.

q: Which of the following statement is not correct?
o: Lysosomes are formed by the process of packaging in the endoplasmic reticulum
The hydrolytic enzymes of lysosomes are active under acidic pH
e: Lysosomes are formed by the process of packaging in the GOLGI APPARATUS, not the endoplasmic reticulum. This makes statement 2 incorrect.

q: Which of the following statements with respect to Endoplasmic Reticulum is incorrect?
o: RER has ribosomes attached to ER
In prokaryotes only RER are present
SER are the sites for lipid synthesis
e: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound endoplasmic reticulum altogether (neither RER nor SER), so the statement that 'only RER are present in prokaryotes' is incorrect.

q: Which of the following components provides sticky character to the bacterial cell?
e: The glycocalyx, a loose sheath surrounding the bacterial cell wall (which can be a slime layer or capsule), gives the bacterial cell its sticky character, aiding attachment to surfaces.

q: The Golgi complex participates in
e: The Golgi complex is primarily involved in the packaging, modification and sorting of proteins and lipids into secretory vesicles for transport within or out of the cell.

t: Structure and function of the nucleolus
q: Which of the following is true for nucleolus?
o: Larger nucleoli are present in dividing cells.
It is a site for active ribosomal RNA synthesis.
It takes part in spindle formation.
e: The nucleolus is the site of synthesis of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembly of ribosomal subunits; it is a non-membrane-bound structure and is typically larger in metabolically active (non-dividing, protein-synthesizing) cells.

q: Which of the following events does not occur in rough endoplasmic reticulum?
e: Phospholipid synthesis primarily occurs in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER), not the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER), which is mainly involved in protein synthesis, folding, glycosylation and signal peptide cleavage.

q: Which of the following statements about inclusion bodies is incorrect?
o: They are not bound by any membrane.
These are involved in ingestion of food particles.
They lie free in the cytoplasm.
These represent reserve material in cytoplasm.
e: Inclusion bodies are reserve/storage granules (like glycogen, lipid droplets) lying free in the cytoplasm without any surrounding membrane; they are not involved in ingestion of food particles, making this statement incorrect.

t: Site of glycoprotein and glycolipid formation
q: Which is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids in eukaryotic cells?
e: The Golgi apparatus (Golgi bodies) is the primary site for the glycosylation of proteins and lipids, forming glycoproteins and glycolipids, which are then packaged for secretion or transport.

t: Arranging cell layers around female gamete
q: Arrange the following cell layers/structures around the female gamete, from outer to inner side: A. Zona pellucida, B. Perivitelline space, C. Corona radiata, D. Plasma membrane of ovum.
e: From outer to inner: corona radiata (C) → zona pellucida (A) → perivitelline space (B) → plasma membrane of ovum (D): C, A, B, D.

q: Which one of the following is an appropriate example of 'sexual deceit' type statement — select the correct statements regarding cell membrane in eukaryotic cell. A. Membrane of human RBCs has approximately 52% protein. B. Major phospholipids are arranged in a bilayer. C. Extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell form mesosomes. D. Tails towards the inner part of lipids are hydrophobic and thus protected from aqueous medium. E. Glycocalyx is present on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
e: B (bilayer arrangement), D (hydrophobic tails inward), and E (glycocalyx on outer surface) are correct. A is false (mesosomes are a bacterial, not human RBC feature); C is false (mesosomes are prokaryotic plasma membrane extensions, not found in human cells). B, D and E only.

q: Select the correct statements regarding cell membrane in eukaryotic cell. A. Membrane of human RBCs has approximately 52% protein. B. Major phospholipids are arranged in a bilayer. C. Extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell form mesosomes. D. Tails towards the inner part of lipids are hydrophobic and thus protected from aqueous medium. E. Glycocalyx is present on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
o: A, B, D and E only
e: A (human RBC membrane ~52% protein), B (phospholipid bilayer), D (hydrophobic tails inward), E (glycocalyx outer surface) are all correct. C is false (mesosomes are a bacterial feature, not present in human/eukaryotic cells). A, B, D and E only.

t: Correct statements about cell organelles and their inclusions
q: Choose the correct statements regarding cell organelles and their inclusions. A. The endomembrane system includes Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. B. Rough endoplasmic reticulum bears ribosomes on its surface. C. Both mitochondria and plastids have circular DNA. D. A network of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments present in the cytoplasm is called cytoskeleton. E. Mitochondrion is a single membrane-bound structure.
e: B (RER has ribosomes), C (mitochondria/plastids have circular DNA), and D (cytoskeleton description) are correct. A is false (mitochondria are not part of the endomembrane system); E is false (mitochondrion is double membrane-bound, not single). B, C and D only.

q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Cristae, (b) Thylakoids, (c) Centromere, (d) Cisternae with (i) Primary constriction in chromosome, (ii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus, (iii) Infoldings in mitochondria, (iv) Flattened membranous sacs in stroma of plastids.
e: Cristae are infoldings in mitochondria (iii); Thylakoids are membranous sacs in plastid stroma (iv); Centromere is the primary constriction in chromosome (i); Cisternae are disc-shaped sacs in the Golgi apparatus (ii). (a)-(iii),(b)-(iv),(c)-(i),(d)-(ii).

q: The inner membrane of mitochondria is folded into finger-like projections called cristae. What is the primary functional significance of cristae?
o: They increase the volume of the matrix to accommodate more enzymes
They increase the surface area for ATP synthesis
They facilitate entry of pyruvate into the mitochondria
They store calcium ions required for oxidative phosphorylation
e: Cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane that greatly increase the surface area available for the enzymes and proteins involved in the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis (oxidative phosphorylation), making energy production more efficient.

q: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) differs from Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) primarily because RER:
o: Is connected to the Golgi apparatus while SER is not
Has ribosomes attached to its surface
e: RER has ribosomes attached to its cytoplasmic surface, giving it a 'rough' appearance. These ribosomes synthesize proteins destined for secretion or membrane insertion. SER lacks ribosomes and is involved primarily in lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification.

q: Lysosomes are often called 'suicidal bags' of the cell. Which organelle is primarily responsible for packaging the hydrolytic enzymes found in lysosomes?
e: Hydrolytic enzymes of lysosomes are synthesized on the RER and then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where they are packaged into vesicles that bud off to form lysosomes. The Golgi is the key packaging and sorting organelle.

q: The nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope serve which critical function?
o: They allow passive diffusion of all molecules regardless of size
They provide structural rigidity to the nuclear envelope
They facilitate selective transport of macromolecules like mRNA and proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm
They act as sites of DNA replication
e: Nuclear pores are complex proteinaceous channels that regulate the selective bidirectional transport of molecules. mRNA exits the nucleus, and proteins (like transcription factors and histones) enter through these pores, making communication between nucleus and cytoplasm possible.

q: A common characteristic feature of plant sieve tube cells and most mammalian erythrocytes is
e: Mature sieve tube cells lose their nucleus to facilitate conduction of food, and mature mammalian erythrocytes also lose their nucleus to maximise oxygen-carrying space — both lack a nucleus at maturity.

q: Which one of these is not a eukaryote?
e: Anabaena is a cyanobacterium (blue-green alga), a prokaryote lacking a true membrane-bound nucleus, whereas Euglena, Spirogyra, and Agaricus are all eukaryotic organisms.

t: Shared Features of Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
q: Which of the following features is common to prokaryotes and many eukaryotes?
e: A cell wall is present in prokaryotes (bacteria) and also in many (though not all) eukaryotes, such as plants and fungi, unlike a true nuclear membrane or membrane-bound organelles, which are exclusively eukaryotic features.

t: Features Not True of Eukaryotic Cells
q: Which of the following is not true of a eukaryotic cell?
o: Cell wall is made up of peptidoglycans.
80S type of ribosomes are present in the cytoplasm.
e: Peptidoglycan cell walls are a characteristic feature of bacteria (prokaryotes), not eukaryotic cells (which have cellulose in plants or chitin in fungi, and no cell wall in animals), so this statement is not true of eukaryotic cells.

q: Which of the following statements is not true for the plasma membrane?
o: It is present in both plant and animal cells.
Lipid is present as a bilayer in it.
Proteins are present, both integrated and loosely associated.
Carbohydrate is never found in it.
e: Carbohydrates are in fact found in the plasma membrane, typically attached to lipids (glycolipids) or proteins (glycoproteins) on the outer surface, so the statement that carbohydrate is 'never' found in it is false.

q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into structures called cristae. What is the primary functional significance of these folds?
o: They increase the volume of the matrix for DNA storage
They increase the surface area for ATP synthesis
They separate the intermembrane space from the cytoplasm
They facilitate import of cytoplasmic ribosomes into mitochondria
e: The cristae increase the surface area of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which houses the electron transport chain components (including ATP synthase), thereby maximizing ATP production. The matrix is the space enclosed by the inner membrane, not related to DNA storage via cristae.

q: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) differs functionally from Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) primarily because RER:
o: Bears ribosomes and is involved in protein synthesis
Is involved in detoxification of drugs
Stores calcium ions for muscle contraction
e: RER has ribosomes on its surface, making it the site of synthesis of secretory and membrane proteins. SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification of drugs, and calcium storage (especially in muscle cells).

q: The Golgi apparatus is often described as the 'post office' of the cell. Which of the following best describes the cis face of the Golgi apparatus?
o: It is the face that faces toward the plasma membrane and releases secretory vesicles
It is the face that receives vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum
It is the face where final modifications of glycoproteins occur
It is the face where lysosomes bud off
e: The cis face (forming face) of the Golgi apparatus faces the endoplasmic reticulum and receives transport vesicles from the ER. The trans face (maturing face) faces the plasma membrane and releases secretory vesicles, including those forming lysosomes.

q: Lysosomes are sometimes called 'suicidal bags' of the cell. This property is related to their role in:
o: Autolysis — self-digestion of the cell during injury or disease
Synthesis of hydrolytic enzymes in the cytoplasm
Packaging of proteins for secretion outside the cell
Producing reactive oxygen species to destroy pathogens
e: Lysosomes contain powerful hydrolytic enzymes capable of digesting all types of macromolecules. Under certain conditions (injury, stress, or programmed cell death), lysosomal membranes rupture and release enzymes that digest the cell's own components — a process called autolysis, hence the term 'suicidal bags.'

q: In prokaryotic cells, the genetic material is located in a region called the nucleoid. Which of the following statements about prokaryotic genetic material is CORRECT?
o: Prokaryotic DNA is linear and associated with histone proteins
Prokaryotic DNA is circular, naked, and not bound by a membrane
Prokaryotic cells contain membrane-bound chromosomes in the nucleoid
Prokaryotic DNA is linear and located in the cytoplasm without any protein association
e: In prokaryotic cells, the DNA is circular, naked (not associated with histone proteins), and not enclosed within a membrane-bound nucleus. The region where DNA is present is called the nucleoid. Histones are associated with eukaryotic DNA, not prokaryotic DNA.

q: Which of the following organelles is NOT considered a part of the endomembrane system of eukaryotic cells?
e: The endomembrane system includes the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, and vacuoles. Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) are NOT part of the endomembrane system because they have their own genetic material, double membranes, and are believed to have evolved semi-autonomously (endosymbiotic theory).

q: Which of the following is not a steroid hormone?
e: Glucagon is a peptide hormone secreted by pancreatic alpha cells, not a steroid hormone. Progesterone, Cortisol, and Testosterone are all steroid hormones derived from cholesterol.

q: Leydig cells produce a group of hormones called
e: Leydig cells in the testes produce androgens, primarily testosterone, under stimulation by LH.

q: The corpus luteum secretes a hormone called
e: The corpus luteum, formed after ovulation, secretes progesterone, which maintains the uterine lining in preparation for pregnancy.

q: Cortisol is secreted by the
e: Cortisol, a glucocorticoid involved in stress response and metabolism, is secreted by the adrenal cortex.

q: A hormone responsible for the normal sleep-wake cycle is
e: Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland, regulates the body's circadian rhythm, including the sleep-wake cycle.

t: Hormone-Secreting Organs (Match List: Heart, Kidney, GI tract, Adrenal Cortex)
q:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I: (A) Heart (B) Kidney (C) Gastro-intestinal tract (D) Adrenal Cortex
List-II: (I) Erythropoietin (II) Aldosterone (III) Atrial natriuretic factor (IV) Secretin
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Atrial wall of the Heart secretes the peptide hormone Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF), which decreases blood pressure (III). JG cells of the Kidney secrete Erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (I). The Gastro-intestinal tract secretes hormones including Secretin, which acts on the exocrine pancreas (IV). The Adrenal Cortex secretes mineralocorticoids like Aldosterone, which maintains water and electrolyte balance (II). So A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II. 11th NCERT, Page No.- 247, 244.
