Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct: Mendel studied seven contrasting trait pairs in pea plants (seed shape, seed color, flower color, pod shape, pod color, flower position, and stem height) and formulated the Laws of Inheritance based on his findings.

q: Which one from those given below is the period for Mendel's hybridization experiments?
e: Gregor Mendel conducted his hybridization experiments on garden pea plants between 1856 and 1863, publishing his results in 1865.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (a) Metacentric chromosome (b) Acrocentric chromosome (c) Submetacentric (d) Telocentric chromosome
List-II: (i) Centromere situated close to the end forming one extremely short and one very long arms (ii) Centromere at the terminal end (iii) Centromere in the middle forming two equal arms of chromosomes (iv) Centromere slightly away from the middle forming one shorter arm and one longer arm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Metacentric: centromere in middle, equal arms(iii). Acrocentric: centromere near end, one short one long arm(i). Submetacentric: centromere slightly away from middle(iv). Telocentric: centromere at terminal end(ii). So (a)-(iii),(b)-(i),(c)-(iv),(d)-(ii).

q: All genes located on the same chromosome
o: form different groups depending upon their relative distance.
will not form any linkage groups.
form interactive groups that affect the phenotype.
e: All the genes present on a single chromosome tend to be inherited together and constitute one linkage group, since they travel together during gamete formation unless separated by crossing over.

q: Occasionally, a single gene may express more than one effect. This phenomenon is called
e: Pleiotropy is the phenomenon where a single gene influences multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits.

t: Pedigree Analysis - X-linked Recessive Inheritance Probability
q:
With the help of given pedigree, find out the probability for the birth of a child having no disease and being a carrier (has the disease mutation in one allele of the gene) in F3 generation.
[Pedigree: F0 - unaffected male x affected female; F1 - unaffected male x carrier female, carrier female x unaffected male; F2 - carrier female, carrier female, affected male x unaffected female, unaffected female; F3 - four children marked '?' from the carrier female x affected male cross]
e: The pedigree pattern (disease in both sexes, carrier females, skips generations) indicates X-linked recessive inheritance. In F2, a carrier female (XᶜX) is crossed with an affected male (XᶜY). Gametes: Female gives Xᶜ or X; Male gives Xᶜ or Y. Possible F3 offspring: XᶜX (carrier female) = 1/4, XᶜXᶜ (affected female) = 1/4, XY (normal male) = 1/4, XᶜY (affected male) = 1/4. The probability of a child being unaffected AND a carrier (XᶜX) is 1/4. Class 12th NCERT Page No.73.

t: Mendel's Law of Dominance - Explanatory Statements
q:
Which one of the following can be explained on the basis of Mendel's Law of Dominance?
(A) Out of one pair of factors one is dominant and the other is recessive.
(B) Alleles do not show any expression and both the characters appear as such in F2 generation.
(C) Factors occur in pairs in normal diploid plants.
(D) The discrete unit controlling a particular character is called factor.
(E) The expression of only one of the parental characters is found in a monohybrid cross.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: A, B, C, D and E
A, C, D and E only
e: The Law of Dominance explains: one factor of a pair is dominant and other recessive (A); factors occur in pairs (C); the discrete unit controlling a character is called a factor (D); and only one parental character is expressed in a monohybrid cross (E). Statement B is incorrect/not part of this law (alleles don't both appear unexpressed in F2 - it describes something else entirely, like codominance absence). So A, C, D and E only. 12th NCERT Page No. 59.

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I (Sub phases of prophase I): (A) Diakinesis (B) Pachytene (C) Zygotene (D) Leptotene
List II (Specific characters): (I) Synaptonemal complex formation (II) Completion of terminalisation of chiasmata (III) Chromosomes look like thin threads (IV) Appearance of recombination nodules
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Diakinesis involves completion of terminalisation of chiasmata (A-II). Pachytene shows appearance of recombination nodules (B-IV). Zygotene involves synaptonemal complex formation (C-I). Leptotene shows chromosomes looking like thin threads (D-III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III is correct.

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Down's syndrome (B) α-Thalassemia (C) β-Thalassemia (D) Klinefelter's syndrome
List II: (I) 11th chromosome (II) 'X' chromosome (III) 21st chromosome (IV) 16th chromosome
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of the 21st chromosome (A-III). α-Thalassemia is linked to genes on the 16th chromosome (B-IV). β-Thalassemia is linked to a gene on the 11th chromosome (C-I). Klinefelter's syndrome results from an extra X chromosome (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is correct.

q:
As per ABO blood grouping system, the blood group of father is B+, mother is A+ and child is O+. Their respective genotype can be:
A. I^B i / I^A i / ii
B. I^B I^B / I^A I^A / ii
C. I^A I^B / i I^A / I^B i
D. I^A i / I^B i / I^A i
E. i I^B / i I^A / I^A I^B
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
e: For the child to have blood group O (genotype ii), both parents must carry a recessive 'i' allele. The father (B+) must be I^B i and the mother (A+) must be I^A i, giving the child ii genotype. This matches option A only: I^B i / I^A i / ii.

q: The recombination frequency between the genes a & c is 5%, b & c is 15%, b & d is 9%, a & b 20%, c & d is 24% and a & d is 29%. What will be the sequence of these genes on a linear chromosome?
e: Testing order a-c-b-d: ac=5, cb=15 ⟹ ab=5+15=20 ✓ (matches given 20); bd=9 ⟹ cd=15+9=24 ✓ (matches given 24); ad=5+15+9=29 ✓ (matches given 29). All distances are consistent with the order a, c, b, d. (NCERT Class 12, Pg 83-84)

q: If a colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal colour vision, the probability of their son being colour-blind is:
e: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. Father: X(c)Y, Mother: X(C)X(C) (homozygous normal). All sons receive the Y chromosome from the father and X(C) from the mother, so all sons are X(C)Y (normal); probability of a colour-blind son = 0.

q: If a colour blind female marries a man whose mother was also colour blind, what are the chances of her progeny having colour blindness?
e: A colour-blind man's mother being colour blind (XcXc) means the man himself must be XcY (colour blind, since he gets one Xc from his mother). Crossing a colour-blind woman (XcXc) with a colour-blind man (XcY) gives all daughters XcXc (colour blind) and all sons XcY (colour blind), so 100% of the progeny will be colour blind.

q: The recombination frequency between the genes a & c is 5%, b & c is 15%, b & d is 9%, a & b is 20%, c & d is 24% and a & d is 29%. What will be the sequence of these genes on a linear chromosome?
e: Using the recombination frequencies as approximate map distances and arranging genes so that distances between adjacent and non-adjacent genes are consistent (a-c=5, c-b=15, b-d=9, a-b=20, c-d=24, a-d=29), the gene order that fits is a, c, b, d.

q: Thalassemia and sickle cell anemia are caused due to a problem in globin molecule synthesis. Select the correct statement.
o: Both are due to a quantitative defect in globin chain synthesis.
Thalassemia is due to less synthesis of globin molecules.
Sickle cell anemia is due to a quantitative problem of globin molecules.
Both are due to a qualitative defect in globin chain synthesis.
e: Thalassemia is a quantitative disorder caused by reduced synthesis (less production) of normal globin chains (alpha or beta), while sickle cell anemia is a qualitative disorder caused by a mutation producing an abnormal (structurally defective) globin protein, not a quantity problem.

q: The genotypes of a Husband and Wife are IAIB and IAi. Among the blood types of their children, how many different genotypes and phenotypes are possible?
e: Crossing IAIB x IAi gives offspring genotypes IAIA, IAIB, IAi, and IBi (4 genotypes). Phenotypically, IAIA and IAi are both blood group A, IAIB is group AB, and IBi is group B, giving only 3 distinct phenotypes (A, AB, B).

t: Linkage, sex determination and inheritance patterns
q: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Starch synthesis in pea : Multiple alleles
e: Starch synthesis in pea is actually an example of incomplete dominance (not multiple alleles), making this pairing incorrect; the correct associations are T.H. Morgan with linkage, XO type sex determination with grasshoppers, and ABO blood grouping with co-dominance.

q: Select the incorrect match:
e: Polytene chromosomes are characteristically found in the salivary gland cells of dipteran insects (like Drosophila), not in oocytes of amphibians; lampbrush chromosomes are the ones associated with amphibian oocytes (diplotene stage), making this pairing incorrect.

q: If a genetic disease is transferred from a phenotypically normal, carrier female to only some of the male progeny, the disease is
e: A phenotypically normal carrier female transmitting a disease to only some of her sons is the hallmark of X-linked (sex-linked) recessive inheritance: the mother is heterozygous (unaffected carrier), and each son has a 50% chance of inheriting the affected X chromosome and expressing the disease.

t: Codon for Valine in Sickle Cell Anaemia
q: In sickle cell anaemia, glutamic acid is replaced by valine in the beta-globin chain. Which one of the following codon triplets codes for valine?
e: Glutamic acid is coded by GAG (among others), and the classic sickle-cell point mutation changes the middle base A→U, converting GAG to GUG, which codes for valine.

q: Turner's syndrome chromosomal formula is:
e: Turner's syndrome (45,X0) — female with only one X chromosome. Features: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, infertility. Klinefelter's = 47,XXY. Down syndrome = 47+21.

t: Incomplete Dominance - Snapdragon Flower Color Cross
q: A pink flowered Snapdragon plant was crossed with a red flowered Snapdragon plant. What type of phenotype/s is/are expected in the progeny?
o: Red, Pink as well as white flowered plants
Red flowered as well as pink flowered plants
e: In Snapdragon, flower colour shows incomplete dominance where red (RR) and white (rr) produce pink (Rr) in F1. Crossing pink (Rr, heterozygous) with red (RR, homozygous dominant) gives offspring in ratio 1 RR (red) : 1 Rr (pink), so both red and pink flowered plants are expected, no white. 12th NCERT Page No. 60.

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Two or more alternative forms of a gene (B) Cross of F1 progeny with homozygous recessive parent (C) Cross of F1 progeny with any of the parents (D) Number of chromosome sets in plant
List II: (I) Back cross (II) Ploidy (III) Allele (IV) Test cross
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Alleles are alternative forms of a gene (A-III). A cross of F1 with homozygous recessive parent is a test cross (B-IV). A cross of F1 with any parent is a back cross (C-I). The number of chromosome sets is ploidy (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is correct.

q: The phenomenon of pleiotropism refers to:
o: presence of two alleles, each of the two genes controlling a single trait.
a single gene affecting multiple phenotypic expressions.
more than two genes affecting a single character.
presence of several alleles of a single gene controlling a single crossover.
e: Pleiotropy refers to a single gene influencing multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits, as seen classically in the starch synthesis gene in garden pea.

q: Frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes to map their position on the chromosome, was used for the first time by:
e: Alfred Sturtevant was the first to use the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes, to construct the first genetic linkage map.

q: Broad palm with single palm crease is visible in a person suffering from:
e: A broad palm with a single palm crease (simian crease) is a characteristic phenotypic feature of Down's syndrome, caused by trisomy of chromosome 21.

q: Which one of the following symbols represents mating between relatives (consanguineous mating) in human pedigree analysis?
o: A double horizontal line connecting a square and a circle (indicating consanguineous mating)
A square and circle connected with a single line, with a filled square offspring below connected to another couple above
A filled square, filled circle, and filled diamond shown side by side
A square connected to a circle by a single horizontal line (normal mating symbol)
e: In pedigree analysis, a double horizontal line connecting a square (male) and a circle (female) represents consanguineous mating (mating between relatives), as opposed to a single line which represents a normal (non-related) mating.

q: Which one of the following is NOT an advantage of inbreeding?
o: It exposes harmful recessive genes that are eliminated by selection.
Elimination of less desirable genes and accumulation of superior genes takes place due to it.
It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.
e: Decreased productivity of an inbred population after continuous inbreeding (inbreeding depression) is a disadvantage, not an advantage, of inbreeding. The other options describe genuine advantages of inbreeding — exposing and eliminating harmful recessive genes and accumulating superior genes (note: inbreeding actually increases, not decreases, homozygosity, but that aspect is treated as an advantage statement here).

q: For a person with blood group 'O', which of the following is not a possible combination of parents' blood group genotypes?
e: Blood group O requires genotype ii, meaning both parents must be able to contribute an 'i' allele. Father IAIB has only IA and IB alleles to contribute (no 'i' allele), so this parent can never contribute an 'i' allele to produce an ii offspring -- making option (3) impossible. In options (1), (2), and (4), both parents carry an 'i' allele that they can pass on, making an ii (blood group O) offspring possible.

t: Chromosomal Disorders - Down's and Turner's Syndrome
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Down's syndrome is caused by the absence of one of the X-chromosomes.
Statement II: Turner's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional copy of the chromosomes.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
e: Down's syndrome is actually caused by the presence of an extra copy (trisomy) of chromosome 21, not the absence of an X-chromosome -- Statement I is incorrect (this description actually fits Turner's syndrome, which is monosomy of X). Turner's syndrome is actually caused by the ABSENCE of one X-chromosome (45, X0), not the presence of an additional chromosome (which would describe conditions like Klinefelter's or Down's syndrome) -- Statement II is incorrect. Both statements describe the conditions in reverse of reality.

q: The mechanism that causes a gene to move from one linkage group to another is called:
e: Translocation is the chromosomal mutation in which a segment of a chromosome (and its genes) is transferred to a non-homologous chromosome, moving a gene from one linkage group to another.

q: A true breeding plant is:
o: Always homozygous recessive in its genetic constitution
One that is able to breed on its own
Produced due to cross-pollination among unrelated plants
Near homozygous and produces offspring of its own kind
e: A true-breeding plant is (near) homozygous for the traits of interest and, upon self-pollination, consistently produces offspring identical to itself, as used by Mendel in his pea experiments.

q: In a cross between a male and female, both heterozygous for sickle cell anaemia gene, what percentage of the progeny will be diseased?
e: Sickle cell anaemia is autosomal recessive. Cross Aa × Aa gives genotypic ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Only the homozygous recessive (aa) progeny (25%) will be diseased.

q: The shorter and longer arms of a submetacentric chromosome are referred to as:
e: The shorter arm of a chromosome is called the p-arm, and the longer arm is called the q-arm.

q: In Antirrhinum (Snapdragon), a red flower was crossed with a white flower and in F1 generation, pink flowers were obtained. When pink flowers were selfed, the F2 generation showed white, red and pink flowers. Choose the incorrect statement from the following:
o: Law of segregation does not apply in the experiment.
This experiment does not follow the principle of Dominance.
Pink colour in F1 is due to incomplete dominance.
e: The law of segregation DOES apply in this experiment (it's a case of incomplete dominance, where alleles still segregate normally during gamete formation) - only the principle of dominance doesn't apply. So statement 2 (claiming law of segregation doesn't apply) is the incorrect statement.

q: What map unit (centimorgan) is adopted in the construction of genetic maps?
o: A unit of distance between genes on chromosomes, representing 1% cross over.
A unit of distance between genes on chromosomes, representing 50% cross over.
A unit of distance between two expressed genes, representing 10% cross over.
A unit of distance between two expressed genes, representing 100% cross over.
e: A centimorgan (map unit) represents 1% recombination/cross over frequency between genes on a chromosome, used to construct genetic linkage maps.

q: The frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes was explained by:
e: Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes, to construct the first genetic linkage map.

q: The appearance of recombination nodules on homologous chromosomes during meiosis characterizes:
o: Sites at which crossing over occurs
e: Recombination nodules are structures that appear on the synaptonemal complex during pachytene stage of meiosis I, marking the sites at which crossing over occurs between homologous chromosomes.

q: Which of the following occurs due to the presence of autosome linked dominant trait?
e: Myotonic dystrophy is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Sickle cell anaemia and thalassemia are autosomal recessive, while haemophilia is X-linked recessive.

q: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Mendel's law of Independent assortment does not hold good for the genes that are located closely on the same chromosome. Reason (R): Closely located genes assort independently. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
e: Assertion (A) is correct: genes located closely together (linked genes) tend to be inherited together, violating independent assortment. Reason (R) is incorrect: closely located (linked) genes do NOT assort independently - that is precisely why linkage violates Mendel's law.

q: Among the following characters, which one was not considered by Mendel in his experiments on pea?
e: Mendel studied seven contrasting characters in garden pea: seed shape, seed colour, pod shape, pod colour, flower colour, flower/pod position, and stem height. Trichome type (glandular or non-glandular) was not among the characters Mendel studied.

q: A disease caused by an autosomal primary non-disjunction is:
e: Down's Syndrome is caused by non-disjunction of an autosome (chromosome 21), resulting in trisomy 21. Klinefelter's and Turner's syndromes result from non-disjunction of sex chromosomes, while Sickle Cell Anemia is a point mutation disorder, not a non-disjunction disorder.

q: A woman has an X-linked condition on one of her X chromosomes. This chromosome can be inherited by
e: A mother passes one of her two X chromosomes to each child regardless of sex (sons receive their only X from the mother, daughters receive one X from each parent), so the X-linked condition can be inherited by both sons and daughters.

q: Which of the following characteristics represent 'Inheritance of blood groups' in humans? a. Dominance, b. Co-dominance, c. Multiple allele, d. Incomplete dominance, e. Polygenic inheritance
e: The ABO blood group system exhibits multiple allelism (three alleles IA, IB, i), dominance (IA and IB are dominant over i), and co-dominance (IA and IB are co-dominant with each other when both present), matching options a, b and c.

q: The stage during which separation of the paired homologous chromosomes begins is
e: During diplotene, the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the paired homologous chromosomes (bivalents) begin to separate, though they remain connected at chiasmata.

t: Meiotic prophase I: synaptonemal complex breakdown
q: Dissolution of the synaptonemal complex occurs during:
e: The synaptonemal complex, formed during zygotene to hold homologous chromosomes together, begins to dissolve during diplotene, allowing the homologous chromosomes to start separating while remaining connected at chiasmata.

t: Mendel's choice of contrasting pea varieties
q: How many true breeding pea plant varieties did Mendel select as pairs, which were similar except in one character with contrasting traits?
e: Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties (7 pairs, each pair contrasting in one of the seven characters he studied).

t: Multiple alleles: ABO blood group system
q: Identify the wrong statement with reference to the gene 'I' that controls ABO blood groups.
o: A person will have only two of the three alleles.
When IA and IB are present together, they express same type of sugar.
Allele 'i' does not produce any sugar.
e: When IA and IB alleles are present together, they are co-dominant and express both types of sugars (A and B antigens) simultaneously (AB blood group), not the 'same type' of sugar; this statement is incorrect.

q: Match the following with respect to meiosis: (a) Zygotene, (b) Pachytene, (c) Diplotene, (d) Diakinesis with (i) Terminalization, (ii) Chiasmata, (iii) Crossing over, (iv) Synapsis
e: Zygotene is characterised by synapsis (pairing of homologous chromosomes) (iv), Pachytene involves crossing over (iii), Diplotene shows chiasmata (ii), and Diakinesis is marked by terminalization of chiasmata (i). This matches a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.

q: Experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance was done by:
e: Thomas Hunt Morgan provided experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance through his studies on Drosophila, demonstrating gene linkage on chromosomes.

t: Probability of O blood group offspring
q: What is the probability of having children with 'O' blood group, where both mother and father are heterozygous for 'A' and 'B' blood group, respectively?
e: Mother IAi × Father IBi: offspring genotypes IAIB, IAi, IBi, ii in 1:1:1:1 ratio, so 25% chance of 'O' (ii) blood group.

q: Karyotype conditions of 2n ± 1 and 2n ± 2 are called
e: Aneuploidy refers to a gain or loss of one or a few individual chromosomes from the normal diploid (2n) set, such as 2n±1 or 2n±2, as opposed to polyploidy, which involves whole extra sets of chromosomes.

q: The distance between genes on a chromosome and the percentage of recombination between them shows
e: Genes that are farther apart on a chromosome are more likely to have a crossover occur between them, so the percentage of recombination increases directly with the physical distance between the genes (up to a maximum of about 50%).

t: Co-dominance in the ABO Blood Group System
q: A person with genotype IᴬIᴮ shows blood group AB. This is because of
e: Both the Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles are expressed fully and simultaneously on the red blood cell surface without either masking the other, which is the defining feature of co-dominance (not a blended, intermediate phenotype as in incomplete dominance).

q: In a dihybrid cross, obtaining a 9:3:3:1 ratio in the offspring denotes that
o: the alleles of the two genes are interacting with each other.
it is a case of multigenic (polygenic) inheritance.
it is a case of multiple allelism.
the alleles of the two genes are segregating (assorting) independently.
e: The classic 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio arises precisely when the two gene pairs assort independently of each other during gamete formation, as described by Mendel's law of independent assortment, without any gene interaction modifying the expected ratio.

q: Which of the following will NOT result in variation among siblings?
e: Linkage causes genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together as a group, reducing the chance of new allele combinations being passed on, so it does not generate variation among siblings the way independent assortment, crossing over, and mutation do.

t: Scope of the Law of Independent Assortment
q: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds good for genes situated on
e: Independent assortment applies to genes located on different (non-homologous) chromosomes, which separate into gametes independently of one another; genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together (linked) instead.

q: Which one of the following generates new genetic combinations leading to variation?
e: Sexual reproduction involves meiosis and fertilization (fusion of gametes from two parents), generating new genetic combinations through recombination, unlike asexual modes which produce genetically identical clones.

t: Role of Meristematic Nodes in Vegetative Propagation
q: The appearance of vegetative propagules from the nodes of plants such as sugarcane and ginger is mainly because
o: nodes are located near the soil.
e: Nodes contain meristematic tissue capable of active cell division, which allows new shoots and roots to develop from them, enabling vegetative propagation in plants like sugarcane and ginger.

q: Choose the correct statement from amongst the following:
o: Dioecious organisms are seen only in animals.
Dioecious organisms are seen only in plants.
Dioecious organisms are seen in both plants and animals.
Dioecious organisms are seen only in vertebrates.
e: Dioecious organisms (having separate male and female individuals) occur in both the plant kingdom (e.g. papaya, date palm) and the animal kingdom (e.g. most vertebrates and many invertebrates), so they are not restricted to just one group.

t: Factors Determining the Type of Reproduction
q: There are various types of reproduction. The type of reproduction adopted by an organism depends on
o: the habitat and morphology of the organism.
the morphology of the organism alone.
the morphology and physiology of the organism.
the organism's habitat, physiology, and genetic makeup.
e: The type of reproduction an organism undergoes is influenced by a combination of factors — its habitat, physiological state, and genetic constitution — not any single factor alone.

q: Which of the following is a post-fertilisation event in flowering plants?
e: Embryo development occurs only after fertilisation has taken place, making it a post-fertilisation event, unlike pollen formation, flower formation, and pollen transfer, which all occur before fertilisation.

q:
Study the four statements (A-D) given below and select the two correct ones out of them:
A. Definition of biological species was given by Ernst Mayr.
B. Photoperiod does not affect reproduction in plants.
C. Binomial nomenclature system was given by R. H. Whittaker.
D. In unicellular organisms, reproduction is synonymous with growth.
The two correct statements are:
e: Ernst Mayr gave the biological species concept, and in unicellular organisms reproduction (cell division) is synonymous with growth — both are correct (A and D). Photoperiod does affect plant reproduction (flowering), and binomial nomenclature was given by Carolus Linnaeus, not Whittaker.

t: Haplontic Life Cycle of a Filamentous Alga
q: A multicellular, filamentous alga exhibits a type of sexual life cycle in which meiotic division occurs only after the formation of the zygote. The adult filament of this alga has
o: haploid vegetative cells and diploid gametangia.
diploid vegetative cells and diploid gametangia.
diploid vegetative cells and haploid gametangia.
haploid vegetative cells and haploid gametangia.
e: In a haplontic life cycle, the zygote is the only diploid stage, and meiosis occurs immediately after zygote formation. This means the entire adult filament — including both its vegetative cells and its gametangia (reproductive structures) — remains haploid throughout its growth.

t: Evidence That Sexual Reproduction Evolved Later
q: Which combination of statements supports the view that the elaborate sexual reproductive process appeared much later in organic evolution? (i) Lower groups of organisms have simpler body designs. (ii) Asexual reproduction is common in lower groups of organisms. (iii) Asexual reproduction is common in higher groups of organisms. (iv) There is a high incidence of sexual reproduction in angiosperms and vertebrates.
e: If asexual reproduction predominates among simpler, more primitive (lower) groups of organisms, while sexual reproduction predominates among evolutionarily advanced (higher) groups like angiosperms and vertebrates, this pattern supports the idea that elaborate sexual reproduction is an evolutionarily later development — matching statements (ii) and (iv).

t: Chromosome Number in the Microspore Mother Cell
q: The number of chromosomes in the shoot tip cells of a maize plant is 20. The number of chromosomes in the microspore mother cells of the same plant shall be
e: Shoot tip cells are somatic (diploid, 2n = 20) cells of the sporophyte. The microspore mother cell (microsporocyte) is also a diploid sporophytic cell — it has not yet undergone meiosis — so it too has 20 chromosomes; only after meiosis do the resulting microspores become haploid with 10 chromosomes.

q: Offsets are produced by
e: Offsets are a form of vegetative propagation, produced through mitotic (asexual) cell divisions of the parent plant, giving rise to genetically identical offspring.

t: Position of ovule attachment to the funicle
q: The body of the ovule is fused within the funicle at:
e: The body of the ovule is fused with the funicle at the chalaza, the basal region of the ovule opposite the micropyle.

t: Features Common to Asexual and Sexual Reproduction
q: A few statements describing certain features of reproduction are given below: (i) Gametic fusion takes place. (ii) Transfer of genetic material takes place. (iii) Reduction division (meiosis) takes place. (iv) Progeny have some resemblance with the parents. Select the option with statements true for BOTH asexual and sexual reproduction.
e: Gametic fusion and reduction division occur only in sexual reproduction, not asexual reproduction. However, transfer of genetic material from parent to offspring, and resemblance of progeny to parents, occur in both modes of reproduction.

t: Why 'Clone' Doesn't Apply to Sexually Reproduced Offspring
q: The term 'clone' cannot be applied to offspring formed by sexual reproduction because
o: offspring do not possess exact copies of the parental DNA.
the DNA of only one parent is copied and passed on to the offspring.
offspring are formed at different times.
the DNA of the parent and the offspring are completely different.
e: Sexual reproduction involves meiosis and fusion of gametes from two parents, which shuffles genetic material (via recombination and independent assortment), so offspring are not exact genetic copies of either parent — hence they cannot be called clones.

q: Asexual reproduction by binary fission is common among: A. Some eukaryotes, B. All eukaryotes, C. Some prokaryotes, D. All prokaryotes. Choose the correct combination.
e: Binary fission occurs in some eukaryotes (e.g. Amoeba) and in prokaryotes, but it is safer to say 'some' rather than claim it applies universally to every single eukaryote or prokaryote, so the correct combination is 'some eukaryotes and some prokaryotes' (A and C).

q: A few statements regarding sexual reproduction are given below: (i) Sexual reproduction does not always require two individuals. (ii) Sexual reproduction generally involves gametic fusion. (iii) Meiosis never occurs during sexual reproduction. (iv) External fertilisation is a rule during sexual reproduction. Choose the correct statements.
e: Sexual reproduction can occur even without two individuals, as in self-fertilising hermaphrodites, and it generally involves gametic fusion — both (i) and (ii) are true. Meiosis does occur (during gamete formation), and external fertilisation is not a universal rule, so (iii) and (iv) are false.

t: Chromosome Numbers Across Generations in Rice
q: The male gametes of a rice plant have 12 chromosomes in their nucleus. The chromosome numbers in the female gamete, the zygote, and the cells of the seedling will be, respectively,
e: Since the male gamete is haploid with n = 12, the female gamete of the same species is also haploid with 12 chromosomes. Fusion of the two gametes gives a diploid zygote with 24 chromosomes, and the seedling's somatic cells (derived from the zygote by mitosis) also retain 24 chromosomes.

q: Given below are statements related to external fertilisation: (i) The male and female gametes are formed and released simultaneously. (ii) Only a few gametes are released into the medium. (iii) Water is the medium in a majority of organisms exhibiting external fertilisation. (iv) Offspring formed as a result of external fertilisation have a better chance of survival than those formed inside an organism. Choose the correct statements.
e: External fertilisation requires synchronized release of male and female gametes, usually into water, which is true for (i) and (iii). In reality, a very large (not few) number of gametes are released to compensate for losses in the open medium, and offspring formed this way generally have a lower, not better, chance of survival due to predation and lack of protection — so (ii) and (iv) are false.

t: Source of Variation in Sexually Reproduced Offspring
q: Offspring formed by sexual reproduction exhibit more variation than those formed by asexual reproduction because
o: sexual reproduction is a lengthy process.
the gametes of the parents have qualitatively different genetic composition.
genetic material comes from parents of two different species.
a greater amount of DNA is involved in sexual reproduction.
e: During gamete formation, meiotic events like crossing over and independent assortment generate gametes with qualitatively different combinations of genes, and the fusion of genetically distinct gametes from two parents results in offspring showing greater variation than asexually produced, genetically identical offspring.

t: Why Single-Celled Organisms Show No Natural Death
q: There is no natural death in single-celled organisms like Amoeba and bacteria because
o: the parental body is distributed among the offspring.
e: In binary fission, the entire parental cell body divides to form the two daughter cells, so there is no separate 'parent' left behind to die — the parent's substance is wholly distributed among the offspring, meaning there is no natural death as conventionally understood.

q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The presence or absence of hymen is not a reliable indicator of virginity.
Statement II: The hymen is torn during the first coitus only.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from options given below:
o: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
e: The presence or absence of the hymen is not a reliable indicator of virginity since it can be torn due to reasons other than coitus, such as physical exercise. So Statement I is true. Statement II is false because the hymen can be torn due to various non-sexual reasons, not only the first coitus.

q: Which of the following is not a natural/traditional contraceptive method?
e: Vaults (like cervical caps) are barrier contraceptive devices, not natural/traditional methods. Lactational amenorrhea, coitus interruptus, and periodic abstinence are all natural/traditional contraceptive methods that don't involve any device or medication.

q: The method of directly injecting a sperm into ovum in assisted reproductive technology is called:
e: Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI) is the assisted reproductive technique where a sperm is directly injected into the cytoplasm of an ovum (egg) to facilitate fertilization, typically used in cases of male infertility.

q: Which one of the following is an example of Hormone releasing IUD?
e: LNG-20 (Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD) is a hormone-releasing IUD; the others (Multiload 375, CuT, Cu7) are copper-releasing IUDs.

q: Natality refers to
o: Number of individuals entering a habitat
Number of individuals leaving the habitat
e: Natality is the birth rate within a population, representing the number of new individuals added through reproduction.

q: The method of directly injecting a sperm into an ovum, used in assisted reproductive technology, is called
e: ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection) involves directly injecting a single sperm into the cytoplasm of an ovum to achieve fertilisation in vitro.

q: Emergency contraceptives are effective if used within
e: Emergency contraceptive pills work by preventing or delaying ovulation and/or fertilisation, and are effective only when taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse (coitus).

q: In case of a couple where the male is having a very low sperm count, which technique will be suitable for fertilisation?
e: As per the official NTA answer key, Artificial Insemination (AI), in which semen collected from the husband or a donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or uterus, is the indicated technique for this scenario.

q: Which of the following statements about STIs is INCORRECT?
o: Hepatitis-B is caused by a virus and can be transmitted sexually
Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium and is curable with antibiotics
Genital herpes is caused by a virus and once acquired, remains permanently curable with antiviral drugs
Syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum
e: The incorrect statement is option C. Genital herpes, caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), is NOT permanently curable. The virus remains latent in nerve ganglia and can reactivate, causing recurrent episodes. Antiviral drugs only suppress symptoms but do not eliminate the virus. Hepatitis-B (viral, sexually transmitted), Gonorrhoea (bacterial, curable), and Syphilis (caused by Treponema pallidum) are all correctly described.

q: What are the potential drawbacks in adoption of the IVF method? A. High fatality risk to mother. B. Expensive instruments and reagents. C. Husband/wife necessary for being donors. D. Less adoption of orphans. E. Not available in India. F. Possibility that the early embryo does not survive. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
e: Drawbacks of IVF include: B (expensive instruments/reagents), D (less adoption of orphans, since couples prefer biological children via IVF), and F (early embryo may not survive). A, C, and E are not accurate drawbacks of IVF as described in NCERT (Class 12, Pg 48).

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Non-Medicated IUD (B) Copper releasing IUD (C) Hormone releasing IUD (D) Implants
List II: (I) Multiload 375 (II) Progestogens (III) Lippes loop (IV) LNG-20
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Non-medicated IUDs include the Lippes loop (A-III). Copper releasing IUDs include Multiload 375 (B-I). Hormone releasing IUDs include LNG-20 (C-IV). Implants deliver progestogens (D-II). So A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II is correct.

t: Drugs and Alcohol Abuse - Source Plants
q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Cocaine (B) Heroin (C) Morphine (D) Marijuana
List II: (I) Effective sedative in surgery (II) Cannabis sativa (III) Erythroxylum (IV) Papaver somniferum
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Cocaine is obtained from Erythroxylum coca plant (A-III). Heroin is derived from morphine, sourced from Papaver somniferum (B-IV). Morphine is an effective sedative used in surgery (C-I). Marijuana is obtained from Cannabis sativa (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is correct.

q: Given below are two statements: Assertion A: Amniocentesis for sex determination is one of the strategies of Reproductive and Child Health Care Programme. Reason R: Ban on amniocentesis checks increasing menace of female foeticide. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
e: Assertion A is false — amniocentesis for sex determination is NOT a strategy of the Reproductive and Child Health Care Programme; rather, sex determination using amniocentesis is legally banned in India. Reason R is true — the ban on amniocentesis for sex determination helps check the increasing menace of female foeticide.

q: Match List I with List II: A. Vasectomy, B. Coitus interruptus, C. Cervical caps, D. Saheli. List II: I. Oral method, II. Barrier method, III. Surgical method, IV. Natural method. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Vasectomy is a surgical method of contraception (A-III). Coitus interruptus is a natural method (B-IV). Cervical caps are a barrier method (C-II). Saheli is an oral contraceptive pill (D-I). So the correct match is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

q: Which of the following is a hormone-releasing IUD?
e: LNG-20 (Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, e.g. Mirena) is a hormone-releasing IUD. Cu7, Multiload 375 are copper-releasing IUDs, and Lippes loop is a non-medicated IUD.

q: Which of the following is incorrect regarding vasectomy?
o: No sperm occurs in seminal fluid
Vasa deferentia is cut and tied
e: Vasectomy involves cutting and tying the vas deferens, so sperm still forms in testes and reaches the epididymis (storage site), just cannot pass beyond the vas deferens. It is reversible in many cases too, so 'irreversible sterility' is also debatable, but the clearly incorrect statement is that no sperm occurs in epididymis.

q: Embryo with more than 16 blastomeres formed due to in vitro fertilization is transferred into:
e: In IVF (test-tube baby program), embryos with more than 8 blastomeres (typically beyond 16-cell stage) are transferred into the uterus to assist pregnancy (ZIFT uses fallopian tube for embryos up to 8 cells).

q:
Match List - I with List - II.
List I: (a) Vaults (b) IUDs (c) Vasectomy (d) Tubectomy
List-II: (i) Entry of sperm through Cervix is blocked (ii) Removal of Vas deferens (iii) Phagocytosis of sperms within the Uterus (iv) Removal of fallopian tube
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Vaults cause phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus; IUDs block entry of sperm through the cervix; Vasectomy removes the vas deferens; Tubectomy removes/blocks the fallopian tube.

q: Which of the following contraceptive methods do involve a role of hormone?
e: Lactational amenorrhea, Pills, and Emergency contraceptives all involve hormonal mechanisms - lactational amenorrhea relies on prolactin-induced suppression of ovulation, while pills and emergency contraceptives directly use hormones.

q: Select the hormone-releasing intra-uterine devices.
e: Progestasert and LNG-20 are hormone-releasing IUDs. Lippes Loop and Multiload 375 are non-hormonal copper-releasing or inert IUDs.

q: Lippe's loop is a type of contraceptive used as:
e: Lippes loop is a non-medicated (inert) intrauterine device (IUD), made of plastic, unlike medicated IUDs like Copper-T which release copper ions.

q: The function of copper ions in copper releasing IUD's is:
o: They make uterus unsuitable for implantation.
They suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity of sperms.
e: Copper ions released by copper-releasing IUDs (like CuT) increase phagocytosis of sperm and suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity, acting as a spermicidal agent within the uterus.

q: The contraceptive 'SAHELI' is
o: a drug that blocks estrogen receptors in the uterus, preventing eggs from getting implanted.
a drug that increases the concentration of estrogen and prevents ovulation in females.
e: SAHELI is a non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill containing centchroman, which acts by blocking the action of estrogen in the uterus, preventing implantation of the fertilised egg.

q: In which of the following techniques, the embryos are transferred to assist those females who cannot conceive?
e: ZIFT (Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer) involves transferring the zygote/early embryo into the fallopian tube, and IUT (Intra Uterine Transfer) involves transferring the embryo into the uterus; both are embryo-transfer assisted reproductive techniques.

t: Example of sexual deceit in pollination/mating
q: Which one of the following is an appropriate example of 'sexual deceit'?
e: Ophrys orchid mimics the female bumblebee to attract male bumblebees for pollination — this is an example of 'sexual deceit'.

t: Correct statement about GIFT to overcome infertility
q: Choose the correct statement regarding GIFT (Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer) to overcome infertility.
o: Ova collected from a female donor are transferred to the uterus of an infertile female
Early embryos with up to 8 blastomeres are transferred into the fallopian tube of an infertile female
Early embryos with up to 8 blastomeres are transferred to the uterus of an infertile female
It is the transfer of an ovum collected from a donor female who cannot produce ovum but can provide suitable environment for fertilization and development
e: GIFT involves transferring early embryos (up to 8 blastomeres) into the fallopian tube of an infertile female.

q: Match List-I with List-II: (a) Vaults, (b) IUDs, (c) Vasectomy, (d) Tubectomy with (i) Entry of sperm through cervix is blocked, (ii) Removal of Vas deferens, (iii) Phagocytosis of sperms within the Uterus, (iv) Removal of fallopian tube.
e: Vaults (barrier method) block sperm entry through cervix (i); IUDs cause phagocytosis of sperm within uterus (iii); Vasectomy is removal/cutting of vas deferens (ii); Tubectomy is removal/blocking of fallopian tubes (iv). (a)-(i),(b)-(iii),(c)-(ii),(d)-(iv).

q: Which of the following contraceptive methods works primarily by preventing implantation of the fertilized egg rather than preventing fertilization?
e: Copper-T (Intrauterine Device) works primarily by creating a hostile uterine environment that prevents implantation of the fertilized ovum. It also affects sperm motility and viability. Condoms and diaphragms act as physical barriers preventing fertilization, while vasectomy prevents sperm release by cutting/tying the vas deferens.

q: Intensely lactating mothers do not generally conceive due to the
e: High prolactin levels during intense lactation suppress the secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) from the pituitary, which in turn suppresses ovulation, making conception unlikely during this period — a phenomenon known as lactational amenorrhea.

t: History of India's Reproductive Health Programme
q: A national-level approach to building up a reproductively healthy society was taken up in our country in the
e: India launched its Family Planning Programme at a national level in 1951, making the 1950s the decade when a nationwide approach toward reproductive health was first undertaken; this was later renamed and expanded as the Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programme.

q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are produced at the end of glycolysis from 206 molecules of glucose?
e: In glycolysis, each molecule of glucose (6 carbon) is broken down into 2 molecules of pyruvic acid (3 carbon each). So 206 molecules of glucose yield 206 × 2 = 412 molecules of pyruvic acid.

q: The ultimate electron acceptor of respiration in an aerobic organism is
e: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons at the end of the electron transport chain, being reduced to water.

t: Mitochondria as the Powerhouse of the Cell
q: Mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell. Which of the following observations best supports this statement?
o: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle are found in mitochondria.
Mitochondria are found in almost all plant and animal cells.
e: Mitochondria are called the cell's powerhouse specifically because they synthesise ATP (the cell's main energy currency) through oxidative phosphorylation.

q: Which statement is wrong for Krebs' cycle?
o: There is one point in the cycle where FAD+ is reduced to FADH2
During conversion of succinyl CoA to succinic acid, a molecule of GTP is synthesised
The cycle starts with condensation of acetyl group (acetyl CoA) with pyruvic acid to yield citric acid
There are three points in the cycle where NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+
e: The Krebs cycle actually starts with the condensation of the acetyl group (acetyl CoA) with oxaloacetic acid (OAA), not pyruvic acid, to yield citric acid, making statement (3) the wrong one.

q: A plant tissue is found to have a respiratory quotient (RQ) of 0.7. Which of the following substrates is most likely being respired, and what does this RQ value indicate?
o: Carbohydrates; complete oxidation with CO₂ released equal to O₂ consumed
Fats; CO₂ released is less than O₂ consumed because fats are more reduced than carbohydrates
Organic acids; CO₂ released is more than O₂ consumed due to the pre-existing oxygen in the substrate
Proteins; CO₂ released is slightly less than O₂ consumed due to nitrogen excretion
e: Respiratory Quotient (RQ) = Volume of CO₂ released / Volume of O₂ consumed. For carbohydrates, RQ = 1. For fats (lipids), RQ is approximately 0.7 because fats are more reduced (hydrogen-rich) compounds compared to carbohydrates. They require proportionally more oxygen for complete oxidation and release less CO₂ relative to O₂ consumed. For example, tripalmitin oxidation gives an RQ of about 0.7. Organic acids have RQ > 1 because they already contain oxygen. Proteins have RQ close to 0.9. Thus, an RQ of 0.7 strongly indicates fat as the respiratory substrate.

q: The complex II of mitochondrial electron transport chain is also known as
e: Complex I is NADH dehydrogenase, Complex II is Succinate dehydrogenase (oxidizes succinate to fumarate, passing electrons via FAD), Complex III is Cytochrome bc1, Complex IV is Cytochrome c oxidase.

q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: (A) Citric acid cycle (B) Glycolysis (C) Electron transport system (D) Proton gradient
List II: (I) Cytoplasm (II) Mitochondrial matrix (III) Intermembrane space of mitochondria (IV) Inner mitochondrial membrane
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: The citric acid cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (A-II). Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm (B-I). The electron transport system is on the inner mitochondrial membrane (C-IV). The proton gradient builds up in the intermembrane space (D-III). So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III is correct.

q: Identify the step in tricarboxylic acid cycle, which does not involve oxidation of substrate.
e: The conversion of Succinyl-CoA to Succinic acid is a substrate-level phosphorylation step that generates GTP/ATP but does not involve oxidation of the substrate, unlike the other listed steps which are oxidation reactions coupled to NAD+/FAD reduction.

q: Given below are two statements: Assertion A: ATP is used at two steps in glycolysis. Reason R: First ATP is used in converting glucose into glucose-6-phosphate and second ATP is used in conversion of fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-disphosphate. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
o: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
e: Assertion A is true — ATP is utilized at two steps in glycolysis. Reason R correctly explains this — the first ATP phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, and the second ATP phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

q: Melonate inhibits the growth of pathogenic bacteria by inhibiting the activity of:
e: Malonate is a classic competitive inhibitor of succinic dehydrogenase (succinate dehydrogenase), an enzyme of the Krebs cycle, and this inhibition can restrict growth of pathogenic bacteria dependent on this respiratory enzyme.

t: Enzymes of Glycolysis, Krebs Cycle and ETS
q: Match List I with List II: A. Oxidative decarboxylation, B. Glycolysis, C. Oxidative phosphorylation, D. Tricarboxylic acid cycle. List II: I. Citrate synthase, II. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, III. Electron transport system, IV. EMP pathway. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate is catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase (A-II). Glycolysis is also known as the EMP (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas) pathway (B-IV). Oxidative phosphorylation occurs via the electron transport system (C-III). The tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle begins with the enzyme citrate synthase (D-I). So the correct match is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

q: Which of the following biomolecules is common to respiration-mediated breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins?
e: Acetyl CoA is the common intermediate formed from breakdown of fats (via beta-oxidation), carbohydrates (via glycolysis+pyruvate oxidation), and proteins (via amino acid catabolism), entering the Krebs cycle.

q: Which of the following is a common intermediate for aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
e: Pyruvic acid (pyruvate), formed at the end of glycolysis, is the common intermediate for both aerobic respiration (enters Krebs cycle via Acetyl CoA) and anaerobic respiration/fermentation (converted to ethanol or lactic acid).

q: Oxidative phosphorylation is:
o: Formation of ATP by energy released from electrons removed during substrate oxidation
Formation of ATP by transfer of phosphate group from a substrate to ADP
Oxidation of phosphate group in ATP
Addition of phosphate group to ATP
e: Oxidative phosphorylation is the process of ATP formation using energy released from the transfer of electrons (removed during substrate oxidation) through the electron transport chain to oxygen.

q: Respiratory quotient (RQ) value of tripalmitin is:
e: Tripalmitin is a fat, and the RQ for fats is less than 1, typically around 0.7, since fats require more oxygen for complete oxidation relative to the CO2 produced.

q: Conversion of glucose-6-phosphate, the first irreversible reaction of glycolysis, is catalyzed by:
e: Hexokinase catalyzes the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which is the first irreversible reaction in glycolysis.

q: What is the net gain of ATP when each molecule of glucose is converted to two molecules of pyruvic acid?
e: In glycolysis, glucose to pyruvate conversion: 4 ATP are produced (gross) but 2 ATP are consumed in the initial steps, giving a net gain of 2 ATP molecules.

q: What amount of energy is released from glucose during lactic acid fermentation?
e: Lactic acid fermentation is an inefficient anaerobic process, releasing less than 7% of the energy content of glucose (compared to about 686 kcal/mol total available via complete aerobic oxidation).

t: Role of NAD+ in cellular respiration
q: What is the role of NAD+ in cellular respiration?
o: It is the final electron acceptor for anaerobic respiration.
It is a nucleotide source for ATP synthesis.
It functions as an electron carrier.
e: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) acts as an electron carrier in cellular respiration, accepting electrons and hydrogen (becoming NADH) during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, and later donating them in the electron transport chain.

q: Which of these statements is incorrect?
o: Enzymes of TCA cycle are present in mitochondrial matrix.
Oxidative phosphorylation takes place in outer mitochondrial membrane.
Glycolysis operates as long as it is supplied with NAD that can pick up hydrogen atoms.
e: Oxidative phosphorylation actually takes place in the inner mitochondrial membrane (where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located), not the outer mitochondrial membrane, making this statement incorrect.

t: Substrate level phosphorylation in Krebs cycle
q: The number of substrate level phosphorylations in one turn of citric acid cycle is:
e: In one turn of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, substrate level phosphorylation occurs once, at the step where succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate, generating one GTP (equivalent to ATP).

q: 2(C51H98O6)+145O2 → 102CO2+98H2O+energy. The Respiratory Quotient (RQ) of a biomolecule used for respiration, as per the above equation, would be:
e: RQ=CO2 evolved/O2 consumed=102/145≈0.70, which is between 0.5 and 0.95 (this is a fat, giving RQ<1).

q: Match List I with List II: List I (Process) — A. Glycolysis, B. ETS, C. Accumulation of protons, D. Krebs' cycle. List II (Location) — I. Inner mitochondrial membrane, II. Mitochondrial matrix, III. Cytoplasm, IV. Intermembrane space.
e: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm (III); ETS occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane (I); protons accumulate in the intermembrane space (IV); Krebs' cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (II). A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

q: During glycolysis, which of the following steps results in the net gain of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation?
o: Conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate and phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate
e: In glycolysis, substrate-level phosphorylation occurs at two steps: (1) conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate (catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase) and (2) conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate (catalyzed by pyruvate kinase). Each step produces 1 ATP per molecule, and since two 3-carbon molecules are processed, a total of 4 ATP are produced. After accounting for the 2 ATP invested in the preparatory phase, the net gain is 2 ATP. Options A and D represent ATP-consuming steps, while option B involves no ATP production.

q: Phosphorylation of glucose during glycolysis is catalysed by
e: Hexokinase catalyses the first step of glycolysis — the phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, using ATP.

q: Pyruvic acid, the key product of glycolysis, can have many metabolic fates. Under aerobic conditions it forms
e: Under aerobic conditions, pyruvic acid is oxidatively decarboxylated (via pyruvate dehydrogenase) to form acetyl CoA and CO2, which then enters the Krebs cycle.

t: Location of the Electron Transport System
q: The Electron Transport System (ETS) is located in the mitochondrial
e: The electron transport chain complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the proton gradient for ATP synthesis is generated.

t: Rate of Respiration in Plant Tissues
q: Which of the following exhibits the highest rate of respiration?
e: A germinating seed shows an exceptionally high rate of respiration due to intense metabolic activity mobilising stored food reserves to fuel rapid growth.

q: The end product of oxidative phosphorylation is
e: Oxidative phosphorylation couples the electron transport chain (where oxygen is reduced to water) with ATP synthesis, so its end products are ATP and water.

q: Which is a character of insect-pollinated flowers?
e: Entomophilous (insect-pollinated) flowers are brightly coloured, fragrant, produce nectar, have sticky/spiny pollen. Wind-pollinated flowers are small with light pollen and feathery stigma.

q: Large, colourful, fragrant flowers with nectar are seen in:
e: Insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers are typically large, colourful, fragrant, and nectar-producing to attract insect pollinators.

q: Which of the following plant produces non-albuminous seeds?
e: Non-albuminous (exalbuminous) seeds are those where the endosperm is completely consumed during seed development and food is stored in the cotyledons instead. Pea is a classic example of a non-albuminous seed. Maize, barley, and wheat are all albuminous seeds (retain endosperm at maturity).

q: Pollination in water hyacinth and water lily is brought about by the agency of:
e: Despite growing in water, water hyacinth and water lily flowers emerge above the water surface and are pollinated by insects or wind, not by water (they are not hydrophilous in pollination).

q: Double fertilization is exhibited by:
e: Double fertilization, where one male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote and another fuses with the secondary nucleus to form the triploid endosperm, is a unique characteristic feature of angiosperms (flowering plants).

q: Pollen grains can be stored for several years in liquid nitrogen having a temperature of
e: Liquid nitrogen, used for cryopreservation of pollen grains (pollen cryobanks), is maintained at a temperature of approximately -196°C.

q: Which of the following flowers only once in its life-time?
e: Many bamboo species are monocarpic, flowering only once (often after several decades) before dying, unlike papaya, mango and jackfruit which flower repeatedly (polycarpic) across their lifetime.

q: Which one of the following is a triploid cell?
e: The primary endosperm cell (formed by triple fusion of 2 polar nuclei + 1 male gamete) is triploid (3n).

t: Pollination type bringing genetically different pollen
q: Which one of the following types of pollination brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma?
e: Xenogamy is cross-pollination between genetically different plants, bringing genetically different pollen to the stigma.

q: Embryo sac is to ovule as ___ is to anther.
e: The embryo sac is the female gametophyte produced inside the ovule; the analogous male gametophyte produced inside the anther is the pollen grain.

q: In a typical complete, bisexual, and hypogynous flower, the arrangement of floral whorls on the thalamus from the outermost to the innermost is
e: In a typical flower, the whorls are arranged from outermost to innermost as calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), and gynoecium (pistil) at the centre.

q: The phenomenon wherein the ovary develops into a fruit without fertilisation is called
e: Parthenocarpy refers specifically to the development of a fruit from the ovary in the absence of fertilisation, typically resulting in seedless fruits.

q:
Identify the set of correct statements:
A. The flowers of vallisneria are colourful and produce nectar.
B. The flowers of waterlily are not pollinated by water.
C. In most of water-pollinated species, the pollen grains are protected from wetting.
D. Pollen grains of some hydrophytes are long and ribbon like.
E. In some hydrophytes, the pollen grains are carried passively inside water.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: A, C, D and E only
B, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
e: Vallisneria flowers are small, inconspicuous and not colourful/nectar-producing (A, false, since it is a water-pollinated plant relying on water transport). Waterlily and lotus flowers are pollinated by insects, not water (B, true). In most water-pollinated species pollen grains are protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering (C, true). Pollen grains of some hydrophytes like Vallisneria and Zostera are long, ribbon-like (D, true). In some hydrophytes like Vallisneria, pollen grains are carried passively inside water (E, true). So B, C, D and E only. 12th NCERT Page No. 13.

q:
Match Column-I with Column-II and select the correct option using the codes given below:
Column-I: a. Pistils fused together, b. Formation of gametes, c. Hyphae of higher Ascomycetes, d. Unisexual female flower
Column-II: (i) Gametogenesis, (ii) Pistillate, (iii) Syncarpous, (iv) Dikaryotic
Codes:
(1) a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii
(2) a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii
(3) a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii
(4) a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii
e: Pistils fused together = Syncarpous; Formation of gametes = Gametogenesis; Hyphae of higher Ascomycetes = Dikaryotic; Unisexual female flower = Pistillate. So a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.

t: Alternation of generations within plant structures
q: The plant parts which consist of two generations - one within the other: (a) Pollen grains inside the anther, (b) Germinated pollen grain with two male gametes, (c) Seed inside the fruit, (d) Embryo sac inside the ovule
e: Pollen grains (the male gametophyte generation) develop inside the anther (sporophyte tissue) representing one generation within another (a); similarly, the embryo sac (female gametophyte) develops inside the ovule (sporophyte tissue), also representing one generation within another (d). This matches (a) and (d).

q: Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Both wind and water pollinated flowers are not very colourful and do not produce nectar. Reason (R): The flowers produce enormous amount of pollen grains in wind and water pollinated flowers. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
e: Both statements are true: abiotically pollinated flowers (wind/water) lack colour and nectar since these are attractants for biotic pollinators which aren't needed; and they produce enormous pollen since pollination is non-directional/random. However R does not directly explain why they lack colour/nectar (A) — the large pollen production is a separate adaptation for non-directional pollen dispersal, not the explanation for the lack of colour/nectar.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: In a floral formula ⊕ stands for zygomorphic nature of the flower, and G stands for inferior ovary. Statement II: In a floral formula ⊕ stands for actinomorphic nature of the flower and G stands for superior ovary. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: ⊕ symbol stands for actinomorphic (radial symmetry) nature of the flower (not zygomorphic, which uses %), and an underlined G (G̲) stands for superior ovary (not inferior — overline Ḡ indicates inferior ovary). So Statement I is incorrect, Statement II is correct.

q: Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A) : A typical unfertilised, angiosperm embryo sac at maturity is 8 nucleate and 7-celled. Reason (R) : The egg apparatus has 2 polar nuclei. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
e: Assertion is correct: a typical mature angiosperm embryo sac is 8-nucleate, 7-celled (3 antipodals, 2 synergids, 1 egg cell, 1 central cell with 2 polar nuclei). Reason is false: the egg apparatus consists of 2 synergids and 1 egg cell, not 2 polar nuclei (the polar nuclei are in the central cell).

q:
Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): Cells of the tapetum possess dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.
Reason (R): Presence of more than one nucleus in the tapetum increases the efficiency of nourishing the developing microspore mother cells.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
e: Tapetum cells possess dense cytoplasm and are often multinucleate - A is true. This multinucleate, dense-cytoplasm nature helps the tapetum efficiently nourish the developing pollen grains (microspores), not the microspore mother cells directly as nutritive tissue - however as per the given answer key, R is considered the correct explanation of A. Both A and R are true and R explains A.

t: Megasporogenesis - Meiotic/Mitotic Divisions for Female Gametophyte
q: How many meiotic and mitotic divisions need to occur for the development of a mature female gametophyte from the megaspore mother cell in an angiosperm plant?
e: The megaspore mother cell undergoes one meiotic division (meiosis) to form four haploid megaspores, and the functional megaspore undergoes 3 successive mitotic divisions to form the 8-nucleate, 7-celled mature embryo sac (female gametophyte). 12th NCERT - Page 11.

t: Structures of the Fertilized Embryo Sac
q: In angiosperm, the haploid, diploid and triploid structures of a fertilized embryo sac sequentially are:
o: Antipodals, synergids, and primary endosperm nucleus
Synergids, Zygote and Primary endosperm nucleus
Synergids, Primary endosperm nucleus and zygote
e: After fertilization, synergids remain haploid, the zygote (formed by fusion of egg and one male gamete) is diploid, and the primary endosperm nucleus (formed by triple fusion of the two polar nuclei and the other male gamete) is triploid. So the sequence haploid, diploid, triploid corresponds to synergids, zygote, and primary endosperm nucleus.

t: Corn Cob Structure - Function of Tassels
q: What is the function of tassels in the corn cob?
e: Tassels in corn bear the staminate (male) flowers at the top of the plant, and the silky styles/stigmas of the female flowers hang to trap pollen grains released from the tassels during wind pollination. (Per the NCERT reference, tassels here trap pollen grains.)

q: How many theca are present in each lobe of a typical bilobed angiosperm anther?
e: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed (dithecous), and each lobe contains two theca (pollen sacs/microsporangia), giving a total of four microsporangia in the whole anther.

q: If the diploid chromosome number of a typical angiosperm is 36, what would be the chromosome number in its endosperm?
e: If the diploid (2n) chromosome number is 36, then the haploid (n) number is 18. The endosperm in angiosperms is formed by triple fusion (one male gamete + two polar nuclei), making it triploid (3n) = 3 × 18 = 54.

q: Which of the following in female gametophyte of an angiosperm helps in guiding the pollen tube for fertilizing the eggs?
e: Synergid cells, located at the micropylar end of the embryo sac alongside the egg cell, possess a specialized filiform apparatus that helps guide and attract the pollen tube towards the egg for fertilization.

q: In majority of angiosperms:
o: A small central cell is present in the embryo sac
Reduction division occurs in the megaspore mother cells
e: In most angiosperms, meiosis (reduction division) occurs in the megaspore mother cell to form megaspores, one of which develops into the embryo sac. The synergids (not the egg) have the filiform apparatus, there are typically 3 antipodal cells (not numerous), and the central cell is large, not small.

q: The ovule of an angiosperm is technically equivalent to:
e: The ovule is technically equivalent to the megasporangium, which is integumented and contains the megaspore mother cell that undergoes meiosis to form megaspores.

q: The term used for transfer of pollen grains from anthers of one plant to stigma of a different plant which, during pollination, brings genetically different types of pollen grains to stigma, is:
e: Xenogamy is cross-pollination between genetically different plants (pollen from one plant to stigma of another plant of the same species), bringing genetically different pollen to the stigma.

q: A typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity is:
e: A typical mature angiosperm embryo sac is 8-nucleate but 7-celled, since the central cell contains two polar nuclei (not yet fused into separate cells).

q: In some members of which of the following pairs of families, pollen grains retain their viability for months after release?
e: In some members of Rosaceae and Leguminosae, pollen grains retain viability for months, unlike members of Poaceae where pollen loses viability within 30 minutes of release.

q: From evolutionary point of view, retention of the female gametophyte with development young embryo on the parent sporophyte for some time, is first observed in:
e: Pteridophytes were the first group to show retention of the female gametophyte with the developing young embryo on the parent sporophyte, a trend that evolved further in seed plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms).

q: Persistent nucellus in the seed is known as:
e: The persistent, dry remnant of the nucellus that remains in some mature seeds is known as perisperm.

q: Placentation, in which ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or in peripheral part is:
e: In parietal placentation, ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on the peripheral part, as seen in mustard and Argemone.

q: Which of the following statements regarding post fertilization development in flowering plants is incorrect?
e: Ovules develop into SEEDS after fertilization, not into embryo sac (the embryo sac develops before fertilization, within the ovule, during megagametogenesis). This makes statement 2 incorrect.

q: In some plants the female gamete develops into embryo without fertilization. This phenomenon is known as:
e: Parthenogenesis is the phenomenon where the female gamete develops into an embryo without fertilization.

q: What is the fate of the male gametes discharged in the synergid?
o: One fuses with the egg, other(s) fuse(s) with synergid nucleus.
One fuses with the egg and other fuses with central cell nuclei.
One fuses with the egg, other(s) degenerate(s) in the synergid.
e: After the pollen tube discharges its two male gametes into the synergid, one male gamete fuses with the egg cell (syngamy), and the other fuses with the central cell nuclei (triple fusion) to form the primary endosperm nucleus.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous. Statement II: Cleistogamy is disadvantageous as there is no chance for cross pollination. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct: cleistogamous flowers never open, so they are necessarily self-pollinated (autogamous), and this is disadvantageous because it eliminates any possibility of cross-pollination, reducing genetic variation.

q: Identify the incorrect statement related to Pollination:
o: Pollination by water is quite rare in flowering plants
Pollination by wind is more common amongst abiotic pollination
Flowers produce foul odours to attract flies and beetles to get pollinated
Moths and butterflies are the most dominant pollinating agents among insects
e: Bees, not moths and butterflies, are considered the most dominant and common pollinating agents among insects. The other statements about water pollination being rare, wind pollination being common abiotically, and foul-smelling flowers attracting flies/beetles are correct.

q: Flowers which have single ovule in the ovary and are packed into inflorescence are usually pollinated by:
e: Flowers with a single ovule packed into dense inflorescences (such as in grasses) are typically small, inconspicuous, and anemophilous, relying on wind for pollination, which can disperse large quantities of light pollen efficiently.

q: A dioecious flowering plant prevents both:
e: In dioecious plants, male and female flowers are borne on separate plants entirely, which prevents both autogamy (self-pollination within the same flower) and geitonogamy (pollination between different flowers of the same plant).

q: Attractants and rewards are required for:
e: Entomophily (pollination by insects) requires attractants (like colour, scent) and rewards (like nectar, pollen) to lure pollinators, unlike wind or water pollination (anemophily, hydrophily) or self-pollinating cleistogamous flowers.

q: Functional megaspore in an angiosperm develops into:
e: The functional megaspore undergoes successive mitotic divisions to develop into the female gametophyte, the embryo sac (megagametophyte).

q: Double fertilization is
o: Fusion of two male gametes of a pollen tube with two different eggs
Fusion of two male gametes with one egg
Fusion of one male gamete with two polar nuclei
e: Double fertilization involves two fusion events: syngamy (fusion of one male gamete with the egg cell to form the zygote) and triple fusion (fusion of the second male gamete with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm).

t: Winged pollen grains (adaptation for wind dispersal)
q: Winged pollen grains are present in
e: Pinus (a conifer, wind-pollinated gymnosperm) has pollen grains with two air sacs (wings), which aid in their buoyancy and dispersal by wind.

q: Ray florets have:
e: Ray florets, found in composite inflorescences of the Asteraceae family, have an inferior ovary, where the ovary is positioned below the point of attachment of other floral parts.

q: In water hyacinth and water lily, pollination takes place by:
e: Despite being aquatic plants, water hyacinth and water lily hold their flowers above the water surface and are pollinated by insects or wind (entomophily/anemophily), not by water.

q: The ovary is half inferior in:
e: In plum flowers, the ovary is half-inferior (perigynous), positioned partway between superior and inferior, with the floral parts arising from around the middle of the ovary.

q: Arrange the following in the correct developmental sequence related to microsporogenesis: A. Microspore tetrads, B. Sporogenous tissue, C. Pollen grains, D. Pollen mother cells.
e: Sequence: sporogenous tissue (B) → pollen mother cells (D) → microspore tetrads (A) → pollen grains (C): B, D, A, C.

t: Ovules not enclosed by ovary wall
q: In which one of the following is the ovule not enclosed by an ovary wall and remain exposed, both before and after fertilization?
e: Pinus (a gymnosperm) has naked ovules not enclosed within an ovary wall, unlike angiosperms.
