q: Match List I with List II: List I (Placentation) — A. Marginal, B. Axile, C. Parietal, D. Basal. List II (Example) — I. Mustard, II. Pea, III. Marigold, IV. Lemon.
e: Marginal placentation example is pea (II); axile is lemon (IV); parietal is mustard (I); basal is marigold (III). A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

t: Why a Dicot Plant May Never Bear Fruit
q: A dicotyledonous plant bears flowers but never produces fruits and seeds. The most probable cause for this is that the
o: plant is dioecious and bears only pistillate flowers.
plant is dioecious and bears both pistillate and staminate flowers.
plant is dioecious and bears only staminate flowers.
e: A dioecious plant that bears only staminate (male) flowers has no ovary at all, so it is structurally incapable of ever producing fruits or seeds on its own, unlike a plant bearing pistillate flowers, which could still potentially be pollinated by another plant.

t: Conditions for Autogamy in a Chasmogamous Flower
q: Autogamy can occur in a chasmogamous flower (one that opens, exposing its anthers and stigma) if
o: the pollen matures well before the ovule matures.
the ovule matures well before the pollen matures.
both the pollen and the ovule mature simultaneously.
the anther and stigma are of equal length.
e: In a chasmogamous flower, self-pollination (autogamy) requires the pollen and the ovule to be receptive at the same time, since both the anther and stigma are already exposed to each other within the same open flower.

q: Choose the correct statement from the following:
o: Cleistogamous flowers exhibit both autogamy and geitonogamy.
e: Cleistogamous flowers never open at all, so their anthers and stigma remain in close, enforced contact, guaranteeing self-pollination (autogamy) within the same flower every time.

q: A particular species of plant produces light, non-sticky pollen in large numbers, and its stigmas are long and feathery. These modifications facilitate pollination by
e: Light, non-sticky, abundantly produced pollen that can be easily carried by air currents, together with long, feathery stigmas adapted to catch airborne pollen, are classic adaptations for wind (anemophilous) pollination.

q: From among the situations given below, choose the one that prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
o: A monoecious plant bearing unisexual flowers.
A dioecious plant bearing only male or only female flowers on separate individuals.
A monoecious plant with bisexual flowers.
A dioecious plant with bisexual flowers.
e: In a dioecious species, each individual plant bears flowers of only one sex. Since no single plant has both male and female flowers (or bisexual flowers), neither self-pollination within a flower (autogamy) nor pollination between flowers of the same plant (geitonogamy) is possible — pollination must occur between two separate plants.

q: The phenomenon observed in some plants wherein parts of the sexual apparatus are used to form embryos without fertilisation is called
e: Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction, in which embryos form directly from certain cells of the ovule (part of the sexual apparatus) without the actual fusion of gametes.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following are fused in somatic hybridization involving two varieties of plants?
e: Somatic hybridization involves the fusion of protoplasts (cells with the cell wall removed) from two different plant varieties or species to produce a hybrid cell, which is then cultured to regenerate a hybrid plant.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Among the following edible fishes, which one is a marine fish having rich source of omega-3 fatty acids?
e: Mackerel is a marine fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids, while Mystus, Mangur (catfish) and Mrigala are freshwater fishes.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Breeding crops with higher levels of vitamins and minerals or higher proteins and healthier fats is called:
e: Biofortification is the breeding of crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, proteins, and healthier fats to improve nutritional value.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in plant breeding?
o: Hybridization → Collection of variability → Evaluation → Selection
Collection of variability → Evaluation → Hybridization → Selection
Collection of variability → Hybridization → Selection → Evaluation and release
Selection → Collection of variability → Hybridization → Evaluation
e: The correct sequence in plant breeding is: (1) Collection of variability (germplasm collection), (2) Evaluation and selection of parents, (3) Hybridization, (4) Selection and testing of superior recombinants, (5) Testing, release and commercialization of new varieties.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is NOT a method of animal breeding?
e: Somatic hybridization is a technique used in plant breeding where protoplasts of two different plants are fused. It is NOT a method of animal breeding. Animal breeding methods include inbreeding, outbreeding (outcrossing, crossbreeding, interspecific hybridization) and artificial insemination.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
t: Plant Breeding for Improved Varieties - Green Revolution
q: The Green Revolution in India was primarily associated with which of the following?
o: Introduction of high-yielding varieties of sugarcane and cotton
Development of high-yielding semi-dwarf varieties of wheat and rice
Large-scale adoption of organic farming practices in Punjab
Introduction of hybrid maize varieties from Mexico
e: The Green Revolution in India during the 1960s-70s was primarily associated with the introduction of high-yielding, semi-dwarf varieties of wheat (by Norman Borlaug) and rice. In India, M.S. Swaminathan introduced these varieties, leading to dramatic increases in food grain production. Semi-dwarf genes allowed heavy grain-bearing without lodging.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in a plant breeding programme?
o: Hybridization → Collection of variability → Evaluation → Selection
Collection of variability → Evaluation → Hybridization → Selection
Collection of variability → Hybridization → Selection → Evaluation and release
Selection → Hybridization → Collection of variability → Evaluation
e: The correct sequence in a plant breeding programme is: (1) Collection of variability (germplasm collection), (2) Evaluation and selection of parents, (3) Hybridization, (4) Selection and testing of superior recombinants, (5) Testing, release, and commercialization of new varieties.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following pairs of breeds correctly represents a cross between an Indian breed and an exotic breed of cattle done for producing improved dairy breeds?
e: Crosses between Indian breeds like Sahiwal and exotic breeds like Brown Swiss are done to improve milk production and disease resistance. The goal is to combine the high milk-yielding capacity of exotic breeds with the disease resistance of Indian breeds. Jersey × Holstein-Friesian is a cross between two exotic breeds, while Red Sindhi, Gir, and Ongole are all Indian breeds.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: A group of animals that are related by descent and share many similarities is referred to as a
e: A breed is a group of animals related by descent that share common characteristics such as general appearance, features, and performance, distinguishing it from other groups within the same species.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Fungicides and antibiotics are chemicals that
o: kill pathogenic fungi and bacteria, respectively.
kill pathogenic bacteria and fungi, respectively.
e: Fungicides specifically target and kill pathogenic fungi, while antibiotics specifically target and kill pathogenic bacteria — each acting selectively on its respective class of pathogen, not microbes in general.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Somaclonal variation refers to which of the following phenomena observed in plant tissue culture?
o: Genetic variation arising due to mutation induced by the culture medium chemicals
Genetic variation observed among plants regenerated from somatic cells in culture
Variation in somatic embryo development due to temperature fluctuations
Epigenetic variation that disappears in subsequent generations
e: Somaclonal variation refers to the genetic variation that is observed among plants regenerated from somatic cells grown in tissue culture. These variations arise due to chromosome number changes, DNA sequence alterations, or gene expression changes during the culture process, and are heritable. They can be exploited as a source of variability in crop improvement.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Inbreeding depression in animals occurs due to continued inbreeding. Which of the following correctly explains the genetic basis of inbreeding depression?
o: Accumulation of heterozygous loci leading to expression of dominant deleterious alleles
Increased homozygosity leading to expression of recessive deleterious alleles
Introduction of foreign alleles that disrupt the existing gene combinations
Reduction in mutation rate leading to decreased genetic variation
e: Inbreeding depression occurs because continued inbreeding increases homozygosity throughout the genome. When homozygosity increases, recessive deleterious alleles (which were previously masked in heterozygous condition) get expressed in homozygous form, leading to reduced fitness, fertility, and productivity — a phenomenon called inbreeding depression.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: In Multiple Ovulation Embryo Transfer (MOET) technology, superovulation is induced by administering:
o: Progesterone to suppress normal ovulation followed by FSH
Gonadotropins (FSH-like hormones) to produce multiple eggs
Luteinizing hormone (LH) to stimulate corpus luteum formation
e: In MOET technology, a cow (high milk-yielding breed) is administered gonadotropins (specifically FSH-like hormones) to induce superovulation — production of 6–8 eggs per cycle instead of the usual one. The animal is then mated with an elite bull, and the fertilized embryos are recovered and transferred to surrogate mothers, allowing rapid multiplication of desirable traits.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Single Cell Protein (SCP) produced from Spirulina is considered a good dietary supplement. Which of the following statements about Spirulina and SCP is INCORRECT?
o: Spirulina can be grown on waste water from potato processing industries
Spirulina is rich in proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals
SCP production reduces environmental pollution as it uses industrial effluents as substrate
Spirulina is a fungus and therefore classified as a heterotrophic organism for SCP production
e: Spirulina is a cyanobacterium (blue-green alga), not a fungus. It is an autotrophic photosynthetic organism. It can be grown on waste water from potato processing, sewage, and other effluents. It is rich in proteins (up to 70% dry weight), fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals, making it an excellent dietary supplement and contributing to reduction of environmental pollution.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: In aquaculture practices, 'composite fish culture' or 'polyculture' is used to increase fish yield. Which of the following combinations is most ideal for composite fish culture, and why is it considered advantageous?
o: Catla and Rohu only, because both feed on surface water plankton
Catla, Rohu, Mrigal, Grass carp, Silver carp, and Common carp, because they occupy different food niches in the same pond
Only exotic species like Silver carp and Grass carp, because they have higher growth rates than Indian species
Catla and Common carp only, because they are both column feeders and maximize mid-water food utilization
e: In composite fish culture, a combination of five or six fish species like Catla (surface feeder), Rohu (column feeder), Mrigal and Common carp (bottom feeders), Grass carp (macrophyte feeder), and Silver carp (surface feeder) are cultured together. Since they occupy different food niches (surface, column, bottom, and vegetation), they do not compete with each other, and all the available food in the pond is used efficiently, thereby maximizing fish yield per unit area.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Interspecific hybridization is the mating of:
o: More closely related individuals within same breed for 4-6 generations
Animals within same breed without having common ancestors
Superior males and females of different breeds
e: Interspecific hybridization involves mating between males and females of two different but related species.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is not a step in Multiple Ovulation Embryo Transfer Technology (MOET)?
o: Fertilized eggs are transferred to surrogate mothers at 8-32 cell stage
Cow is administered hormone having LH like activity for super ovulation
Cow yields about 6-8 eggs at a time
Cow is fertilized by artificial insemination
e: In MOET, the cow is administered FSH-like hormone (not LH-like) for superovulation to yield 6-8 eggs, which are then fertilized by artificial insemination and transferred to surrogate mothers at the 8-32 cell stage.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Homozygous purelines in cattle can be obtained by:
o: mating of unrelated individuals of same breed.
mating of individuals of different breed.
mating of individuals of different species.
mating of related individuals of same breed.
e: Inbreeding, the mating of closely related individuals within the same breed, increases homozygosity, allowing desirable recessive traits to be exposed and homozygous purelines to be developed.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Norman Borlaug developed semi-dwarf varieties of wheat. Which of the following traits was specifically introduced to prevent lodging in these varieties?
o: Disease resistance genes from wild relatives
Dwarfing genes (Rht genes) that reduce stem elongation
High tillering capacity from Mexican wheat
Increased root depth to absorb more nutrients
e: Norman Borlaug introduced dwarfing genes (Rht genes) into wheat that reduce stem elongation, preventing lodging (falling over) when the plant produces heavy grain. This was central to the Green Revolution, allowing plants to support heavier grain loads without falling.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Himgiri, a variety of wheat developed through hybridization and selection, is resistant to which of the following diseases?
o: Leaf and stripe rust, hill bunt
Brown rust, yellow mosaic, and smut
e: Himgiri is a variety of wheat developed through hybridization and selection for disease resistance. It is resistant to leaf and stripe rust, as well as hill bunt. This example is specifically mentioned in the NCERT textbook for Class 12.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Single Cell Protein (SCP) is considered an alternative protein source. Which of the following organisms is used to produce SCP from industrial effluents?
e: Spirulina can be grown on industrial effluents (waste water from potato processing plants, animal manure, etc.) to produce Single Cell Protein (SCP). Methylophilus methylotrophus is used to produce SCP from methanol, while Chlorella and Anabaena are microalgae used differently. NCERT specifically mentions Spirulina as an SCP grown on waste materials.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is a correct example of biofortification in crop plants as mentioned in NCERT?
o: Maize hybrids with twice the amount of lysine and tryptophan
IR-36 rice variety with enhanced iron content
Pusa Komal cowpea with increased vitamin C
Sonalika wheat with higher zinc content
e: Biofortification involves breeding crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, protein, and healthier fats. NCERT specifically mentions that maize hybrids have been developed with twice the amount of amino acids lysine and tryptophan compared to existing maize varieties. This is a classic example of biofortification mentioned in the textbook.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Mung bean variety resistant to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew was developed using which breeding technique?
e: Mutation breeding involves inducing mutations artificially using mutagens (physical or chemical). The mung bean variety resistant to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew was developed through mutation breeding. Atom bomb explosions at Hiroshima and Nagasaki also demonstrated the effect of radiation-induced mutations, which led to the development of this technique.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: The ability of a single explant to grow into a complete plant on a suitable culture medium is known as:
e: Totipotency is the property of a living plant cell to have the genetic potential to generate a whole new individual plant. This concept was proposed by Haberlandt. Micropropagation is the technique that uses totipotency to produce thousands of plants. Somatic hybridization involves fusion of protoplasts from different plants, and morphogenesis refers to the process of development of form and structure.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
q: Which of the following is an example of biofortification achieved through plant breeding to address protein-calorie malnutrition?
o: Atlas 66 wheat variety with high protein content
Sharbati Sonora wheat with better grain quality
IR-8 rice variety with high yield
Pusa Komal cowpea with disease resistance
e: Atlas 66, a wheat variety with high protein content, has been used as a donor for improving cultivated wheat. It is an example of biofortification — breeding crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, or proteins. IR-8 is a high-yielding rice variety, Sharbati Sonora is a quality improvement variety, and Pusa Komal is disease resistant — but none specifically address protein enrichment through biofortification like Atlas 66.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
t: Bird Flu and Properly Cooked Poultry
q: The chances of contracting bird flu from a properly cooked (above 100°C) chicken or egg are
e: The bird flu (avian influenza) virus is inactivated by heat; thoroughly cooking chicken or eggs above 100°C destroys the virus, eliminating the risk of transmission.

c: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
t: Purpose of Inbreeding in Animal Husbandry
q: Inbreeding is carried out in animal husbandry because it
e: Inbreeding (mating closely related individuals of the same breed) increases homozygosity, which helps evaluate and select for desirable superior genes while eliminating undesirable, less desirable recessive genes from the breed.

q: In water, frogs respire using _________
e: When submerged in water, frogs rely primarily on cutaneous respiration (gas exchange through their moist, vascularized skin), since lungs and buccal cavity respiration require access to air.

q: Which of the following is not a connective tissue?
e: Neuroglia are supporting cells of the nervous system (neural tissue), not connective tissue. Blood, adipose tissue, and cartilage are all types of connective tissue.

q: Male frogs can be distinguished from female frogs due to the presence of: A. Bulging eyes. B. Vocal sacs. C. Webbed digits in feet. D. Copulatory pad on first digit of fore limbs. E. Olive green-coloured skin with dark irregular spots.
e: Male frogs have vocal sacs for croaking (B) and copulatory pads on the first digit of forelimbs for amplexus (D); these are distinguishing male features. B and D only.

q: Which type of epithelium lines the inner surface of the urinary bladder, allowing it to stretch when filled with urine?
e: Transitional epithelium (also called urothelium) lines the urinary bladder. Its cells can change shape — from cuboidal when the bladder is empty to squamous-like when distended — allowing the bladder to stretch and accommodate varying volumes of urine.

q: Which connective tissue is characterized by a fluid matrix called plasma and contains cells like erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes?
e: Blood is a specialized connective tissue with a liquid matrix called plasma. It contains red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes) suspended in plasma. Lymph is similar but lacks erythrocytes and has a different protein composition.

q: In an earthworm (Pheretima), the clitellum is located on which segments?
e: In Pheretima posthuma (earthworm), the clitellum is a glandular, saddle-shaped structure found on segments 14–16. It secretes mucus for copulation and forms the cocoon for egg deposition. It appears as a distinct, darker girdle on the body.

q: To which one of the following categories does adipose tissue belong?
e: Adipose tissue, which stores fat, is a type of loose connective tissue.

q: Out of 'X' ribs in humans only 'Y' pairs are true ribs. Select the option that correctly represents values of X and Y and provides their explanation:
o: X=12, Y=5: True ribs are attached dorsally to vertebral column and sternum on the two ends.
X=24, Y=7: True ribs are dorsally attached to vertebral column but are free on ventral side.
X=24, Y=12: True ribs are dorsally attached to vertebral column but are free on ventral side.
X=12, Y=7: True ribs are attached dorsally to vertebral column and ventrally to the sternum.
e: As accepted in the official NTA answer key, X=24 (total individual ribs, forming 12 pairs) and Y=7 pairs are classified as true ribs since they attach directly (dorsally to the vertebral column, and via their own costal cartilage ventrally) to the sternum, while the remaining pairs are false or floating ribs.

q: Select the correct route for the passage of sperms in male frogs:
o: Testes -> Vasa efferentia -> Kidney -> Seminal Vesicle -> Urinogenital duct -> Cloaca
Testes -> Vasa efferentia -> Bidder's canal -> Ureter -> Cloaca
Testes -> Vasa efferentia -> Kidney -> Bidder's canal -> Urinogenital duct -> Cloaca
Testes -> Bidder's canal -> Kidney -> Vasa efferentia -> Urinogenital duct -> Cloaca
e: In male frogs, sperms travel from the testes through the vasa efferentia into the kidney, then via Bidder's canal to the urinogenital duct, and finally to the cloaca.

q: In the cockroach (Periplaneta americana), which of the following statements about its excretory system is CORRECT?
o: Excretion occurs through nephridia which open into the coelom
Malpighian tubules absorb nitrogenous wastes from haemolymph and empty them into the midgut
Malpighian tubules absorb nitrogenous wastes and empty them at the junction of midgut and hindgut
The fat body is the primary excretory organ, storing uric acid permanently
e: In cockroaches, excretion is carried out by Malpighian tubules — about 100–150 yellow thread-like structures. They absorb nitrogenous wastes (mainly uric acid) from the haemolymph (blood) and empty them at the junction of the midgut and hindgut (ileum), from where wastes are expelled with feces. Nephridia are found in annelids, not insects.

q: In a frog, the vasa efferentia from the testes open into the kidneys. This means the frog's kidney serves as which of the following?
o: A urinogenital organ since the same duct (Bidder's canal/Wolffian duct) carries both urine and sperms
Only a reproductive organ during the breeding season
A separate reproductive organ unrelated to urine transport
e: In male frogs, the vasa efferentia from the testes enter the kidneys and open into the Bidder's canal (longitudinal canal in the kidney). Sperms then pass through uriniferous tubules into the Wolffian duct (ureter), which opens into the cloaca. Thus, the same duct carries both urine and spermatozoa, making the kidney a urinogenital organ in male frogs.

q: Microvilli are finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase the absorptive surface area. Which type of epithelium characteristically shows a 'brush border' formed by microvilli?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium of the oesophagus
Simple columnar epithelium of the small intestine
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the trachea
Simple cuboidal epithelium of kidney tubules
e: The simple columnar epithelium lining the small intestine has densely packed microvilli on its apical surface, forming the characteristic 'brush border' (striated border). This dramatically increases the surface area for absorption of digested nutrients. The trachea has cilia (not microvilli) for mucus movement, and the oesophageal epithelium is protective stratified squamous type.

q: Setae help in locomotion in earthworm but are not uniformly present in all the segments. They are present in
e: Setae are absent in the first segment, the last segment, and the clitellar segments (14th-16th) of the earthworm, but are present in ordinary body segments such as the 20th-22nd segment.

q: In an earthworm, the typhlosole is a structure found in the intestine. What is its primary function and in which region of the intestine is it present?
o: It secretes digestive enzymes and is present throughout the entire length of the intestine
It increases the absorptive surface area and is present from the 26th segment onwards
It produces mucus to lubricate food passage and is present only in the anterior intestine up to the 25th segment
It stores glycogen and is present only in the posterior region near the rectum
e: The typhlosole is a deep dorsal fold of the intestinal wall (internal fold) that runs from the 26th segment to the last few segments in the earthworm. Its primary function is to increase the effective absorptive surface area of the intestine, thereby enhancing the absorption of digested nutrients. It does not secrete enzymes or produce mucus as its main role.

q:
Match List I with List II:
List I: (A) Unicellular glandular epithelium (B) Compound epithelium (C) Multicellular glandular epithelium (D) Endocrine glandular epithelium
List II: (I) Salivary glands (II) Pancreas (III) Goblet cells of alimentary canal (IV) Moist surface of buccal cavity
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Unicellular glandular epithelium is exemplified by goblet cells of the alimentary canal (A-III). Compound epithelium lines the moist surface of the buccal cavity (B-IV). Multicellular glandular epithelium forms salivary glands (C-I). Endocrine glandular epithelium forms glands like the pancreas (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is correct.

q:
Match List I with List II related to digestive system of cockroach.
List I: (A) The structures used for storing of food. (B) Ring of 6-8 blind tubules at junction of foregut and midgut. (C) Ring of 100-150 yellow coloured thin filaments at junction of midgut and hindgut. (D) The structures used for grinding the food.
List II: (I) Gizzard (II) Gastric Caeca (III) Malpighian tubules (IV) Crop
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: The crop stores food (A-IV). Gastric caeca are a ring of 6-8 blind tubules at the junction of foregut and midgut (B-II). Malpighian tubules form a ring of 100-150 thin filaments at the junction of midgut and hindgut (C-III). The gizzard grinds food (D-I). So A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I is correct.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Ligaments are dense irregular tissue. Statement II: Cartilage is dense regular tissue. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
e: Statement I is true — ligaments are made of dense irregular connective tissue (highly elastic). Statement II is false — cartilage is not a dense regular tissue; it is a specialized connective tissue with a solid matrix (chondrin), distinct from dense regular connective tissue like tendons.

q: Match List I with List II: A. Mast cells, B. Inner surface of bronchiole, C. Blood, D. Tubular parts of nephron. List II: I. Ciliated epithelium, II. Areolar connective tissue, III. Cuboidal epithelium, IV. Specialised connective tissue. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Mast cells are found in areolar connective tissue (A-II). The inner surface of the bronchiole is lined by ciliated epithelium (B-I). Blood is a specialised connective tissue (C-IV). Tubular parts of the nephron are lined by cuboidal epithelium (D-III). So the correct match is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

q: Smooth muscles are:
e: Smooth muscles are involuntary, fusiform (spindle-shaped) in appearance, uninucleate, and non-striated — found in the walls of internal organs.

q: The ciliated epithelial cells are required to move particles or mucus in a specific direction. In humans, these cells are mainly present in:
e: Ciliated epithelial cells that move particles or mucus in a specific direction are mainly present in the bronchioles (respiratory tract, to move mucus) and fallopian tubes (to move the ovum towards the uterus).

q: Choose the correct statements regarding frog's anatomy. A. Hepatic portal system is the special venous connection between liver and intestine. B. There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain. C. The ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca in female frogs. D. Hind-brain consists of cerebellum, medulla oblongata and optic lobes. E. Sinus venosus joins the right atrium of heart.
e: A (hepatic portal system between intestine and liver), C (ureters/oviducts open separately into cloaca), and E (sinus venosus joins right atrium) are correct. B is false (frogs have 10, not 12, pairs of cranial nerves); D is false (optic lobes are part of the midbrain, not hindbrain). A, C and E only.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes cardiac muscle from skeletal muscle?
o: Cardiac muscle is voluntary and striated; skeletal muscle is involuntary and non-striated
Cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated with intercalated discs; skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated without intercalated discs
Cardiac muscle is non-striated and involuntary; skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary
Cardiac muscle has multiple nuclei per cell; skeletal muscle has a single central nucleus
e: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated, and has branched cells joined by intercalated discs that enable synchronized contraction. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated but lacks intercalated discs; its cells are multinucleated (peripheral nuclei). Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

q: Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system are functionally analogous to which cells in the central nervous system?
e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath around axons in the peripheral nervous system. Oligodendrocytes perform the equivalent function in the central nervous system by myelinating CNS axons. Astrocytes provide structural and metabolic support, microglia are immune cells, and ependymal cells line brain ventricles.

q: In the earthworm's digestive system, which structure is responsible for grinding food particles?
e: The gizzard (found in segments 8–9 in Pheretima) is a muscular organ that grinds soil and organic matter using its thick muscular walls and ingested sand grains. The pharynx and buccal cavity are anterior structures for food ingestion, and the stomach (segments 9–14) is involved in chemical digestion.

q: The compound eyes of the cockroach are composed of numerous visual units called:
e: Each compound eye of the cockroach consists of about 2,000 hexagonal units called ommatidia (singular: ommatidium). Each ommatidium functions as an independent photoreceptive unit. The compound eyes provide a mosaic (apposition) image. Ocelli are simple eyes (present on the dorsal head surface), while rhabdom is a component within each ommatidium.

q: Which one of the following types of cells is involved in making the inner walls of blood vessels?
e: The inner lining (endothelium) of blood vessels is composed of squamous epithelium — flat, thin cells that facilitate smooth movement of blood and easy diffusion of materials.

q: Which one of the following is not a connective tissue?
e: Bone, cartilage, and blood are all types of connective tissue, while muscle is a distinct tissue type specialised for contraction, not classified as connective tissue.

q: Which one of the following statements is true for cockroach?
o: The number of ovarioles in each ovary is ten.
The larval stage is called caterpillar.
Anal styles are absent in females.
e: A pair of anal styles is present only in male cockroaches and is absent in females — a useful feature for distinguishing sexes. (Cockroaches have 6-8 ovarioles per ovary, their larval stage is called a nymph not a caterpillar, and they are uricotelic, not ureotelic.)

q: Which type of epithelium lines the inner surface of the fallopian tubes (oviducts) and aids in the movement of the egg towards the uterus?
e: The fallopian tubes are lined by ciliated columnar epithelium. The cilia on these cells beat in a coordinated manner to create a current that helps transport the ovum (egg) from the ovary towards the uterus. Squamous epithelium is found in blood vessels and alveoli; cuboidal epithelium is found in kidney tubules; stratified epithelium is found in skin.

q: Which one of the following statements refers to Reductionist Biology?
o: Physico-chemical approach to study and understand living organisms.
Physiological approach to study and understand living organisms.
Chemical approach to study and understand living organisms.
Behavioural approach to study and understand living organisms.
e: Reductionist Biology applies the physico-chemical approach — concepts and techniques of physics and chemistry — to study and understand the function and structure of living organisms at the molecular level.

q:
Arrange the following taxonomic categories in ascending order.
(a) Genus (b) Class (c) Order (d) Phylum (e) Family (f) Kingdom (g) Species
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: The taxonomic hierarchy in ascending order (from most specific/narrow to broadest) is: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom. This matches the sequence (g) Species, (a) Genus, (e) Family, (c) Order, (b) Class, (d) Phylum, (f) Kingdom.

q: The label of a herbarium sheet does not carry information on:
e: A herbarium sheet label carries date of collection, collector's name, and local names, but not the height of the plant.

q: Which one of the following statements is not true about the universal rules of binomial nomenclature?
o: The first word in a biological name represents the specific epithet, while the second component denotes the genus
The specific epithet in the biological name starts with a small letter
Both the words in a biological name, when handwritten, are separately underlined or printed in italics
Biological names are generally in Latin
e: In binomial nomenclature, the first word is the genus and the second is the specific epithet — the reverse of what statement 1 says, making it the incorrect statement.

q: Which of the following is considered the most fundamental characteristic that distinguishes living organisms from non-living things?
e: Reproduction is considered the most fundamental characteristic of living organisms. While growth and response to stimuli can also occur in non-living things (e.g., crystals grow, iron responds to a magnet), reproduction — the ability to produce offspring — is unique to living organisms. However, among all options, reproduction is the defining feature emphasized in NCERT as the most inclusive criterion.

q: The branch of science that deals with identification, nomenclature, and classification of organisms is called:
e: Taxonomy is the branch of science dealing with identification, nomenclature, and classification of organisms. Systematics is broader and includes evolutionary relationships, while taxonomy is the practical aspect of naming and classifying. Ecology deals with interactions between organisms and their environment, and morphology deals with external structure.

q: The system of binomial nomenclature for naming organisms was introduced by:
e: Carolus Linnaeus introduced the system of binomial nomenclature in his work 'Systema Naturae.' In this system, each organism is given a two-part name — the first part is the genus name and the second is the species epithet. Both are written in Latin and italicized when printed.

q: Which of the following 'suffixes' used for units of classification in plants indicates a taxonomic category of 'family'?
e: In plant taxonomy, the suffix '-aceae' is used to denote the family level (e.g., Solanaceae, Poaceae).

q: The term 'systematics' refers to
o: identification and study of organ systems of plants and animals.
identification and preservation of plants and animals.
diversity of kinds of organisms and their relationships.
study of habitats of organisms and their classification.
e: Systematics is the branch of science concerned with the diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships to one another, as established through classification.

q: Botanical gardens and zoological parks have
o: a collection of endemic living species only.
a collection of exotic living species only.
a collection of endemic and exotic living species.
a collection of only local plants and animals.
e: Botanical gardens and zoos maintain living collections of both native (endemic) and non-native (exotic) plant and animal species for study, conservation and public education.

q: Which of the following is considered the most defining and unique property of living organisms?
e: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the body and is considered the most defining feature of life. Even non-living entities like crystals can grow, and mules cannot reproduce, but no non-living object has metabolism.

q: Which of the following represents the correct descending order of taxonomic hierarchy?
o: Kingdom → Order → Class → Phylum → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Phylum → Order → Class → Family → Genus → Species
e: The correct descending order of taxonomic hierarchy is: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. A helpful mnemonic is 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.

q: The scientific name of humans is Homo sapiens. According to binomial nomenclature, which part of this name denotes the genus?
e: In binomial nomenclature proposed by Carolus Linnaeus, the first word denotes the genus and the second word denotes the specific epithet (species). So 'Homo' is the genus name and 'sapiens' is the species name.

q: A herbarium is a store house of collected plant specimens. Which of the following statements about a herbarium is INCORRECT?
o: Herbarium sheets are arranged according to a universally accepted classification system.
Herbarium specimens are dried, pressed, and preserved on sheets.
A herbarium serves as a quick referral system for taxonomists in the field.
Herbarium sheets contain information about the collector, date and place of collection, and local name.
e: A herbarium is a collection of dried, pressed, and preserved plant specimens mounted on herbarium sheets along with information such as collection date, place, local name, and collector's name. They are arranged according to universally accepted classification systems and serve as quick referral systems in the laboratory, NOT in the field. In the field, botanical gardens and field guides are more useful. Hence, option C is incorrect.

q: According to the NCERT definition, a 'species' is best described as:
o: A group of organisms that look identical and are found in the same geographical area.
A group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The lowest taxonomic category with organisms sharing the maximum number of common characters.
A group of organisms classified together based on morphological characters alone.
e: According to NCERT, a species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities. It is the lowest level of taxonomic hierarchy. Organisms within a species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. While options A and D are partially correct, they are incomplete and misleading. Option C refers to the concept of species as the lowest category but does not capture its complete definition as provided in NCERT.

q: Which of the following pairs of taxonomic aids and their primary purposes is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Monograph — Provides information on any one taxon
Flora — Contains a list of plants found in a particular area with their description
Museum — Stores only wet specimens preserved in formalin for reference
Key — Used for identification of organisms based on similarities and differences
e: A museum is a taxonomic aid that houses collections of both preserved specimens (in fluids/formalin — wet specimens) AND dry preserved specimens, as well as skeletons, models, and photographs. It is NOT limited to only wet specimens. Hence option C is incorrectly matched. Monographs cover one particular taxon in detail, Flora describes plants of a given area, and Keys are aids for identification — all correctly matched.

q: All living organisms are linked to one another because
o: they have common genetic material of exactly the same type.
they share common genetic material but to varying degrees.
e: All living organisms share genetic material (nucleic acids) as the basis of heredity, but the specific genetic content, complexity, and cellular organisation vary considerably across different groups of organisms — it is not identical across all life forms.

q: A biologist identifies a new organism. It belongs to the same family as Panthera leo but a different genus. Which of the following pairs could represent its classification?
e: Panthera leo (lion) belongs to Family Felidae. If the new organism belongs to the same family (Felidae) but a different genus, it could belong to genus Felis (e.g., domestic cat, Felis catus). Canidae and Ursidae are different families entirely.

q: Which of the following statements best explains why reproduction is NOT considered an all-inclusive defining characteristic of life?
o: Reproduction requires two organisms and hence is not a property of an individual
Worker bees and mules are living organisms that do not reproduce, yet they clearly exhibit other properties of life
Viruses can reproduce and hence reproduction cannot distinguish living from non-living
Reproduction only occurs in multicellular organisms, not in unicellular ones
e: Reproduction is not an all-inclusive characteristic because certain living organisms like mules (sterile hybrids) and worker bees are incapable of reproduction, yet they are undeniably alive. This shows reproduction alone cannot define life universally.

q: A taxonomic key used to identify plants and animals works on the principle of:
o: Phenetics — grouping based purely on overall morphological similarity
Offering a series of contrasting characters in pairs (couplets) to lead to identification
Phylogenetic — grouping based solely on evolutionary relationships
Listing all characters of organisms alphabetically for comparison
e: Taxonomic keys are analytical tools based on contrasting characters presented in pairs called couplets. At each step, one of two contrasting characters is chosen, and this process is repeated until the organism is identified. They are used in field guides and manuals.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Family, (B) Genus, (C) Class, (D) Phylum, (E) Order
List-II: (I) Sapindales, (II) Dicotyledonae, (III) Anacardiaceae, (IV) Angiospermae, (V) Mangifera
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: For the mango plant's taxonomic hierarchy: Family = Anacardiaceae (III), Genus = Mangifera (V), Class = Dicotyledonae (II), Phylum = Angiospermae (IV), Order = Sapindales (I). So A-III, B-V, C-II, D-IV, E-I.

q: In the taxonomic hierarchy, which of the following represents the correct descending order from the highest to the lowest category?
o: Kingdom → Phylum → Order → Class → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Family → Order → Genus → Species
e: The correct descending taxonomic hierarchy is: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. A common mnemonic is 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.' This is the standard classification system used in biological taxonomy.

q: Which of the following statements about growth in living organisms is CORRECT?
o: Growth in plants is limited to certain phases of life, unlike animals where it is continuous.
Growth in living organisms always occurs from inside (intrinsic growth), unlike non-living objects.
Non-living objects like mountains also show intrinsic growth similar to living organisms.
Growth in living organisms requires addition of new cells, so unicellular organisms cannot grow.
e: Growth in living organisms occurs from within (intrinsically) due to the synthesis of new protoplasm. This is called intrinsic growth. In contrast, non-living objects like mountains and crystals grow by external addition of material (extrinsic growth). Unicellular organisms also grow by increase in cell size and mass. Growth in plants is continuous (in meristematic regions), unlike animals which stop growing after maturity.

q: Which of the following best explains why metabolism is considered a defining characteristic of life?
o: Metabolic reactions only occur in multicellular organisms, making them truly alive.
The sum of all chemical reactions occurring in a living body, which can be demonstrated in a cell-free system, still defines life.
No living organism can survive without an external supply of metabolic substrates from the environment.
Metabolic reactions are unique to living organisms and cannot be demonstrated outside a living system.
e: Metabolism is the sum total of all chemical reactions occurring in a living body. While isolated metabolic reactions can be demonstrated in vitro (in cell-free systems), the isolated reactions outside the body are not living. It is the totality of metabolic reactions occurring in a living context that defines life. All living organisms without exception have metabolism, making it a defining criterion of life.

q: As we go from species to kingdom in a taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics
e: Moving up the hierarchy from species towards kingdom, each level includes more diverse organisms, so the number of shared/common characteristics among them decreases.

q: The taxonomic unit 'Phylum' in the classification of animals is equivalent to which hierarchical level in the classification of plants?
e: In plant taxonomy, 'Division' is the rank equivalent to 'Phylum' used in animal taxonomy, both sitting between Kingdom and Class.

q: A taxonomic key is one of the taxonomic tools used in the identification and classification of plants and animals. It is used in the preparation of
e: Taxonomic keys, consisting of a series of contrasting character choices, are used as identification aids in both monographs (detailed accounts of a single taxon) and floras (accounts of plants of an area).

q: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of living organisms?
e: While growth and response to stimuli can also be observed in some non-living systems (e.g., crystals growing, or metals responding to temperature), reproduction — self-replication leading to increase in number of individuals of the same kind — has no true parallel in the non-living world, making it the most defining characteristic of living organisms.

q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes growth in living organisms from growth in non-living objects?
o: Non-living objects cannot grow at all
Growth in living organisms is always external, whereas in non-living objects it is internal
Growth in living organisms occurs by cell division from inside, whereas in non-living objects growth is by accumulation of material on the surface
Living organisms grow only during a specific period of their life cycle
e: Growth in living organisms is intrinsic — it occurs from inside by cell division and differentiation. In contrast, non-living objects like crystals or mountains grow by addition of material on their external surface (extrinsic growth).

q: Systematics differs from taxonomy primarily in that systematics:
o: Only deals with nomenclature and classification of organisms
Takes into account evolutionary and phylogenetic relationships between organisms
Is limited to the study of morphological characters of organisms
Does not involve classification of organisms
e: Taxonomy involves identification, nomenclature, and classification. Systematics goes further — it takes into account evolutionary relationships and phylogenetic history of organisms. The word 'systematics' comes from the Latin word 'systema' meaning systematic arrangement.

q: Approximately how many species of plants and animals have been described so far on Earth, as mentioned in NCERT?
e: As per the NCERT Class 11 Biology textbook, more than 1.5 million species of animals and plants have been described so far. The actual total biodiversity on Earth is estimated to be much higher.

q: Which of the following rules is NOT followed in binomial nomenclature?
o: The generic name starts with a capital letter
The scientific name should be italicized when printed
The name of the author appears in full after the specific epithet
The specific epithet starts with a capital letter
e: In binomial nomenclature, the generic name begins with a capital letter while the specific epithet (species name) begins with a small letter. For example, Mangifera indica. The author's name may appear abbreviated after the name, e.g., Mangifera indica Linn.

q: Movement and accumulation of ions across a membrane against their concentration gradient can be explained by:
e: Active transport uses energy (ATP) to move ions and molecules across a membrane against their concentration gradient, unlike passive transport, facilitated diffusion, or osmosis, which all move substances along their gradient.

q: Xylem translocates:
o: Water mineral salts and some organic nitrogen only
Water mineral salts some organic nitrogen and hormones
e: Xylem translocates water, mineral salts, some organic nitrogen compounds, and hormones (like cytokinins synthesized in roots) upward to the shoot system.

q: What is the direction of movement of sugars in phloem?
e: Sugars move bi-directionally in phloem, from source to sink, which can be upward or downward depending on the location of the source (site of synthesis) and sink (site of storage/utilization).

q: Addition of more solutes in a given solution will:
o: not affect the water potential at all
e: Adding solutes to a solution decreases its solute potential, which in turn lowers (makes more negative) the overall water potential of the solution.

q: The water potential of pure water is:
o: More than zero but less than one
e: By convention, the water potential of pure water at standard temperature and pressure is taken to be zero, the maximum possible value, since any solute added lowers it below zero.

q: A plant cell is placed in a solution and its turgor pressure becomes zero. This state of the cell is called:
e: Incipient plasmolysis is the condition when the turgor pressure (pressure potential) of the cell becomes exactly zero. At this point, the cell is neither gaining nor losing water by osmosis, and the protoplast just begins to pull away from the cell wall. Flaccidity refers to a limp state but turgor pressure is not necessarily zero; plasmolysis is a further stage where the protoplast actually shrinks away from the cell wall.

q: The form of sugar transported through phloem is
e: Sucrose, a disaccharide, is the primary form in which sugar (photosynthate) is transported through phloem tissue in plants.

q: Which of the following is an example of imbibition?
o: Uptake of water by root hair.
Swelling of a seed when put in soil.
e: Imbibition is the absorption of water by solid hydrophilic (colloidal) substances without forming a true solution, as seen when a dry seed swells after absorbing water from the soil.

q: Water potential of pure water at standard temperature is equal to
e: By convention, pure water at standard atmospheric pressure and temperature is assigned a water potential of zero, serving as the reference point against which all other water potentials are measured.

q:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I: (a) Cohesion, (b) Adhesion, (c) Surface tension, (d) Guttation
List-II: (i) More attraction in liquid phase, (ii) Mutual attraction among water molecules, (iii) Water loss in liquid phase, (iv) Attraction towards polar surfaces
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
(1) a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii
(2) a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii
(3) a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i
(4) a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii
e: Cohesion = mutual attraction among water molecules (ii); Adhesion = attraction towards polar surfaces (iv); Surface tension = more attraction in liquid phase (i); Guttation = water loss in liquid phase (iii). So a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

q: According to the Pressure Flow (Mass Flow) hypothesis of phloem transport, which of the following sequences correctly describes the movement of sucrose from source to sink?
o: Sucrose loaded into phloem at source → water moves in by osmosis → high turgor at source pushes sap toward sink → sucrose unloaded at sink → water exits phloem at sink.
Sucrose loaded into phloem at sink → water moves out by osmosis → low turgor at sink pulls sap from source → sucrose unloaded at source.
Water moves into phloem at source by active transport → sucrose follows passively → sap moves toward sink by diffusion.
Sucrose moves from source to sink entirely by symplastic diffusion without any involvement of turgor pressure.
e: According to Munch's Pressure Flow hypothesis: (1) Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source (e.g., leaf), increasing solute concentration. (2) This decreases the water potential of phloem sap, causing water to enter by osmosis from the xylem/surrounding cells, building high turgor pressure at the source end. (3) At the sink (e.g., root, fruit), sucrose is unloaded and used or stored, lowering the solute concentration. (4) Water then exits the phloem at the sink, reducing turgor pressure there. (5) The resulting turgor pressure gradient drives bulk flow of phloem sap from high pressure (source) to low pressure (sink). This is a pressure-driven mass flow mechanism.

t: Transpiration - Cohesion-Tension Theory and Cooling Effect
q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The forces generated by transpiration can lift a xylem-sized column of water over 130 meters height. Statement II: Transpiration cools leaf surfaces sometimes 10 to 15 degrees, by evaporative cooling. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
e: Both statements are correct per the NCERT textbook — the forces generated by transpiration pull (cohesion-tension) can lift water columns over 130 meters, and transpiration provides evaporative cooling that can lower leaf surface temperature by 10 to 15 degrees in some cases.

t: Water Properties - Cohesion, Adhesion, Surface Tension, Guttation
q: Match List I with List II: A. Cohesion, B. Adhesion, C. Surface tension, D. Guttation. List II: I. More attraction in liquid phase, II. Mutual attraction among water molecules, III. Water loss in liquid phase, IV. Attraction towards polar surfaces. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Cohesion is the mutual attraction among water molecules (A-II). Adhesion is attraction of water molecules towards polar surfaces (B-IV). Surface tension results from greater attraction among molecules in the liquid phase than towards the air (C-I). Guttation is the loss of water in the liquid phase from leaf margins (D-III). So the correct match is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

q: A few drops of sap were collected by cutting across a plant stem by a suitable method. The sap was tested chemically. Which one of the following test results indicates that it is phloem sap?
e: Phloem sap is alkaline (slightly basic, pH ~8), while xylem sap tends to be acidic; this distinguishes phloem sap in the test.

q: The chemical test for phloem sap shows that it is usually:
e: Phloem sap is slightly alkaline (pH around 8-8.5), unlike xylem sap which tends to be acidic.

q: Grass leaves curl inwards during very dry weather. Select the most appropriate reason from the following:
o: Shrinkage of air spaces in spongy mesophyll
e: Grass leaves curl inward during dry weather due to flaccidity (loss of turgor) of bulliform cells, which reduces water loss by decreasing the exposed leaf surface area.

q: 'Girdling Experiment' was performed by Plant Physiologists to identify the plant tissue through which:
o: for both water and food transportation
e: The girdling (ringing) experiment involves removing a ring of bark (including phloem) from a tree stem. Since the region above the girdle swells (accumulation of food) while the tree continues to survive (water still moves via xylem), this experiment demonstrated that food is transported through phloem.

q: Which of the following is not observed during apoplastic pathway?
o: Movement of water occurs through intercellular spaces and wall of the cells
The movement does not involve crossing of cell membrane
The movement is aided by cytoplasmic streaming
Apoplast is continuous and does not provide any barrier to water movement
e: Cytoplasmic streaming is associated with the symplastic pathway (movement through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata), not the apoplastic pathway, which involves movement through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing membranes or involving cytoplasm.

q: Which of the following facilitates opening of stomatal aperture?
o: Decrease in turgidity of guard cells
Radial orientation of cellulose microfibrils in the cell wall of guard cells
Longitudinal orientation of cellulose microfibrils in the cell wall of guard cells
Contraction of outer wall of guard cells
e: The radial (micellation) orientation of cellulose microfibrils in the guard cell wall causes the guard cells to bulge outward more at the thinner outer wall when turgid, bowing the pair apart and opening the stomatal pore.

t: Guttation and loss of water from leaf tips
q: The process responsible for facilitating loss of water in liquid form from the tip of grass blades at night and in early morning is:
e: Guttation, the loss of water in liquid form from leaf tips (especially of grasses), occurs due to root pressure pushing water up through the xylem when transpiration is minimal (at night/early morning).

q: Which of the following correctly explains the mechanism by which stomata open in the presence of light?
o: Light causes breakdown of starch to glucose in guard cells, increasing osmotic concentration and causing water influx.
Light activates photosynthesis in mesophyll cells, which directly pumps K⁺ ions into guard cells.
Light stimulates active transport of K⁺ ions out of guard cells, reducing their osmotic pressure.
Light triggers breakdown of ATP in guard cells, releasing energy that directly inflates them.
e: In the presence of light, starch (insoluble) in guard cells is converted to glucose (soluble), increasing the osmotic concentration of guard cells. This leads to endosmosis — water moves into guard cells from surrounding cells. The increased turgor pressure causes the thin outer wall of guard cells to stretch outward and the thick inner wall to curve, thus opening the stomatal pore. (Note: The K⁺ ion hypothesis is also accepted, but among the given options, the starch-glucose conversion explanation is the one that is correctly stated.)

q: An experiment shows that mineral ion absorption by root cells continues even when the concentration of ions inside the root is already higher than in the external soil solution. This observation best demonstrates:
o: Osmosis, because water carries minerals along with it into the root.
Passive transport along an electrochemical gradient.
Active transport requiring metabolic energy against the concentration gradient.
Facilitated diffusion through specific carrier proteins down the gradient.
e: Mineral ions are often absorbed against their concentration gradient (from lower concentration outside to higher concentration inside root cells). This type of transport requires expenditure of metabolic energy (ATP) and is called active transport. Passive transport and facilitated diffusion both occur along the concentration/electrochemical gradient and do not require energy, so they cannot explain absorption against the gradient. Osmosis involves movement of water, not mineral ions.

q: Which of the following statements does not apply to reverse osmosis?
o: It is used for water purification.
In this technique, pressure greater than osmotic pressure is applied to the system.
e: Reverse osmosis requires externally applied pressure (greater than the osmotic pressure) to force water across a membrane against its natural gradient — this makes it an active process, not a passive one.

q: Which one of the following will not directly affect transpiration?
e: Transpiration rate is directly influenced by environmental factors like temperature, light, and wind speed (which affect stomatal opening and evaporation), but chlorophyll content relates to photosynthesis, not transpiration directly.

q: The process of guttation takes place
o: when the root pressure is high and the rate of transpiration is low.
when the root pressure is low and the rate of transpiration is high.
when the root pressure equals the rate of transpiration.
when both the root pressure and rate of transpiration are high.
e: Guttation (exudation of water droplets from leaf margins) occurs under conditions of high root pressure combined with low transpiration (such as high humidity or early morning), when excess water is forced out through specialised pores.

q: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
e: 2-Butanol (CH3-CHOH-CH2-CH3) has the hydroxyl group attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbons, making it a secondary alcohol. 1-Butanol and 2-methyl-1-propanol are primary alcohols, while 2-methyl-2-propanol is a tertiary alcohol.

q: The boiling points of alcohols are higher than those of alkanes with comparable molecular masses. This is primarily due to:
o: Greater van der Waals forces in alcohols
Intermolecular hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules
The polar C–O bond increasing molecular polarity alone
Alcohols having higher molecular weights than alkanes
e: Alcohols exhibit strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding (O–H···O) due to the highly electronegative oxygen atom bonded to hydrogen. This significantly increases their boiling points compared to alkanes of similar molecular mass, which only have weaker van der Waals/London dispersion forces.

q: The IUPAC name of m-cresol is
e: m-Cresol is the common name for 3-methylphenol, a phenol with a methyl substituent at the meta (3-) position relative to the hydroxyl group.

t: Structural and Stereoisomers of Cyclic Ethers
q: Total number of possible isomers (both structural as well as stereoisomers) of cyclic ethers of molecular formula C4H8O is :
e: Cyclic ethers with formula C4H8O include: oxetane derivatives (4-membered ring with O) and epoxide derivatives (3-membered ring with O + extra carbons), and tetrahydrofuran. Counting all structural isomers plus their stereoisomers (cis/trans and enantiomers where applicable) gives a total of 10 isomers.

q: Consider the following reaction: Benzyl phenyl ether (PhCH2-O-Ph) reacts with HI/Δ to give A + B. Identify products A and B.
o: A = Benzyl alcohol (PhCH2OH) and B = 4-iodophenyl derivative
A = Benzyl iodide (PhCH2I) and B = Phenol (PhOH)
e: In the cleavage of an unsymmetrical ether like benzyl phenyl ether with HI, the iodide ion attacks the benzylic carbon (SN1-like, since the benzylic cation is highly stabilized), displacing the phenoxide as phenol, while the aryl-oxygen bond of the phenyl ring is not cleaved (aryl ethers do not undergo SN2 attack at the aromatic carbon). This gives A = benzyl iodide (PhCH2I) and B = phenol (PhOH).

q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The acidic strength of monosubstituted nitrophenol is higher than phenol because of electron withdrawing nitro group.
Statement II: o-nitrophenol, m-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol will have same acidic strength as they have one nitro group attached to the phenolic ring.
In the light of the above statement, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
e: Statement I is correct - nitro group is electron withdrawing, increasing acidic strength of nitrophenol compared to phenol. Statement II is incorrect because o-, m-, and p-nitrophenol do NOT have the same acidic strength; they differ due to differences in resonance and inductive effects based on position (order: p-nitrophenol > o-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol in Ka, though exact order can vary by effect considered).

q: The compound that is most difficult to protonate is:
e: In phenol, the lone pair on the oxygen atom is delocalised into the benzene ring through resonance, which reduces the electron density available on oxygen for protonation, making phenol the most difficult to protonate among the given options.

q: Phenol undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution more readily than benzene. When phenol reacts with dilute HNO3 at room temperature, the major products are:
e: With dilute HNO3 at room temperature, phenol undergoes mononitration giving a mixture of ortho (2-nitrophenol) and para (4-nitrophenol) products because the –OH group is an ortho/para director. 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) is formed only with concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4.

q: When diethyl ether is treated with excess HI, the products formed are:
o: Two moles of ethyl iodide and one mole of water
e: With excess HI, diethyl ether first cleaves to give ethanol and ethyl iodide (with 1 mol HI). The ethanol then reacts with the second equivalent of HI to give another mole of ethyl iodide and water. So the overall reaction with excess HI gives 2 mol ethyl iodide (C2H5I) and 1 mol water.

q: 2-methylbutan-2-ol undergoes acid-catalyzed dehydration. According to Saytzeff's rule, the major alkene product is:
e: 2-Methylbutan-2-ol on dehydration forms a tertiary carbocation intermediate. According to Saytzeff's rule, the major product is the more substituted (more stable) alkene. Elimination of H from C1 gives 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted, more stable), while elimination from C3 gives 2-methylbut-1-ene (less substituted). Hence, 2-methylbut-2-ene is the major product.

q: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, phenol is treated with CHCl3 and NaOH. The initial electrophile attacking the ring is:
e: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, CHCl3 is treated with strong base (NaOH), which causes α-elimination to form dichlorocarbene (:CCl2), a highly reactive electrophilic intermediate. This dichlorocarbene attacks the electron-rich ortho position of the phenoxide ion, eventually giving salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) after hydrolysis.

t: Reactions of Ethers — Cleavage by HI
q: When anisole (methoxybenzene, C6H5–O–CH3) is treated with excess HI, which of the following best describes the products formed?
o: Chlorobenzene and methanol, because the C–O bond on the methyl side cleaves preferentially
Phenol and iodomethane, formed because the weaker alkyl C–O bond cleaves to give a carbocation that reacts with I⁻
Iodobenzene and methanol, because the aryl C–O bond is weaker than the alkyl C–O bond in this ether
Phenol and iodomethane initially; with excess HI, phenol is further converted to iodobenzene
e: In the acid-catalyzed cleavage of ethers by HI, the protonated ether undergoes nucleophilic attack by I⁻. In aryl alkyl ethers like anisole, the aryl C–O bond cannot be cleaved under normal conditions because it has partial double-bond character due to resonance between the oxygen lone pairs and the ring (making it very strong). Therefore, cleavage always occurs at the weaker alkyl C–O bond. I⁻ attacks the methyl carbon (SN2), yielding phenol (C6H5OH) and iodomethane (CH3I). Option A is wrong as no chlorine is involved. Option C is wrong because the aryl C–O bond is actually stronger, not weaker. Option D is incorrect because phenol does not react further with HI to give iodobenzene under standard conditions — electrophilic aromatic substitution would give iodophenol, not iodobenzene.

t: Product of Toluene's Side-Chain Chlorination Followed by Hydrolysis
q: Monochlorination of toluene in sunlight, followed by hydrolysis with aq. NaOH, yields
e: Chlorination in sunlight proceeds by a free-radical mechanism at the benzylic (side-chain methyl) position rather than on the aromatic ring, converting toluene to benzyl chloride (C6H5CH2Cl). Subsequent hydrolysis of this benzylic halide with aqueous NaOH then gives benzyl alcohol (C6H5CH2OH), not a ring-substituted cresol.

t: Counting Chiral Alcohols with Formula C4H10O
q: How many alcohols with molecular formula C4H10O are chiral in nature?
e: The four alcohols with formula C4H10O are 1-butanol, 2-butanol, 2-methyl-1-propanol (isobutanol), and 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butanol). Only 2-butanol (CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3) has a carbon bonded to four different groups (OH, H, CH3, C2H5), making it the sole chiral alcohol among them.

q: Lucas test distinguishes:
e: Lucas test (ZnCl2+conc.HCl): 3° alcohol → turbid immediately; 2° → turbid in 5 min (warm); 1° → no turbidity at room temp. Identifies class of alcohol.

q: The compound which shows metamerism is:
e: C4H10O is applicable for homologous series ether (-O-), a bivalent functional group, and ether with minimum four carbons shows metamerism. CH3-CH2-O-CH2-CH3 and CH3-O-CH2-CH2-CH3 are metamers.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the organic compound formed in the following chemical reaction? Acetone --(i) C2H5MgBr, dry Ether; (ii) H2O, H+--> Product
e: Acetone (CH3-CO-CH3) reacts with C2H5MgBr (Grignard reagent) then H3O+ workup to give 2-methyl butan-2-ol: CH3-C(OH)(C2H5)-CH3

q: The structure of intermediate A in the following reaction is: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) + O2 -> A, then A + H+/H2O -> Phenol + Acetone
o: Phenyl-O-O-CH(CH3)-CH3 structure (isopropyl peroxide attached via O-O to phenyl ring at CH)
e: In the cumene process, cumene reacts with O2 to form cumene hydroperoxide (intermediate A), where the tertiary C-H of the isopropyl group is converted to C-O-O-H. Acid hydrolysis of cumene hydroperoxide then gives phenol and acetone.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: In Lucas test, primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols are distinguished on the basis of their reactivity with conc. HCl + ZnCl2, known as Lucas Reagent. Statement II: Primary alcohols are most reactive and immediately produce turbidity at room temperature on reaction with Lucas Reagent. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Statement I is correct: the Lucas test uses conc. HCl + ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent) and differentiates alcohols by reactivity (rate of turbidity formation). Statement II is incorrect: it is tertiary alcohols that react immediately at room temperature, while primary alcohols react very slowly (need heating) with Lucas reagent.

q: The heating of phenyl-methyl ethers with HI produces:
e: In aryl-alkyl ethers like phenyl methyl ether (anisole), cleavage with HI always occurs such that the alkyl-oxygen bond breaks (since aryl-oxygen bond is stronger due to partial double bond character), giving phenol and methyl iodide.

q: The most suitable method of separation of 1:1 mixture of ortho and para-nitrophenols is:
e: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, making it volatile and steam-distillable, while p-nitrophenol has intermolecular hydrogen bonding, making it less volatile. This difference allows separation of the mixture by steam distillation.

q: Which one is the most acidic compound? (Options: phenol; p-nitrophenol; 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid); p-cresol)
e: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid) is the most acidic because the three strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups stabilise the phenoxide ion through resonance and inductive effects far more than a single nitro group or an electron-donating methyl group.

q: In the reaction of phenol with CHCl3 and NaOH to give the sodium salt of salicylaldehyde, the electrophile involved is
e: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, NaOH generates dichlorocarbene (:CCl2) from CHCl3 by alpha-elimination, which acts as the electrophile attacking the phenoxide ring.

q: The compound A on treatment with Na gives B, and with PCl5 gives C. B and C react together to give diethyl ether. A, B and C are in the order
e: A is ethanol (C2H5OH). With Na it gives sodium ethoxide B (C2H5ONa) releasing H2. With PCl5 it gives ethyl chloride C (C2H5Cl). B and C then react via Williamson synthesis to give diethyl ether.

q: Reaction between acetone and methylmagnesium chloride followed by hydrolysis will give:
e: Acetone (a ketone) reacting with a Grignard reagent (CH3MgCl) followed by hydrolysis gives a tertiary alcohol: (CH3)2C(CH3)OH, which is tert-butyl alcohol.

t: Cleavage of aryl alkyl ethers with HI
q: Anisole on cleavage with HI gives:
e: In the cleavage of anisole (aryl alkyl ether) with HI, the alkyl-oxygen bond is cleaved (due to the instability of forming an aryl cation), giving phenol and methyl iodide (CH3I).

q: Which reagent converts an aldehyde to a primary alcohol and a ketone to a secondary alcohol via hydride transfer?
e: Both LiAlH4 (in dry ether) and NaBH4 (in methanol/ethanol) are hydride reducing agents that reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols via nucleophilic hydride transfer. H2/Ni also reduces carbonyls but by a heterogeneous catalytic mechanism, not hydride transfer.

q: When ethanol reacts with excess HI, the major product is:
e: When ethanol reacts with HI, the OH group is protonated and then the iodide ion acts as a nucleophile to displace water in an SN2 reaction, giving ethyl iodide (iodoethane) and water. This is the standard nucleophilic substitution of alcohols with halogen acids.

q: Which of the following correctly explains why phenol is more acidic than ethanol?
o: Phenol has a higher molecular weight than ethanol
The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance with the aromatic ring, delocalizing the negative charge
The O–H bond in phenol is weaker than in ethanol
Phenol undergoes hydrogen bonding more readily than ethanol
e: Phenol is more acidic (pKa ~10) than ethanol (pKa ~16) because the phenoxide ion formed after deprotonation is stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge into the aromatic ring. No such stabilization exists for the ethoxide ion.

q: Williamson's synthesis is used to prepare ethers. Which combination of reactants will successfully give methyl phenyl ether (anisole)?
e: Williamson's synthesis involves reaction of an alkoxide/phenoxide ion with an alkyl halide via SN2. Sodium phenoxide (C6H5ONa) reacting with methyl bromide (CH3Br) gives anisole (C6H5OCH3). Option C fails because bromobenzene (an aryl halide) does not undergo SN2 due to sp2 carbon. Option A is Fischer–Speier esterification conditions, not ether synthesis.

q: Which of the following correctly explains why phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16)?
o: The O–H bond in phenol is stronger due to the presence of the benzene ring, making proton release easier
The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge into the benzene ring, which is not possible in ethoxide ion
Phenol has a higher molecular mass, which increases the inductive effect and stabilizes the conjugate base
The sp2 carbon attached to –OH in phenol withdraws electrons by hyperconjugation, weakening the O–H bond
e: When phenol loses a proton, the phenoxide ion formed is stabilized by resonance. The negative charge on oxygen is delocalized into the benzene ring through six resonance structures, spreading the charge and lowering the energy of the conjugate base. Ethoxide ion (from ethanol) cannot undergo such delocalization because the oxygen is attached to an sp3 carbon with no π system available. Greater stability of the conjugate base means greater acidity, so phenol is significantly more acidic than ethanol. Options A and C are incorrect — bond strength and molecular mass are not the governing factors here. Option D confuses hyperconjugation with resonance.

t: Compound That Reacts with Aqueous NaOH
q: Which of the following compounds will react with sodium hydroxide solution in water?
e: Phenol (C6H5OH) is acidic enough (its phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the aromatic ring) to react with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide and water, unlike benzyl alcohol, tert-butanol, or ethanol, which are far weaker acids and do not react with NaOH.

t: Comparing the Acidity of Phenol and o-Nitrophenol
q: Phenol is less acidic than
e: The electron-withdrawing nitro group in o-nitrophenol stabilises the phenoxide ion through resonance and induction, making o-nitrophenol considerably more acidic than plain phenol; electron-donating groups like methyl or methoxy, by contrast, make phenol less acidic, not more.

q: Which of the following is most acidic?
e: m-Chlorophenol is the most acidic because the electron-withdrawing chlorine substituent further stabilises the phenoxide ion compared to plain phenol, while benzyl alcohol and cyclohexanol are simple (non-aromatic-stabilised) alcohols and are far weaker acids than any phenol.

q: Weight (g) of two moles of the organic compound, which is obtained by heating sodium ethanoate with sodium hydroxide in presence of calcium oxide, is:
e: Heating sodium ethanoate (CH3COONa) with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) causes decarboxylation to give methane (CH4), which has a molecular weight of 16 g/mol. The weight of two moles of CH4 is 2 x 16 = 32 g.

t: Grignard Reaction with Nitriles and Ketones
q: The major product of the following reaction is: Ph-CO-CH2-CH2-CN treated with (i) CH3MgBr (excess) (ii) H3O+
o: Ph-C(CH3)(OH)-CH2-CN (Grignard adds only to nitrile, ketone untouched)
