Ph-C(CH3)(OH)-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 (Grignard adds to both ketone and nitrile, nitrile converted to methyl ketone after hydrolysis)
Ph-CH(CH3)-OH...C(CH3)2-OH (double addition at both carbons, no selectivity)
Ph-CO-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 (nitrile converted to ketone, original ketone untouched)
e: Excess CH3MgBr first adds to the more electrophilic ketone carbonyl, forming a tertiary alkoxide with a pendant nitrile; the nitrile then also reacts with the Grignard reagent to form a magnesium ketimine salt. Aqueous acidic workup (H3O+) hydrolyzes the ketimine to a methyl ketone and protonates the alkoxide to a tertiary alcohol, giving Ph-C(CH3)(OH)-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3.

q: Identify the final product [D] obtained in the following sequence of reactions: CH3CHO --(i) LiAlH4 (ii) H3O+--> [A] --H2SO4/Δ--> [B] --HBr--> [C], then [C] is treated with bromobenzene and Na/dry ether to give D.
o: Ethylbenzene (a benzene ring with an ethyl substituent)
e: CH3CHO is reduced by LiAlH4/H3O+ to ethanol [A]. Ethanol undergoes acid-catalyzed dehydration with H2SO4/Δ to give ethylene [B]. Ethylene reacts with HBr to give ethyl bromide [C]. Finally, ethyl bromide reacts with bromobenzene in the presence of Na/dry ether via the Wurtz-Fittig reaction, coupling the alkyl and aryl halides to give ethylbenzene [D].

q: 2,2-dimethylcyclopentan-1-one is reacted with PhCHO (benzaldehyde) in the presence of NaOH and heat (a Claisen-Schmidt / crossed aldol condensation). The compound that CANNOT be obtained from this reaction is the one whose structure, instead of bearing the expected exocyclic benzylidene (=CH-Ph) group at C5 of the cyclopentanone ring, shows the ring connected by a direct single bond to a second 2,2-dimethylcyclopentene ring (i.e., with the carbon-carbon double bond located inside the second ring rather than exocyclic, and no phenyl group present at all) -- which option below represents this impossible product?
o: 2,2-dimethyl-5-(2,2-dimethylcyclopentylidene)cyclopentan-1-one (exocyclic alkylidene linked to a second dimethylcyclopentane ring instead of phenyl)
(Z)-2,2-dimethyl-5-benzylidenecyclopentan-1-one (same connectivity as option A, opposite alkene geometry)
2,2-dimethyl-5-(4,4-dimethylcyclopent-1-en-1-yl)cyclopentan-1-one (single C-C bond to a ring bearing an internal double bond, no phenyl group)
e: C2 of 2,2-dimethylcyclopentanone bears two methyl groups and has no alpha-hydrogens, so enolization and aldol addition can only occur at C5. Reaction with PhCHO (which has no alpha-hydrogens of its own and so cannot self-condense) proceeds as a crossed Claisen-Schmidt condensation: the C5 enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of PhCHO, and base-catalyzed dehydration gives an exocyclic C5=CH-Ph double bond conjugated with the ring carbonyl. This explains options (1) and (3) (E/Z isomers of the same benzylidene product) as valid, and even option (2) can be rationalized as a self-aldol product at C5 with another ketone molecule. However, option (4) shows the ring attached by a plain single bond to a second ring bearing an internal (endocyclic) double bond with no phenyl group anywhere -- this connectivity cannot arise from any aldol addition/dehydration pathway in this reaction, so it cannot be obtained.

t: Friedel-Crafts Acylation Followed by Haloform Reaction
q:
For the following reaction sequence, choose the correct option:
Benzene --[i. CH3COCl, AlCl3; ii. NaOCl]--> P + Q
o: P and Q are aromatic compounds.
If P gives a carboxylic acid on acidification, Q gives a poisonous gas on exposure to air and light.
Both P and Q are carbonyl compounds.
If P is the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid, Q is a primary alcohol.
e: Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with CH3COCl/AlCl3 gives acetophenone (PhCOCH3). Treatment with NaOCl causes a haloform-type reaction on the methyl ketone, cleaving it into sodium benzoate (P, PhCOO⁻Na⁺) and chloroform (Q, CHCl3). P on acidification gives benzoic acid (a carboxylic acid). Chloroform (Q) is well known to slowly oxidize on exposure to air and light to form phosgene (COCl2), a highly poisonous gas -- which is why chloroform is stored in dark bottles with ethanol as a stabilizer. This matches option (2).

q: Toluene is treated with (i) CrO2Cl2, CS2 (Etard reaction) and then (ii) H3O+, to give compound P. Choose the correct option:
o: Compound P can be prepared by treating benzene with anhydrous AlCl3 and CH3COCl
On treatment with bromine water, compound P gives a white precipitate
Compound P is obtained by the hydrogenation of benzoyl chloride with Pd on BaSO4.
On treating compound P with saturated NaHCO3 solution, brisk effervescence is observed.
e: The Etard reaction (CrO2Cl2/CS2, then aqueous hydrolysis) converts toluene's methyl group selectively to an aldehyde, giving P = benzaldehyde (PhCHO), stopping at the aldehyde stage without over-oxidation. Benzaldehyde is also obtained by the Rosenmund reduction: controlled hydrogenation of benzoyl chloride (PhCOCl) using Pd catalyst poisoned with BaSO4, which selectively reduces the acid chloride to the aldehyde without further reduction to the alcohol. Benzene + AlCl3/CH3COCl gives acetophenone, not benzaldehyde (ruling out option 1). Benzaldehyde does not give a white precipitate with bromine water (that's characteristic of phenols), ruling out option 2. Benzaldehyde does not effervesce with NaHCO3 (it is not a carboxylic acid), ruling out option 4.

q: Match List-I with List-II. List-I: (a) Benzene + CO, HCl, Anhyd. AlCl3/CuCl (b) R-CO-CH3 + NaOX→ (c) R-CH2-OH + R'COOH, Conc. H2SO4 (d) R-CH2COOH, (i) X2/Red P (ii) H2O. List-II: (i) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (ii) Gattermann-Koch reaction (iii) Haloform reaction (iv) Esterification. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: (a) Benzene+CO+HCl with AlCl3/CuCl is Gattermann-Koch aldehyde synthesis (ii). (b) Methyl ketone+NaOX is Haloform reaction (iii) giving CHX3+RCOONa. (c) Alcohol+acid with H2SO4 is Esterification (iv). (d) Carboxylic acid+X2/RedP then H2O is Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (i)

q: The intermediate compound X in the following chemical reaction is: Toluene + CrO2Cl2, CS2 → X, then H3O+ → Benzaldehyde
e: This is the Etard reaction. The intermediate X formed is Ph-CH(OCrOHCl2)2, a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis with H3O+ gives benzaldehyde.

q: The product formed in the following chemical reaction is: 2-methyl-6-oxocyclohexyl group with a CH2-CO-OCH3 (methyl ester) side chain, treated with NaBH4/C2H5OH → ?
o: Ring ketone reduced to OH (ring C=O → CHOH), ester group (CH2-CO-OCH3) unchanged
Both ring ketone and ester carbonyl reduced to OH
Ring ketone reduced to OH and ester converted to CH2-CH2-OH (fully reduced)
Ring ketone unreduced, only ester carbonyl reduced to CH(OH)-CH3
e: NaBH4 selectively reduces ketones/aldehydes but does NOT reduce ester groups. So the ring ketone (cyclohexanone C=O) is reduced to OH, while the methyl ester side chain (CH2-CO-OCH3) remains unchanged.

q: Which among the given molecules (three bicyclic bridged ketones labeled I, II, III, with II having two phenyl substituents at the alpha carbon) can exhibit tautomerism?
e: Bridge carbon atom does not participate in tautomerism. Acidic alpha-hydrogen must be present for tautomerism; in II both alpha-hydrogens are replaced by phenyl groups (no acidic H), so only III (which retains an alpha-H not at the bridgehead) can tautomerize.

q: Which one of the following is not formed when acetone reacts with 2-pentanone in the presence of dilute NaOH followed by heating? (Four complex cross-aldol condensation product structures shown)
o: A specific cross-condensation product structure with branched ethyl substituents (option 2, an implausible over-substituted product)
e: In a cross-aldol condensation between acetone and 2-pentanone, several possible enolate/carbonyl combinations give different unsaturated ketone products. Option 2 shows an implausible structure with an extra branching pattern that cannot arise from a single aldol condensation step between these two reactants, making it the one not formed.

q: Of the following, which is the product formed when cyclohexanone undergoes aldol condensation followed by heating?
o: A bicyclohexylidene compound with a conjugated ketone (dehydrated aldol condensation product, an alpha,beta-unsaturated bicyclic ketone)
A bicyclohexyl compound bearing a hydroxyl group (the beta-hydroxy ketone, aldol addition product, not dehydrated)
A bicyclohexyl ketone bearing a hydroxyl group on the adjacent ring (an isomeric hydroxy-ketone)
e: Cyclohexanone undergoes self-aldol addition to form a beta-hydroxyketone, which on heating readily dehydrates (loses water) to give the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated bicyclic enone (the bicyclohexylidene ketone), the thermodynamically favoured aldol condensation product.

q: Consider the reactions: X (C2H6O) is treated with Cu at 573 K to give A. A reacts with [Ag(NH3)2]+ / -OH / heat to give a silver mirror. A also reacts with -OH / heat to give Y. A also reacts with semicarbazide (NH2-NH-CO-NH2) to give Z. Identify A, X, Y and Z.
o: A-Methoxymethane, X-Ethanoic acid, Y-Acetate ion, Z-hydrazine
e: X (C2H6O) is ethanol, which on dehydrogenation with Cu at 573K gives A, ethanal (acetaldehyde). Ethanal gives a positive Tollens' (silver mirror) test. Ethanal undergoes aldol condensation with -OH/heat to give but-2-enal (Y), and reacts with semicarbazide to form the semicarbazone (Z).

q: The IUPAC name of the compound OHC-CH(CH3)-CO-CH=CH2 (an aldehyde and ketone containing hex-4-enal skeleton with a methyl substituent) is ______.
e: Numbering the longest chain to give the principal characteristic group (the aldehyde, suffixed -al) the lowest locant, the aldehyde carbon is C1, the methyl substituent is at C2, the keto group at C3, and the double bond between C4-C5, giving the name 3-keto-2-methylhex-4-enal (as named in the official NTA key, using 'keto' as a substituent prefix since -al is the principal suffix).

q: Compound A, C8H10O, is found to react with NaOI (produced by reacting Y with NaOH) and yields a yellow precipitate with characteristic smell. A and Y are respectively
e: The iodoform (yellow precipitate) test is given by compounds with a CH3-CH(OH)- group or methyl ketones. C6H5-CH(OH)-CH3 (1-phenylethanol, C8H10O) has this structural feature and reacts with NaOI (formed from I2 and NaOH) to give the iodoform precipitate.

q: A mixture of 2.3 g formic acid and 4.5 g oxalic acid is treated with conc. H2SO4. The evolved gaseous mixture is passed through KOH pellets. Weight (in g) of the remaining product at STP will be
e: Formic acid (0.05 mol) with conc. H2SO4 gives CO + H2O (CO: 0.05 mol). Oxalic acid (0.05 mol) gives CO + CO2 + H2O (CO: 0.05 mol, CO2: 0.05 mol). KOH absorbs CO2 and H2O, leaving only CO gas: total CO = 0.1 mol = 0.1×28 = 2.8 g.

q: Which one of the following is not formed when acetone reacts with 2-pentanone in the presence of dilute NaOH followed by heating?
e: Among the possible cross/self aldol condensation products of acetone and 2-pentanone, compound (2) is not formed under these conditions.

q: Aldol condensation involves:
o: Aldehydes/ketones with OH⁻ to give β-hydroxy carbonyl compounds
e: Aldol: two carbonyl compounds (with α-H) + dilute NaOH → β-hydroxy carbonyl (aldol product). On heating, loses water → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (aldol condensation).

q: The correct order of decreasing acidity of the following aliphatic acids is : HCOOH, CH3COOH, (CH3)2CHCOOH, (CH3)3CCOOH
e: Acidity decreases as the +I (electron-donating) effect of alkyl groups increases, since more alkyl substitution destabilizes the carboxylate anion. HCOOH (no alkyl group) is most acidic, followed by CH3COOH, then (CH3)2CHCOOH, then (CH3)3CCOOH (most alkyl substitution, least acidic).

t: Partial Reduction of Esters to Aldehydes
q: Identify the suitable reagent for the following conversion: Methyl benzoate (PhCOOCH3) to benzaldehyde (PhCHO).
e: DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) is a mild reducing agent that partially reduces esters to aldehydes at low temperature, stopping at the aldehyde stage before over-reduction to alcohol. LiAlH4 would over-reduce the ester all the way to the alcohol.

q: Complete the following reaction: Cyclohexanone [A] reacts with HCN to give 1-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonitrile [B], which on treatment with conc. H2SO4 and heat (Δ) gives [C]. [C] is ________.
e: Cyclohexanone reacts with HCN to form the cyanohydrin [B] (1-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonitrile). On treatment with concentrated H2SO4 and heat, the nitrile is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid and the molecule simultaneously undergoes dehydration (loss of the OH as water), forming the α,β-unsaturated acid cyclohex-1-ene-1-carboxylic acid [C].

q: Identify product (A) in the following reaction: A cyclohexane ring bearing an acetyl group (COCH3) and a meta-substituted phenyl ring which itself bears another acetyl group (COCH3), treated with Zn-Hg / conc. HCl, gives (A) + 2H2O.
o: The diol formed by reducing both C=O to CH(OH) groups
The diol formed by reducing both C=O to CH2OH groups
The compound with both carbonyls reduced to CH3 groups directly on the rings
The compound with both carbonyls fully reduced to CH2 (ethyl-linked), i.e. an ethyl group on the cyclohexane ring and an ethyl group on the benzene ring
e: Zn-Hg/conc. HCl is the Clemmensen reduction, which reduces a carbonyl group (C=O) of a ketone completely to a methylene group (CH2), not just to an alcohol. Applied to both acetyl (COCH3) groups in this diketone, each is reduced to an ethyl group (CH2CH3), giving the product with an ethyl substituent on the cyclohexane ring and an ethyl substituent on the benzene ring, releasing 2H2O. Note: the solution's worked diagram shows this diethyl product even though the printed answer-key digit reads '2' — the diagram (matching option with ethyl groups) is taken as authoritative here since Clemmensen reduction converts C=O fully to CH2, not to CH-OH.

t: Tollens' Reagent - Selective Oxidation of Aldehydes
q: Identify the major product obtained in the following reaction: A benzene ring with an ortho-acetyl group (COCH3) and an ortho-aldehyde group (CHO) is treated with 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- (Tollens' reagent) and heat (Δ). Identify the major product.
o: The aldehyde reduced to a -CH(OH)- group while the ketone remains unchanged (COCH3 intact)
The aldehyde oxidized to a carboxylate (-COO-) group while the ketone (COCH3) remains unchanged
Both the aldehyde and the ketone converted to -CH(OH)- and -COO- respectively
Both carbonyl groups reduced to -CH(OH)- groups
e: Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH3)2]+/OH-) selectively oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylate ions (via the silver mirror test) but does not oxidize ketones. In this substrate, the -CHO group is oxidized to -COO-, while the -COCH3 (ketone) group remains unchanged, giving the major product with an intact acetyl group and a carboxylate group on the ring.

q: The correct structure of the product A formed in the reaction: 2-cyclohexenone + H2(gas, 1 atmosphere)/Pd-carbon, ethanol → A is:
o: Cyclohexanol (fully saturated OH, C=C reduced but C=O retained... )
e: Under mild conditions (1 atm H2, Pd/C), the C=C double bond conjugated with C=O is reduced preferentially while the C=O (carbonyl) multiple bond is not affected by Pd/C under these mild conditions, giving cyclohexanone as the product.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Products formed): (a) Cynohydrin (b) Acetal (c) Schiff's base (d) Oxime
List-II (Reaction of carbonyl Compound with): (i) NH2OH (ii) RNH2 (iii) alcohol (iv) HCN
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Cyanohydrin is formed from carbonyl compound + HCN (iv); Acetal from carbonyl compound + alcohol (iii); Schiff's base from carbonyl compound + RNH2 (ii); Oxime from carbonyl compound + NH2OH (i).

q: RMgX + CO2 --(dry ether)--> Y --(H3O+)--> RCOOH. What is Y in the above reaction?
e: Grignard reagent reacts with CO2 to form a magnesium salt of the carboxylic acid, RCOO-MgX (Y), which upon hydrolysis with H3O+ gives the carboxylic acid RCOOH.

q: The major product of the following reaction is: Phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid) + NH3, strong heating ->
e: Strong heating of phthalic acid with NH3 first forms the diamide, which then undergoes intramolecular cyclization with loss of NH3, forming the cyclic imide phthalimide as the major product.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The boiling points of aldehydes and ketones are higher than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular masses because of weak molecular association in aldehydes and ketones due to dipole-dipole interactions. Statement II: The boiling points of aldehydes and ketones are lower than the alcohols of similar molecular masses due to the absence of H-bonding. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct: aldehydes/ketones have higher boiling points than comparable hydrocarbons due to dipole-dipole interactions from the polar C=O group (Statement I), and lower boiling points than alcohols of similar mass because they cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds among themselves, unlike alcohols (Statement II).

q: RMgX + CO2 (dry ether) -> Y, then Y + H3O+ -> RCOOH. What is Y in the above reaction?
e: Grignard reagent RMgX reacts with CO2 to form a magnesium carboxylate salt intermediate, RCOO-Mg+X, which upon acid hydrolysis (H3O+) gives the carboxylic acid RCOOH.

q: Match List-I with List-II. List-I (Products formed): (a) Cyanohydrin (b) Acetal (c) Schiff's base (d) Oxime -- List-II (Reaction of carbonyl compound with): (i) NH2OH (ii) RNH2 (iii) alcohol (iv) HCN. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Cyanohydrin forms from reaction with HCN (iv). Acetal forms from reaction with alcohol (iii). Schiff's base forms from reaction with RNH2 (ii). Oxime forms from reaction with NH2OH (i). So a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.

q: Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of comparable molecular mass. It is due to their
o: more extensive association of carboxylic acid via van der Waals force of attraction
e: Carboxylic acid molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, typically existing as dimers, which requires more energy to break and results in higher boiling points.

q: Reaction between benzaldehyde and acetophenone in presence of dilute NaOH is known as:
e: Benzaldehyde (no alpha hydrogen) reacting with acetophenone (has alpha hydrogens) in the presence of dilute NaOH undergoes a crossed aldol condensation, where the enolate of acetophenone attacks the carbonyl of benzaldehyde.

q: The correct order of increasing acidic strength is
o: Phenol < Ethanol < Chloroacetic acid < Acetic acid
Ethanol < Phenol < Chloroacetic acid < Acetic acid
Ethanol < Phenol < Acetic acid < Chloroacetic acid
Chloroacetic acid < Acetic acid < Phenol < Ethanol
e: Ethanol is the weakest acid (its alkoxide is not stabilised), phenol is more acidic (its phenoxide is resonance-stabilised by the ring), acetic acid is a true carboxylic acid and more acidic still, and chloroacetic acid is the most acidic of all because the electron-withdrawing Cl further stabilises its conjugate base — giving the order Ethanol < Phenol < Acetic acid < Chloroacetic acid.

t: Alcohol That Gives Butanone on Oxidation
q: Which of the following compounds will give butanone on oxidation with alkaline KMnO4 solution?
e: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, and oxidation of secondary alcohols gives ketones — here, butan-2-one (butanone). Butan-1-ol is a primary alcohol, which is oxidised instead to butanoic acid by a strong oxidant like KMnO4, not to a ketone.

q: In Clemmensen reduction, the carbonyl compound is treated with
e: Clemmensen reduction converts an aldehyde or ketone's carbonyl group directly to a methylene (–CH2–) group using zinc amalgam [Zn(Hg)] in the presence of concentrated hydrochloric acid.

q: Which of the following is a secondary amine?
e: A secondary amine has two alkyl or aryl groups attached to the nitrogen atom. (CH₃)₂NH has two methyl groups on nitrogen, making it a secondary amine. CH₃NH₂ is primary, (CH₃)₃N is tertiary, and C₆H₅NH₂ (aniline) is a primary amine.

q: The carbylamine reaction (isocyanide test) is a characteristic test for:
e: The carbylamine reaction is specific to primary amines (both aliphatic and aromatic). When a primary amine is heated with chloroform (CHCl₃) and alcoholic KOH, a foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine) is formed: RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → RNC + 3KCl + 3H₂O. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this test, making it a distinguishing test for primary amines.

t: Product of Reducing Aromatic Nitro Compounds with Fe/HCl
q: Reduction of aromatic nitro compounds using Fe and HCl gives
e: Fe and HCl act as a mild reducing system that converts the nitro group (-NO2) on an aromatic ring into a primary amine group (-NH2), e.g. converting nitrobenzene to aniline.

t: Diazonium Salts and Azo Dye Formation
q: A given nitrogen-containing aromatic compound A reacts with Sn/HCl, followed by HNO2 to give an unstable compound B. B, on treatment with phenol, forms a beautiful coloured compound C with the molecular formula C12H10N2O. The structure of compound A is
e: Nitrobenzene → (Sn/HCl) → Aniline → (HNO2) → Benzenediazonium chloride (B, unstable) → (+phenol) → p-Hydroxyazobenzene (C, orange azodye, C12H10N2O)

t: Reactions of Nitriles and Diazonium Salts
q: The product formed from the following reaction sequence is: Benzonitrile (Ph-CN) treated with (i) LiAlH4, H2O (ii) NaNO2 + HCl (iii) H2O
e: Benzonitrile is reduced by LiAlH4/H2O to benzylamine (Ph-CH2-NH2). This reacts with NaNO2+HCl to form an unstable primary aliphatic diazonium salt (Ph-CH2-N2+Cl-), which on treatment with H2O undergoes hydrolysis to give benzyl alcohol (Ph-CH2-OH) releasing N2.

t: Reaction Sequence - Nitrile to Diazonium Hydrolysis
q: The product formed from the following reaction sequence is: Benzonitrile (Ph-CN) -- (i) LiAlH4, H2O (ii) NaNO2 + HCl (iii) H2O -->
e: LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile (PhCN) to a primary amine, PhCH2NH2 (benzylamine). This primary amine reacts with NaNO2+HCl to form an unstable aliphatic diazonium salt, which immediately hydrolyzes with water to give benzyl alcohol (PhCH2OH), releasing N2.

q:
Arrange the following in decreasing order of basic strength:
(P) Aniline  (Q) p-nitroaniline  (R) p-methylaniline  (S) Diphenylamine
e: Basic strength of aromatic amines decreases with electron-withdrawing groups and increases with electron-donating groups on the ring. p-methylaniline (R) has an electron-donating methyl group, making it more basic than aniline (P). Diphenylamine (S) has two phenyl rings delocalizing the lone pair, making it less basic than aniline. p-nitroaniline (Q) has a strong electron-withdrawing nitro group, making it least basic. Order: R > P > S > Q.

q: When aniline undergoes bromination with Br₂/H₂O (bromine water), the major product is:
e: The –NH₂ group in aniline is a powerful ortho/para director and activates the ring strongly towards electrophilic aromatic substitution. With bromine water (a mild reagent but in presence of the highly activated ring), all three activated positions (2, 4, and 6) are brominated simultaneously, giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline as a white precipitate. To obtain monobromination, aniline is first converted to acetanilide to reduce activation.

t: Strongest Base Among Substituted Amines in Water
q: Amongst the following, the strongest base in aqueous medium is
e: Basicity in aqueous solution depends on the balance of the electron-donating inductive (+I) effect, steric hindrance, and solvation. (CH3)2NH has two electron-donating methyl groups increasing electron density on N, making it the strongest base here; NCCH2NH2 is weakened by the strongly electron-withdrawing cyano group, and C6H5NHCH3 is weakened by resonance delocalisation of the N lone pair into the aromatic ring.

t: Reagent That Adds a Carbon While Forming a Primary Amine
q: In order to prepare a 1° amine from an alkyl halide with simultaneous addition of one CH2 group in the carbon chain, the reagent used as a source of nitrogen is
e: Treating an alkyl halide with KCN gives a nitrile (R-CN), adding one carbon atom to the chain; subsequent reduction (e.g. with LiAlH4) converts the nitrile's C≡N into a -CH2-NH2 group, giving a primary amine with one extra CH2 in the chain. Sodium azide, by contrast, directly substitutes to give an alkyl azide which reduces to a primary amine with no added carbon.

t: Decreasing Order of Basic Strength: H2O, NH3, OH-, NH2-
q: The correct decreasing order of basic strength of the species H2O, NH3, OH-, and NH2- is
e: Comparing the conjugate bases of very weak acids (NH3, pKa≈38, and H2O, pKa≈15.7) shows that NH2- (amide ion) is a far stronger base than OH- (hydroxide), since NH3 is a much weaker acid than H2O. Between the neutral molecules, NH3 is more basic than H2O, giving the overall order NH2- > OH- > NH3 > H2O.

q: Diazotization reaction involves:
o: NaNO2 + HCl at 0-5°C with primary aromatic amine
e: Diazotization: ArNH2 + NaNO2 + HCl at 0-5°C → ArN2⁺Cl⁻ (diazonium salt). Temperature critical — above 5°C the salt decomposes. Diazonium salts are versatile intermediates.

q: The correct order of decreasing basic strength of the given amines is : N-methylaniline, benzenamine, ethanamine, N-ethylethanamine
e: Aliphatic amines are more basic than aromatic amines due to +I effect without resonance delocalization of lone pair. Among aliphatic amines, secondary (diethylamine) > primary (ethanamine). Among aromatic amines, N-methylaniline (secondary, +I from methyl) is more basic than benzenamine (aniline, primary). Order: N-ethylethanamine > ethanamine > N-methylaniline > benzenamine.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Benzenediazonium salt is prepared by the reaction of aniline with nitrous acid at 273-278 K. It decomposes easily in the dry state. Statement II: Insertion of iodine into the benzene ring is difficult and hence iodobenzene is prepared through the reaction of benzenediazonium salt with KI. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
e: Both statements are correct: benzenediazonium salt is indeed prepared from aniline + NaNO2/HCl at 273-278K and is unstable/decomposes in dry form; and direct iodination of benzene is difficult, so iodobenzene is made via the Sandmeyer-type reaction of the diazonium salt with KI.

q: Which of the following reactions will NOT give primary amine as the product? (1) CH3CN --(i) LiAlH4 (ii) H3O+--> Product (2) CH3NC --(i) LiAlH4 (ii) H3O+--> Product (3) CH3CONH2 --(i) LiAlH4 (ii) H3O+--> Product (4) CH3CONH2 --Br2/KOH--> Product
e: Reduction of an isocyanide (CH3NC) with LiAlH4 followed by hydrolysis gives a secondary amine (CH3-NH-CH3), not a primary amine. Reduction of a nitrile (CH3CN) or amide (CH3CONH2) with LiAlH4 gives primary amines (CH3CH2NH2), and the Hofmann bromamide reaction (CH3CONH2 with Br2/KOH) also gives a primary amine (CH3NH2). So option 2 is the one that does NOT give a primary amine.

t: Acidity and Basicity - Effect of Substituents (Assertion-Reason)
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement-I: Oxidation of p-nitrotoluene with acidic KMnO4 gives an acid that is stronger than benzoic acid.
Statement-II: Reduction of p-nitrotoluene with Sn/HCl followed by neutralization gives an amine that is more basic than aniline.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
e: Oxidation of p-nitrotoluene with acidic KMnO4 oxidizes the methyl group to -COOH, giving p-nitrobenzoic acid. The electron-withdrawing -NO2 group stabilizes the carboxylate conjugate base, making it a stronger acid than benzoic acid -- Statement-I is correct. Reduction of p-nitrotoluene's -NO2 group with Sn/HCl (followed by neutralization) gives p-toluidine (p-methylaniline). The electron-donating methyl group increases electron density on nitrogen, making p-toluidine more basic than aniline -- Statement-II is correct. Both statements are correct.

q:
Identify the reactions which give aniline as the major product.
A. PhCN --[LiAlH4]--> ?
B. PhCONH2 --[KOH, Br2]--> ?
C. PhNO2 --[NaBH4]--> ?
D. PhNHCOCH3 (acetanilide) --[HCl, H2O, Δ]--> ?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: A: PhCN + LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile to a primary amine with an extra carbon, giving benzylamine (PhCH2NH2), not aniline. B: PhCONH2 (benzamide) + KOH/Br2 undergoes the Hofmann bromamide degradation, directly giving aniline (PhNH2) with loss of the carbonyl carbon as CO2 -- gives aniline. C: NaBH4 is a mild reducing agent and does not reduce aromatic nitro groups under normal conditions, so nitrobenzene is NOT reduced to aniline by NaBH4. D: Acetanilide (PhNHCOCH3) undergoes acidic hydrolysis with HCl/H2O/heat to give aniline and acetic acid -- gives aniline. So only B and D give aniline.

q: The reagent R in the given sequence of chemical reaction is: 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline --NaNO2,HCl, 0-5°C--> 2,4,6-Tribromobenzenediazonium chloride --R--> 1,3,5-Tribromobenzene
e: Diazonium salt treated with ethanol (CH3CH2OH, a reducing agent) undergoes deamination, replacing -N2Cl with -H, giving 1,3,5-tribromobenzene

q: The Kjeldahl's method for the estimation of nitrogen can be used to estimate the amount of nitrogen in which one of the following compounds? (1) Pyridine (nitrogen in aromatic ring) (2) Aniline (benzene with NH2 group) (3) Azobenzene (benzene-N=N-benzene) (4) Nitrobenzene (benzene with NO2 group)
e: Kjeldahl's method is not applicable to nitrogen present in nitro and azo groups, or nitrogen present in a ring (like pyridine). It works for aniline, where the NH2 group nitrogen can be converted to ammonium sulphate.

q: The correct order of the basic strength of methyl substituted amines in aqueous solution is:
e: In aqueous solution, basicity of methylamines follows the order secondary > primary > tertiary, i.e., (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N, due to a balance of inductive effect, steric hindrance, and solvation (hydrogen bonding) effects in water.

t: Diazonium Salt Formation - Aliphatic vs Aromatic Amines
q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Primary aliphatic amines react with HNO2 to give unstable diazonium salts. Statement II: Primary aromatic amines react with HNO2 to form diazonium salts which are stable even above 300 K. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
e: Statement I is correct: aliphatic diazonium salts are highly unstable and decompose immediately even at low temperatures. Statement II is incorrect: aromatic diazonium salts are stable only at low temperatures (0-5°C), not above 300 K, since they decompose readily at higher temperatures.

q: The correct increasing order of basic strength for the following compounds - (I) aniline, (II) p-nitroaniline, (III) p-methylaniline (p-toluidine) - is:
e: The -NO2 group is strongly electron-withdrawing, reducing basicity, so p-nitroaniline (II) is the least basic. The -CH3 group is electron-donating, increasing basicity, so p-toluidine (III) is the most basic. Hence the increasing order is II < I < III.

q: Which of the following reactions is appropriate for converting acetamide to methanamine?
e: The Hoffmann hypobromamide (bromamide) degradation reaction converts an amide (acetamide, CH3CONH2) into a primary amine (methanamine, CH3NH2) with one carbon less, using Br2 and NaOH.

q: Which of the following amine will give the carbylamine test? (options show aniline, N-methylaniline, N,N-dimethylaniline, N-ethylaniline)
e: The carbylamine (isocyanide) test is given only by primary amines. Among the options, only aniline (C6H5-NH2) is a primary amine; the others are secondary amines, which do not give this test.

q:
The correct order of basic strength of the following amines in aqueous solution is:
(i) CH₃NH₂  (ii) (CH₃)₂NH  (iii) (CH₃)₃N  (iv) NH₃
e: In aqueous solution, basicity depends on both inductive effect and solvation (hydration). Dimethylamine (secondary) is most basic because it has enough alkyl groups for electron donation and is still well solvated. The order is: (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃. Trimethylamine, despite having more alkyl groups, is less solvated due to steric hindrance, reducing its effective basicity in water.

q: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used to prepare which type of amines?
e: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis involves the reaction of potassium phthalimide with an alkyl halide followed by hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH or hydrazine. This method exclusively gives primary aliphatic amines. Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by this method because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution under these conditions.

q: When aniline reacts with nitrous acid (HNO₂) at 0–5°C, the product formed is:
e: Aniline (a primary aromatic amine) reacts with nitrous acid (prepared from NaNO₂ + HCl) at 0–5°C to form benzene diazonium chloride (C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻) by a process called diazotization. The low temperature is essential to prevent decomposition of the unstable diazonium salt. N-nitrosoamine is formed with secondary amines, not primary amines.

t: Preparation of Amines – Hofmann Bromamide Reaction
q: Hofmann bromamide degradation of an amide (RCONH₂) gives:
o: An amine with the same number of carbon atoms as the amide
An amine with one less carbon atom than the amide
An amine with one more carbon atom than the amide
A nitrile with the same number of carbon atoms
e: In Hofmann bromamide degradation, RCONH₂ reacts with Br₂ and NaOH to form a primary amine RNH₂. The carbonyl carbon (C=O) is lost as CO₂/carbonate. Therefore, the amine product has one carbon atom less than the original amide. For example, CH₃CONH₂ (2 carbons) gives CH₃NH₂ (1 carbon). This is useful for preparing amines with specific chain lengths.

q: Which of the following is a 3° (tertiary) amine?
e: Triethylamine, N(C2H5)3, has three carbon substituents directly bonded to the nitrogen, making it a tertiary amine. The others are primary (1-methylcyclohexylamine and tert-butylamine both have only one carbon group on N, despite that carbon itself being branched) or secondary (N-methylaniline, with two groups — phenyl and methyl — on N).

t: Nitrogen Source in Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis
q: The source of nitrogen in the Gabriel synthesis of amines is
e: In the Gabriel synthesis, potassium phthalimide's nitrogen is alkylated by an alkyl halide, and the resulting N-alkylphthalimide is then hydrolysed to release a primary amine — making potassium phthalimide the nitrogen source.

t: Gas Evolved When Methylamine Reacts with Nitrous Acid
q: The gas evolved when methylamine reacts with nitrous acid is
e: Primary aliphatic amines react with nitrous acid (HNO2) to form an unstable diazonium salt that decomposes immediately at room temperature, releasing nitrogen gas (N2) and forming the corresponding alcohol.

q: In the nitration of benzene using a mixture of conc. H2SO4 and conc. HNO3, the species which initiates the reaction is
e: Concentrated H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and facilitates the loss of water, generating the nitronium ion (NO2+), which is the electrophile that attacks the benzene ring to initiate nitration.

t: Product of Acid Anhydride Reacting with a Primary Amine
q: Acid anhydrides on reaction with primary amines give
e: A primary amine's nitrogen nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl carbon of an acid anhydride, displacing one carboxylate group and forming an N-substituted amide (an acylated amine).

q: Which sugar is known as 'invert sugar'?
e: Invert sugar = equimolar mixture of glucose + fructose obtained by hydrolysis of sucrose. Called invert because optical rotation changes from +66.5° (sucrose) to -39.3° (invert sugar).

q: Match List - I with List - II. List-I (Name of Vitamin): A. Vitamin B12, B. Vitamin D, C. Vitamin B2, D. Vitamin B6. List-II (Deficiency disease): I. Cheilosis, II. Convulsions, III. Rickets, IV. Pernicious anaemia. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
e: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anaemia (IV). Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets (III). Vitamin B2 deficiency causes cheilosis (I). Vitamin B6 deficiency causes convulsions (II). So A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

q:
Match the vitamins in List I with their sources in List II.
List I: A. vitamin A, B. vitamin B12, C. vitamin E, D. vitamin K
List II: I. meat, II. Sunflower oil, III. green leafy vegetables, IV. carrots
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Vitamin A is sourced from carrots (IV). Vitamin B12 is sourced from meat (I). Vitamin E is sourced from sunflower oil (II). Vitamin K is sourced from green leafy vegetables (III). So A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

q: The RBC deficiency is deficiency disease of:
e: Deficiency of Vitamin B12 causes pernicious anemia (RBC deficiency / low red blood cell count)

q: The central dogma of molecular genetics states that the genetic information flows from:
e: The central dogma of molecular biology: genetic information flows DNA → RNA → Proteins (transcription then translation)

q: The incorrect statement from the following:
o: Like chemical catalysis enzymes reduce the activation energy of bio processes.
Enzymes are very specific for a particular reaction and substrate.
e: Enzymes are proteins, not polysaccharides. They act as biocatalysts, reduce activation energy, and are highly specific to their substrates.

q: The non-essential amino acid among the following is:
e: Alanine is a non-essential amino acid, meaning the human body can synthesize it on its own. Lysine, valine, and leucine are all essential amino acids that must be obtained through diet.

q: Among the following, the narrow spectrum antibiotic is:
e: Penicillin G is a narrow spectrum antibiotic, effective mainly against Gram-positive bacteria. Chloramphenicol, amoxycillin, and ampicillin are broad spectrum antibiotics.

q: The incorrect statement regarding enzymes is:
o: Like chemical catalysts enzymes reduce the activation energy of bio processes.
Enzymes are very specific for a particular reaction and substrate.
e: Enzymes are proteins, not polysaccharides, making statement 3 incorrect. Enzymes do act as biocatalysts, reduce activation energy, and show high specificity for particular reactions and substrates.

q: Which of the following compounds can form a zwitterion?
e: Glycine, an amino acid, has both an acidic -COOH group and a basic -NH2 group in the same molecule, allowing internal proton transfer to form a dipolar zwitterion (+H3N-CH2-COO-).

q: The correct statement with regard to the secondary structure of DNA/RNA is:
o: DNA possesses a double strand helix structure and contains thymine as one of the four bases
DNA possesses a single strand helix structure and contains uracil as one of the four bases
RNA possesses a double strand helix structure and contains uracil as one of the four bases
RNA possesses a single strand helix structure and contains thymine as one of the four bases
e: DNA is a double helix containing thymine (not uracil); RNA is typically single-stranded and contains uracil (not thymine).

q: Which of the following is a non-reducing sugar?
e: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because it has no free aldehyde or ketone group — its anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose are involved in the glycosidic bond. Maltose, lactose, and glucose all have free anomeric/aldehyde groups and can reduce Fehling's solution.

q: Which of the following polymers is stored in the liver of animals?
e: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide in animals, stored mainly in the liver and muscles, analogous to how starch (amylose/amylopectin) serves as the storage carbohydrate in plants.

q: Sucrose (cane sugar) is a disaccharide. One molecule of sucrose on hydrolysis gives
o: 2 molecules of glucose + 1 molecule of fructose.
1 molecule of glucose + 1 molecule of fructose.
e: Sucrose is a disaccharide formed by the glycosidic linkage of one glucose unit and one fructose unit; hydrolysis breaks this linkage to regenerate exactly one molecule each of glucose and fructose.

t: Identifying a Vitamin Among Listed Acids
q: Which of the following acids is a vitamin?
e: Ascorbic acid is the chemical name for vitamin C, unlike aspartic acid (an amino acid), adipic acid (used in nylon manufacture), or saccharic acid (an oxidation product of glucose).

q: Nucleic acids are the polymers of
e: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are built from repeating nucleotide units, each nucleotide itself composed of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.

t: Definition of a Protein's Primary Structure
q: Each polypeptide in a protein has amino acids linked with each other in a specific sequence. This sequence of amino acids is said to be the
e: The primary structure of a protein refers simply to the linear sequence in which amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds; higher-order structures (secondary, tertiary, quaternary) describe the subsequent folding and assembly of this chain.

q: DNA and RNA each contain four bases. Which of the following bases is NOT present in RNA?
e: RNA contains adenine, uracil, cytosine, and guanine — using uracil in place of the thymine found in DNA.

q: Which of the following bases is NOT present in DNA?
e: DNA contains adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine; uracil is instead the base found in RNA in place of thymine.

q: The correct corresponding order of names of four aldoses with Fischer projection configurations given (four 4-carbon aldose structures with different OH orientations at C2 and C3) respectively, is:
e: Based on the Fischer projections: first structure (both OH on right, bottom OH determines D) = D-erythrose, second (OH alternating, bottom right) = D-threose, third (mirror of first) = L-erythrose, fourth (mirror of second) = L-threose

t: Equilibrium constant and Gibbs free energy
q: Hydrolysis of sucrose is given by the following reaction: Sucrose + H2O ⇌ Glucose + Fructose. If the equilibrium constant (Kc) is 2×10^13 at 300 K, the value of ΔrG° at the same temperature will be:
Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes DNA from RNA?
o: DNA contains uracil while RNA contains thymine
DNA is always single-stranded while RNA can be double-stranded
DNA contains deoxyribose sugar and thymine, whereas RNA contains ribose sugar and uracil
DNA is found only in the cytoplasm while RNA is found only in the nucleus
e: DNA contains 2-deoxyribose sugar and the base thymine (instead of uracil), while RNA contains ribose sugar and uracil (instead of thymine). DNA is typically double-stranded and found mainly in the nucleus, while RNA is typically single-stranded and can be found in both nucleus and cytoplasm. Options A, B, and D have the features reversed or incorrectly stated.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about glucose?
o: On heating with HI, it forms n-hexane.
It is present in furanose form.
It does not give the 2,4-DNP test.
e: Glucose exists predominantly in the six-membered pyranose ring form (not furanose, which is the five-membered ring typical of fructose or ribose), making this statement false. The other three statements are all true of glucose: it is an aldohexose, HI reduction of its backbone gives n-hexane, and since it does have a free aldehyde group, it actually DOES give a positive 2,4-DNP test — meaning that particular statement, taken as worded ('does not give'), is also false, but the originally intended NCERT answer is the furanose-form statement.

q: Which bond connects amino acids in proteins?
e: Peptide bond (−CO−NH−) is a covalent amide linkage connecting amino acids. Formed by condensation (loss of H2O) between -COOH of one amino acid and -NH2 of next. Primary structure of protein.

q: Sugar 'X': A. is found in honey. B. is a keto sugar. C. exists in α and β anomeric forms. D. is laevorotatory. 'X' is :
e: Among the options, only D-Fructose is a keto sugar (ketohexose), is found abundantly in honey, exists in α/β anomeric forms, and is laevorotatory (also called levulose).

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: A unit formed by the attachment of a base to the 1' position of sugar is known as nucleoside. Statement II: When nucleoside is linked to phosphoric acid at the 5'-position of sugar moiety, we get nucleotide. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true and Statement II is false.
Statement I is false and Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
e: Statement I is correct: a nucleoside is formed by attachment of a nitrogenous base to the 1' position of the pentose sugar. Statement II is correct: when phosphoric acid is further attached to the 5'-position of the sugar moiety of a nucleoside, the resulting unit is a nucleotide. Both statements are true.

t: Role of Minerals (Ca, Mg) in the Body
q: Which one of the following statements is correct? (1) All enzymes that utilise ATP in phosphate transfer require Ca as the cofactor. (2) The bone in human body is an inert and unchanging substance. (3) Mg plays roles in neuromuscular function and interneuronal transmission. (4) The daily requirement of Mg and Ca in the human body is estimated to be 0.2 - 0.3 g.
o: All enzymes that utilise ATP in phosphate transfer require Ca as the cofactor.
The bone in human body is an inert and unchanging substance.
Mg plays roles in neuromuscular function and interneuronal transmission.
The daily requirement of Mg and Ca in the human body is estimated to be 0.2 - 0.3 g.
e: Statement 1 is incorrect — it is Mg, not Ca, that acts as a cofactor for enzymes utilising ATP in phosphate transfer. Statement 2 is incorrect — bone is continuously being solubilized and redeposited (about 400 mg per day), not inert. Statement 3 is incorrect — it is Ca, not Mg, that plays roles in neuromuscular function and interneuronal transmission. Statement 4 is correct — the daily requirement of Ca and Mg is estimated to be 200-300 mg (0.2-0.3 g).

t: Sodium Fusion Test for Amino Acids
q: The amino acid that gives a red-blood colour on treating its sodium fusion extract with sodium nitroprusside is:
e: Sodium fusion converts any organically bound sulfur present in an amino acid into sodium sulfide (Na2S). Methionine is the only sulfur-containing amino acid among the given options (it has a thioether -S- group), so its sodium fusion extract contains sulfide ions, which react with sodium nitroprusside to give a characteristic red/violet colouration. Threonine, serine and leucine contain no sulfur and give a negative test.

q: The correct statement about peptides and proteins is:
o: Only the proteins having a quaternary structure are biologically active
In β-pleated sheet structures, peptide chains are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds
In α-helices, the polypeptide chain is twisted into a left-handed screw (helix) through intramolecular hydrogen bonds
Tertiary structure of proteins has two or more polypeptide subunits.
e: In β-pleated sheet structures, adjacent polypeptide strands are held together by hydrogen bonds formed between different chains (or different segments of an extended chain), i.e., intermolecular hydrogen bonds -- this is correct. The α-helix is actually a RIGHT-handed (not left-handed) screw, stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonds. Proteins without quaternary structure can still be biologically active. Two or more polypeptide subunits describes the QUATERNARY structure, not tertiary.

q: Enzymes that utilize ATP in phosphate transfer require an alkaline earth metal (M) as the cofactor. M is:
e: Mg2+ is the alkaline earth metal cofactor required by enzymes (kinases) that utilize ATP in phosphate transfer reactions, as it helps stabilize the negative charges on the phosphate groups of ATP.

q: The Kjeldahl's method for the estimation of nitrogen can be used to estimate the amount of nitrogen in which one of the following compounds? (1) Nitrobenzene (NO2 group) (2) Pyridine (3) Aniline (NH2 group) (4) Azobenzene (N=N group)
e: Kjeldahl's method works for compounds where nitrogen can be converted to ammonium sulfate by digestion with concentrated H2SO4, which works for amines like aniline. It does not work for nitro, azo, or diazo compounds, or for pyridine-type ring nitrogen, because the nitrogen in these cannot be easily converted to ammonium sulfate.

q: The difference between amylose and amylopectin is
o: Amylose is made up of glucose and galactose
e: Amylopectin is a branched polysaccharide of glucose units joined by α-1,4 glycosidic linkages along the chain and α-1,6 glycosidic linkages at the branch points.

q: Sucrose on hydrolysis gives:
e: Sucrose, upon hydrolysis, breaks down into one molecule of α-D-glucose and one molecule of β-D-fructose.

t: Classification of amino acids (basic amino acids)
q: Which of the following is a basic amino acid?
e: Lysine contains an additional amino group in its side chain, making it a basic amino acid, unlike serine, alanine and tyrosine which are neutral amino acids.

t: Statements about narcotic and non-narcotic analgesics
q: Statement I: Aspirin and Paracetamol belong to the class of narcotic analgesics. Statement II: Morphine and Heroin are non-narcotic analgesics. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is correct but Statement II is false
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true
e: Aspirin/Paracetamol are actually non-narcotic analgesics, and Morphine/Heroin are narcotic analgesics — both statements as given are reversed/false.

q:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Drug class): (a) Antacids (b) Antihistamines (c) Analgesics (d) Antimicrobials
List-II (Drug molecule): (i) Salvarsan (ii) Morphine (iii) Cimetidine (iv) Seldane
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Antacids-Cimetidine(iii), Antihistamines-Seldane(iv), Analgesics-Morphine(ii), Antimicrobials-Salvarsan(i). So (a)-(iii),(b)-(iv),(c)-(ii),(d)-(i).

q: The secondary structure of a protein refers to which of the following?
o: The sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds
The three-dimensional arrangement of all atoms in the polypeptide chain
The regular coiling or folding of the polypeptide chain stabilised by hydrogen bonds
The association of two or more polypeptide chains held together by non-covalent interactions
e: Secondary structure refers to the regular, repeating conformations such as α-helix and β-pleated sheets that are stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the —NH and —C=O groups of the peptide backbone. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, tertiary is the overall 3D folding, and quaternary involves multiple subunits.

t: Stabilising Force in the α-Helix Structure
q: Proteins have two different secondary structures, the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet. The α-helix structure of a protein is stabilised by
e: The α-helix is held in its coiled shape by intramolecular hydrogen bonds between the N-H of one peptide bond and the C=O of another peptide bond, four residues away along the chain.

t: Carbon Positions Linked by a Phosphodiester Bond
q: A dinucleotide is obtained by joining two nucleotides together by a phosphodiester linkage. Between which carbon atoms of the pentose sugars of the nucleotides are these linkages present?
e: In a dinucleotide, the phosphate group bridges the 5'-carbon of one nucleotide's sugar to the 3'-carbon of the next nucleotide's sugar, forming the characteristic 5'→3' phosphodiester linkage seen throughout DNA and RNA strands.

t: B-Group Vitamin That Can Be Stored in the Body
q: Which of the following B-group vitamins can be stored in our body?
e: Unlike most water-soluble B vitamins, which are excreted and must be replenished regularly, Vitamin B12 can be stored in significant amounts in the liver for later use.

q: Amongst the given options, which of the following molecules/ion acts as a Lewis acid?
e: BF3 has boron with an incomplete octet (only 6 electrons around it), making it electron-deficient and able to accept an electron pair, so it acts as a Lewis acid. H2O, OH-, and NH3 all have lone pairs available to donate and act as Lewis bases.

q: Which of the following molecules is non-polar in nature?
e: SbCl5 has trigonal bipyramidal symmetric geometry making it non-polar, while NO2, POCl3, and CH2O are polar molecules.

q: Which of the following angle corresponds to sp2 hybridisation?
e: sp2 hybridised orbitals are arranged in a trigonal planar geometry with bond angles of 120° between them.

t: Dipole Moment, Lone Pairs, Bond Length, Bond Enthalpy Comparisons
q: Identify the correct orders against the property mentioned: A. H2O > NH3 > CHCl3 – dipole moment. B. XeF4 > XeO3 > XeF2 – number of lone pairs on central atom. C. O–H > C–H > N–O – bond length. D. N2 > O2 > H2 – bond enthalpy. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: A is correct: dipole moments H2O(1.85D) > NH3(1.47D) > CHCl3(1.04D). B is incorrect: lone pairs are XeF4(2) = XeF2(3)... actual order differs (XeF2 has 3 lone pairs, XeF4 has 2, XeO3 has 1), so stated order is wrong. C is incorrect bond length order stated. D is correct: bond enthalpy N2(941) > O2(498) > H2(436) kJ/mol (triple bond strongest). So A, D only.

q: Match List I with List-II. List-I: (a) PCl5 (b) SF6 (c) BrF5 (d) BF3. List-II: (i) Square pyramidal (ii) Trigonal planar (iii) Octahedral (iv) Trigonal bipyramidal. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: PCl5: SN=5, lp=0, trigonal bipyramidal (iv). SF6: SN=6, lp=0, octahedral (iii). BrF5: SN=6, lp=1, square pyramidal (i). BF3: SN=3, lp=0, trigonal planar (ii)

q: Among the following, which one is a wrong statement?
o: PH5 and BiCl5 do not exist
pπ-dπ bonds are present in SO2
SeF4 and CH4 have same shape
e: SeF4 has a see-saw shape (due to one lone pair, sp3d hybridization) while CH4 is tetrahedral - they do not have the same shape, making statement (4) wrong.

q: Which amongst the following is incorrect statement?
o: C2 molecule has four electrons in its two degenerate pi molecular orbitals.
The bond orders of O2+, O2, O2-, and O2(2-) are 2.5, 2, 1.5 and 1, respectively.
e: O2+ ion has 15 electrons (odd number), which means it has an unpaired electron, making it paramagnetic, not diamagnetic. This makes statement 3 incorrect. C2 has 4 electrons in degenerate pi orbitals (correct), H2+ has one electron (correct), and the bond orders listed in statement 4 are correct (2.5, 2, 1.5, 1).

q: Which of the following diatomic molecular species has only pi bonds according to Molecular Orbital Theory?
e: C2 has 12 electrons with configuration sigma1s^2 sigma*1s^2 sigma2s^2 sigma*2s^2 pi2px^2=pi2py^2. Bond order = (8-4)/2 = 2, and both bonds are pi bonds (the last 4 electrons are in pi2px^2 = pi2py^2 orbitals), with no sigma bond from 2p orbitals.

t: Molecular Orbital Theory - Bond Order and Magnetism
q: Which amongst the following is incorrect statement? (1) The bond orders of O2+, O2, O2-, and O2(2-) are 2.5, 2, 1.5 and 1, respectively (2) C2 molecule has four electrons in its two degenerate pi molecular orbitals (3) H2+ ion has one electron (4) O2+ ion is diamagnetic
o: The bond orders of O2+, O2, O2- and O2(2-) are 2.5, 2, 1.5 and 1, respectively
C2 molecule has four electrons in its two degenerate pi molecular orbitals
e: O2+ has an unpaired electron in its pi* antibonding orbital (bond order 2.5), making it paramagnetic, not diamagnetic. So statement 4 is incorrect. The bond orders in statement 1, C2's electron configuration in statement 2, and H2+ having one electron in statement 3 are all correct.

q: Which of the following pairs of compounds is isoelectronic and isostructural?
e: IBr2- and XeF2 both have 22 valence electrons and both adopt a linear shape with 3 lone pairs on the central atom (sp3d hybridisation), making them isoelectronic and isostructural.

t: Bond dissociation energy and enthalpy of formation
q: The bond dissociation energies of X2, Y2 and XY are in the ratio of 1:0.5:1. ΔH for the formation of XY is -200 kJ/mol. The bond dissociation energy of X2 will be
e: Let bond energies be: X2=a, Y2=0.5a, XY=a. ΔH(formation of XY) = (1/2)BE(X2)+(1/2)BE(Y2)-BE(XY) = (1/2)a+(1/4)a-a = -(1/4)a = -200, giving a = 800 kJ/mol, so BE(X2) = 800 kJ/mol.

q: Amongst the following elements whose electronic configurations are given below, the one having the highest ionisation enthalpy is
e: [Ne]3s2 3p3 corresponds to phosphorus, which has an extra-stable half-filled 3p subshell, giving it a higher ionisation enthalpy than its period-3 neighbours Al ([Ne]3s2 3p1) and Si ([Ne]3s2 3p2). It also has higher ionisation enthalpy than arsenic ([Ar]3d10 4s2 4p3), which despite also being half-filled p3, is in a lower period with a larger atomic size and greater shielding, lowering its ionisation enthalpy relative to phosphorus.

q: Shape of NH3 molecule is:
e: N in NH3: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (sp³). VSEPR: lone pair repulsion makes bond angles 107.3° (less than 109.5°). Shape = trigonal pyramidal (electron geometry = tetrahedral).

t: Bond Order and Molecular Orbital Theory
q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: A hypothetical diatomic molecule with bond order zero is quite stable. Statement II: As bond order increases, the bond length increases. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
e: Statement I is false: a bond order of zero means the molecule does not exist/is not stable (e.g., He2). Statement II is false: as bond order increases, bond length actually decreases (bonds become stronger and shorter), not increases. Both statements are false.

t: Sigma Bonds, Pi Bonds and Lone Pairs
q: The number of sigma bonds, pi bonds and lone pairs of electrons in pyridine, respectively, are:
e: Pyridine (C5H5N) has 11 sigma bonds (5 C-C/C-N sigma bonds in the ring plus 5 C-H bonds plus... counted as 11 total sigma bonds in the ring system and substituents), 3 pi bonds (from the three alternating double bonds in the aromatic ring), and 1 lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom (which lies in the plane of the ring and is not part of the aromatic pi system).

q: The correct order of energies of molecular orbitals of N2 molecule is:
o: sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < sigma2pz < (pi2px = pi2py) < (pi*2px = pi*2py) < sigma*2pz
sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < sigma2pz < sigma*2pz < (pi2px = pi2py) < (pi*2px = pi*2py)
sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < (pi2px = pi2py) < (pi*2px = pi*2py) < sigma2pz < sigma*2pz
sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < (pi2px = pi2py) < sigma2pz < (pi*2px = pi*2py) < sigma*2pz
e: For N2 (and other molecules with atomic number up to 7, where there is significant s-p mixing), the correct molecular orbital energy order is: sigma1s < sigma*1s < sigma2s < sigma*2s < (pi2px = pi2py) < sigma2pz < (pi*2px = pi*2py) < sigma*2pz. This is because the pi2p orbitals are lower in energy than the sigma2pz orbital for these lighter diatomic molecules.

q: Amongst the following, the total number of species NOT having eight electrons around the central atom in its outermost shell, is: NH3, AlCl3, BeCl2, CCl4, PCl5.
e: NH3 has 8 electrons around N (3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair) and CCl4 has 8 electrons around C (4 bond pairs) — both satisfy the octet. AlCl3 has only 6 electrons around Al, BeCl2 has only 4 electrons around Be, and PCl5 has 10 electrons around P — none of these three satisfy the octet rule. So 3 species (AlCl3, BeCl2, PCl5) do NOT have eight electrons around the central atom.

q: Match List-I (Oxoacids of Sulphur) with List-II (Bonds): A. Peroxodisulphuric acid, B. Sulphuric acid, C. Pyrosulphuric acid, D. Sulphurous acid. List-II: I. Two S-OH, Four S=O, One S-O-S. II. Two S-OH, One S=O. III. Two S-OH, Four S=O, One S-O-O-S. IV. Two S-OH, Two S=O. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
e: Peroxodisulphuric acid (H2S2O8) has two S-OH, four S=O, and one peroxo S-O-O-S linkage (A-III). Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) has two S-OH and two S=O bonds (B-IV). Pyrosulphuric acid (H2S2O7) has two S-OH, four S=O, and one S-O-S bridging linkage (C-I). Sulphurous acid (H2SO3) has two S-OH and one S=O, plus a lone pair on S (D-II). So the correct match is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

q:
Match the species in List I with their geometry in List II:
List I: A) PCl5, B) BrF5, C) BF4⁻, D) [Ni(CN)4]2⁻
List II: I) Tetrahedral, II) Square Planar, III) Trigonal bipyramidal, IV) Square pyramidal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: PCl5 (sp3d hybridization, no lone pairs on P) is trigonal bipyramidal (III). BrF5 (sp3d2, one lone pair on Br) is square pyramidal (IV). BF4⁻ (sp3, no lone pairs on B) is tetrahedral (I). [Ni(CN)4]2⁻: CN⁻ is a strong field ligand, causing Ni2+ (d8) to adopt dsp2 hybridization, giving a square planar (II) diamagnetic complex. So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

q: The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) for Ne2 is:
e: Ne2 (hypothetical) would have 20 electrons total (10 from each Ne atom), completely filling all 10 molecular orbitals formed from 1s and 2s/2p atomic orbitals: σ1s, σ*1s, σ2s, σ*2s, σ2pz, π2px, π2py, π*2px, π*2py, σ*2pz. With all orbitals completely filled (including the highest, σ*2p), the HOMO is σ*2p, and the bond order is zero (which is why Ne2 does not exist as a stable molecule).

q: BF3 is planar and electron deficient compound. Hybridization and number of electrons around the central atom, respectively are:
e: In BF3, lone pairs on central atom=0, sigma bonds with boron=3, so steric number=3, hybridization=sp2. Number of electrons around central B atom = 6 (3 bond pairs × 2 electrons)

q: Which one of the following compounds shows the presence of intramolecular hydrogen bond?
e: Cellulose exhibits intramolecular hydrogen bonding between OH groups on adjacent glucose units within the same chain, unlike the other options which show intermolecular H-bonding or none.

q: The hybridizations of atomic orbitals of nitrogen in NO2+, NO3- and NH4+ respectively are:
e: NO2+ is linear (sp), NO3- is trigonal planar (sp2), NH4+ is tetrahedral (sp3)

q: Which of the following fluoro-compounds is most likely to behave as a Lewis base?
e: PF3 has a lone pair on phosphorus available for donation, making it capable of behaving as a Lewis base, unlike the other fully saturated/deficient compounds listed.

q: Which of the following pairs of ions is isoelectronic and isostructural?
e: ClO3- and SO3^2- both have the same number of electrons and the same pyramidal structure, making them isoelectronic and isostructural.

q: Which compound amongst the following is not an aromatic compound? (1) Cyclopentadienyl anion (2) Tropylium cation (cycloheptatrienyl cation) (3) Cyclopropenyl cation (4) Cycloheptatrienyl anion (with one double bond missing from full conjugation)
e: The cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons), tropylium cation (6 pi electrons), and cyclopropenyl cation (2 pi electrons) all satisfy Huckel's rule (4n+2) with full conjugation and are aromatic. The structure in option 4 lacks complete conjugation around the ring (not all ring atoms are part of a continuous p-orbital system), so it is not aromatic.

t: Lone Pair-Lone Pair Repulsions in Molecules
q: Amongst the following which one will have maximum 'lone pair - lone pair' electron repulsions?
e: XeF2 has 3 lone pairs on the central Xe atom (trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry with 3 lone pairs in the equatorial plane), giving the maximum lone pair-lone pair repulsions among the given options (ClF3 has 2 lone pairs, SF4 has 1, IF5 has 1).

q: The species, having bond angles of 120 degrees is:
e: BCl3 has a trigonal planar geometry (sp2 hybridisation) with bond angles of exactly 120 degrees. ClF3 is T-shaped (~87.5 degrees), NCl3 and PH3 are pyramidal with angles less than 109.5 degrees.

q: Which one of the following pairs of species have the same bond order?
e: CN- and CO are both isoelectronic with 14 electrons and have a bond order of 3 (triple bond), making them a pair with the same bond order.

t: Acidic nature of oxides (alkaline earth metals)
q: Which of the following oxides is most acidic in nature?
e: Among the alkaline earth metal oxides, BeO is the most acidic (even amphoteric) due to beryllium's small size and high polarising power, which gives its bonds more covalent character compared to the increasingly basic oxides of Mg, Ca and Ba.

q: Among CaH2, BeH2, BaH2, the order of ionic character is
e: Ionic character of the metal hydride increases with increasing metallic/electropositive character of the metal down the group: Be < Ca < Ba, so BeH2 < CaH2 < BaH2.

t: Bond order using molecular orbital theory
q: Consider the following species: CN+, CN-, NO and CN. Which one of these will have the highest bond order?
e: Using molecular orbital theory, CN- has 14 electrons giving a bond order of 3 (triple bond), which is higher than NO (bond order 2.5), neutral CN (bond order 2.5) and CN+ (bond order 2), making CN- the species with the highest bond order.

t: Ionic compound formula from electronic configuration
q: Magnesium reacts with an element (X) to form an ionic compound. If the ground state electronic configuration of (X) is 1s2 2s2 2p3, the simplest formula for this compound is
e: Element X with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3 is nitrogen, which gains 3 electrons to form X3- (N3-). Magnesium forms Mg2+. Balancing charges: 3Mg2+ + 2N3- → Mg3N2, giving the formula Mg3X2.

q: Which of the following set of molecules will have zero dipole moment?
o: Boron trifluoride, hydrogen fluoride, carbon dioxide, 1,3-dichlorobenzene
Boron trifluoride, beryllium difluoride, carbon dioxide, 1,4-dichlorobenzene
e: BF3 (trigonal planar, symmetric), BeF2 (linear, symmetric), CO2 (linear, symmetric), and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (para-substituted, symmetric) are all molecules with symmetric charge distribution, giving them zero net dipole moment.

t: Classifying oxides as acidic, basic, neutral or amphoteric
q: Match the following oxides (CO, BaO, Al2O3, Cl2O7) with their nature (Basic, Neutral, Acidic, Amphoteric). Which of the following is the correct option?
e: CO is a neutral oxide (ii), BaO is a basic oxide (i), Al2O3 is an amphoteric oxide (iv), and Cl2O7 is an acidic oxide (iii). This matches a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.

t: Non-existent molecules based on MO theory
q: Identify a molecule which does not exist.
e: Using molecular orbital theory, He2 has a bond order of 0 (2 electrons in bonding and 2 in antibonding orbitals), meaning it does not exist as a stable molecule, unlike Li2, C2 and O2 which have positive bond orders.

t: Formal charges on oxygen atoms in ozone
q: The structure of ozone (O3) with oxygen atoms numbered 1, 2, 3 is shown. The correct formal charges on oxygen atoms numbered 2, 1 and 3 respectively are:
e: In ozone's resonance structure, the central O (2) has formal charge 0... per official key, formal charges on atoms 2,1,3 are +1, 0, -1.

q: Match List I with List II: List I — A. C2H4, B. C2H2, C. CH4, D. NH3. List II — I. 3σ bonds, 2π bonds, II. 3σ bonds, one lone pair, III. 4σ bonds, IV. 5σ bonds, 1π bond.
e: C2H4 (ethylene) has 5σ+1π bonds (IV); C2H2 (acetylene) has 3σ+2π bonds (I); CH4 has 4σ bonds (III); NH3 has 3σ bonds + 1 lone pair (II). A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II.

q: Polarity in a molecule and hence the dipole moment depends primarily on electronegativity of the constituent atoms and shape of a molecule. Which of the following has the highest dipole moment?
e: CO2 is linear and symmetric, so its bond dipoles cancel (net dipole moment = 0). HI has a small dipole moment due to small electronegativity difference. SO2 has a moderate dipole moment. H2O, being bent with highly electronegative oxygen and large H-O bond polarity, has the highest dipole moment (~1.84 D) among these.

q: Hydrogen bonds are formed in many compounds, e.g., H2O, HF, NH3. The boiling point of such compounds depends to a large extent on the strength of hydrogen bond and the number of hydrogen bonds. The correct decreasing order of the boiling points of the above compounds is
e: Although HF has a stronger individual hydrogen bond, water forms an extensive 3-D hydrogen-bonded network (each molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds), giving it the highest boiling point: H2O (100°C) > HF (19.5°C) > NH3 (−33°C).

q: In which of the following substances will hydrogen bond be strongest?
e: Hydrogen bonding strength depends on the electronegativity and small size of the atom bonded to hydrogen. Oxygen is more electronegative and smaller than Cl, I, or S (in a bonding sense relevant here), making the H-bond in H2O the strongest among these.

q: The electronic configuration of the outermost shell of the most electronegative element is
e: The most electronegative element is fluorine, whose outermost (second) shell has the configuration 2s2 2p5.

q: The role of a catalyst is to change
o: the Gibbs energy of the reaction.
the activation energy of the reaction.
e: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the rate of reaction without altering the thermodynamic quantities (ΔG, ΔH, or the equilibrium constant).

q: For an elementary chemical reaction, the Arrhenius plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line with y-intercept (at 1/T=0) equal to 6 and negative slope. If the energy of activation is 6.64 kJ mol⁻¹ and R = 8.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, the temperature at which the rate constant becomes e² min⁻¹, is:
e: From the Arrhenius equation, ln k = ln A - (Ea/R)(1/T). From the graph, ln A = 6 (y-intercept at 1/T=0). Ea/R = 6640/8.3 = 800 K. We want k = e², i.e., ln k = 2: 2 = 6 - 800(1/T), so 800/T = 4, giving T = 200 K.

t: Rate law and order of reaction
q: Mechanism of a hypothetical reaction X2 + Y2 -> 2XY is given below: (i) X2 -> X + X (fast) (ii) X + Y2 <=> XY + Y (slow) (iii) X + Y -> XY (fast). The overall order of the reaction will be:
e: The rate is determined by the slow step (ii): Rate = k[X][Y2]. Since step (i) is a fast pre-equilibrium-like dissociation, [X] is proportional to [X2]^0.5, so the rate becomes k'[X2]^0.5[Y2], giving an overall order of 1.5.

t: Time for 100% Completion of a First-Order Reaction
q: A first-order reaction is 50% completed in 1.26×10¹⁴ s. How much time would it take for 100% completion?
e: A first-order reaction follows exponential decay and, mathematically, the reactant concentration only approaches zero asymptotically but never reaches it in any finite time, so 100% completion technically requires an infinite amount of time.

q: Half-life of first order reaction is:
e: t½=0.693/k=ln2/k for 1st order. Half-life is INDEPENDENT of initial concentration (unique to 1st order). For 0th order: t½=a/2k.

q: If the half-life (t1/2) for a first order reaction is 1 minute, then the time required for 99.9% completion of the reaction is closest to:
If the rate constant of a reaction is 0.03s⁻¹, how much time does it take for 7.2 mol L⁻¹ concentration of the reactant to get reduced to 0.9 mol L⁻¹? (Given: log 2 = 0.301)

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R: Assertion A: A reaction can have zero activation energy. Reason R: The minimum extra amount of energy absorbed by reactant molecules so that their energy becomes equal to threshold value, is called activation energy. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
e: Assertion A is false — a reaction cannot have zero activation energy; every reaction requires some minimum energy for the reactants to reach the transition state. Reason R correctly defines activation energy as the minimum extra energy needed for reactant molecules to reach the threshold energy. Hence A is false but R is true.

q: 2A →(k)→ B is a zero-order reaction, where k = 1.0 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹ (rate of reaction = k). If the initial concentration of A is 2 M, then the time taken to complete 75% of the reaction will be:
e: Rate of reaction = -(1/2)d[A]/dt = k, so d[A]/dt = -2k = -2.0 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹ (rate of consumption of A). 75% completion means 1.5 M of A (out of initial 2 M) is consumed. Time = (amount consumed)/(rate of consumption) = 1.5/2.0 = 0.75 min.

q: The slope of Arrhenius Plot (lnK vs 1/T) of first order reaction is -5×10^3 K. The value of Ea of the reaction is. Choose the correct option for your answer. [Given R = 8.314 JK^-1mol^-1]
e: lnk=lnA-Ea/RT, slope m=-Ea/R. -Ea/R=-5×10^3, Ea=5×10^3×8.314=41.5 kJ/mol

q: The decomposition of phosphine (PH3) on tungsten at low pressure is a first order reaction. It is because the:
o: rate of decomposition is very slow
rate is proportional to the surface coverage
rate is inversely proportional to the surface coverage
rate is independent of the surface coverage
e: At low pressure, the rate is proportional to the surface coverage of adsorbed PH3, making the reaction first order with respect to pressure/concentration.

q: For a first order reaction A -> Product, initial concentration of A is 0.1 M, which becomes 0.001 M after 5 minutes. Rate constant for the reaction in min-1 is:
For the chemical reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), the correct option is:
e: Rate r = -(1/1)d[N2]/dt = (1/3)d[H2]/dt = (1/2)d[NH3]/dt, based on dividing the rate of change of each species by its stoichiometric coefficient. This gives -d[N2]/dt = (1/2)d[NH3]/dt.

q: If the rate constant for a first order reaction is k, the time (t) required for the completion of 99% of the reaction is given by:
e: For a first order reaction, ln(C0/Ct) = kt. When 99% is consumed, Ct = C0/100, so ln(100) = kt, giving t = (2.303/k) x log(100) = (2.303/k) x 2 = 4.606/k.

q: For a first order reaction A -> Products, initial concentration of A is 0.1 M, which becomes 0.001 M after 5 minutes. Rate constant for the reaction in min^-1 is:
A first order reaction has a specific reaction rate of 10^-2 sec^-1. How much time will it take for 20 g of the reactant to reduce to 5 g?
e: For a first order reaction, t = (2.303/k) log(C0/C) = (2.303/0.01) log(20/5) = 230.3 x log(4) = 230.3 x 0.602 = 138.6 sec.

t: Effect of temperature and pressure on equilibrium yield (exothermic reaction)
q: Which one of the following conditions will favour maximum formation of the product in the reaction, A2(g) + B2(g) ⇌ X2(g), ΔrH = -X kJ?
e: The reaction is exothermic and proceeds with a decrease in the number of gas moles (2 moles reactants → 1 mole product). By Le Chatelier's principle, low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction and high pressure favours the side with fewer moles, so low temperature and high pressure maximise product formation.

q: When initial concentration of the reactant is doubled, the half-life period of a zero order reaction
e: For a zero order reaction, t1/2 = [A]0/(2k), which is directly proportional to the initial concentration. Doubling [A]0 doubles the half-life.

t: Comparing first and second order reactions
q: The correct difference between first- and second-order reactions is that
o: the rate of a first-order reaction does not depend on reactant concentrations; the rate of a second-order reaction does depend on reactant concentrations
the rate of a first-order reaction does depend on reactant concentrations; the rate of a second-order reaction does not depend on reactant concentrations
a first-order reaction can be catalyzed; a second-order reaction cannot be catalyzed
the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on [A]0; the half-life of a second-order reaction does depend on [A]0
e: For a first-order reaction, t1/2 = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration. For a second-order reaction, t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0), which depends on the initial concentration [A]0. This is the correct distinguishing feature.

t: First order reaction: time for given fraction to react
q: The rate constant for a first order reaction is 4.606×10^-3 s^-1. The time required to reduce 2.0 g of the reactant to 0.2 g is:

t: Effect of concentration on rate (collision theory)
q: An increase in the concentration of the reactants of a reaction leads to change in:
e: Increasing the concentration of reactants increases the number of molecules per unit volume, leading to a higher collision frequency between reacting molecules, which increases the rate of reaction, without changing activation energy, threshold energy, or heat of reaction.

q: Given below is an expression for the rate constant of a first order reaction occurring at a certain temperature, T(K): ln k=14.34-1.25×10⁴/T. The energy of activation in kcal mol⁻¹ for the reaction is: (k in s⁻¹, R=1.987 cal mol⁻¹K⁻¹)
e: Comparing with ln k = ln A - Ea/RT, Ea/R=1.25×10⁴ → Ea=1.25×10⁴×1.987 cal/mol ≈ 24840 cal/mol = 24.84 kcal/mol.

t: Matching order of reaction to unit of rate constant
q: Match List I with List II: List I (Order of reaction) — A. Zero order, B. First order, C. Second order, D. Third order. List II (Unit of rate constant) — I. mol⁻¹ L s⁻¹, II. mol⁻¹L²s⁻¹, III. s⁻¹, IV. mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
e: Zero order: mol L⁻¹s⁻¹ (IV); first order: s⁻¹ (III); second order: mol⁻¹Ls⁻¹ (I); third order: mol⁻²L²s⁻¹ (II). A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

q: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 1.386 × 10⁻² min⁻¹. Starting with 10 g of the reactant, how much reactant will remain after 100 minutes?
e: For a first-order reaction, t₁/₂ = 0.693/k = 0.693/(1.386 × 10⁻²) = 50 minutes. After 100 minutes, exactly 2 half-lives have elapsed. After 1st half-life: 10/2 = 5 g remains. After 2nd half-life: 5/2 = 2.5 g remains. Therefore, 2.5 g of reactant remains after 100 minutes.

t: Activation energy from Arrhenius plot slope
q: The slope of Arrhenius Plot (ln k vs 1/T) of first order reaction is -5×10³ K. The value of Ea of the reaction is. Choose the correct option for your answer. [R=8.314 JK⁻¹mol⁻¹]
e: Slope=-Ea/R, so Ea=-slope×R=5×10³×8.314≈41570 J/mol≈41.5 kJ/mol.

t: Effect of a Catalyst on Heat of Reaction
q: In the presence of a catalyst, the heat evolved or absorbed during the reaction
e: A catalyst only speeds up the attainment of equilibrium by lowering the activation energy; it does not alter the enthalpy change of the overall reaction, so the heat evolved or absorbed stays the same.

q: The activation energy of a chemical reaction can be determined by
o: determining the rate constant at a single standard temperature.
determining the rate constants at two different temperatures.
