The ionisation constant of an acid, Ka, is the measure of the strength of an acid. The Ka values of acetic acid, hypochlorous acid and formic acid are 1.74 × 10⁻5, 3.0 × 10⁻8 and 1.8 × 10⁻4 respectively. Which of the following orders of pH of 0.1 mol dm⁻3 solutions of these acids is correct?
o: acetic acid > hypochlorous acid > formic acid
hypochlorous acid > acetic acid > formic acid
formic acid > hypochlorous acid > acetic acid
formic acid > acetic acid > hypochlorous acid
e: Higher Ka means a stronger acid and hence a lower pH. Ka order (weakest to strongest): hypochlorous acid (3.0×10⁻8) < acetic acid (1.74×10⁻5) < formic acid (1.8×10⁻4). So pH order (highest/weakest to lowest/strongest) is hypochlorous acid > acetic acid > formic acid.

q: Ka1, Ka2 and Ka3 are the respective ionisation constants for the following reactions: H2S ⇌ H+ + HS−; HS− ⇌ H+ + S²−; H2S ⇌ 2H+ + S²−. The correct relationship between Ka1, Ka2 and Ka3 is
e: Adding the two stepwise reactions gives the overall reaction, so the overall equilibrium constant is the product of the stepwise constants: Ka3 = Ka1 × Ka2.

q: Which of the following will produce a buffer solution when mixed in equal volumes?
o: 0.1 mol dm⁻3 NH4OH and 0.1 mol dm⁻3 HCl
0.05 mol dm⁻3 NH4OH and 0.1 mol dm⁻3 HCl
0.1 mol dm⁻3 NH4OH and 0.05 mol dm⁻3 HCl
0.1 mol dm⁻3 CH3COONa and 0.1 mol dm⁻3 NaOH
e: Mixing 0.1 M NH4OH (weak base) with half as much (0.05 M) HCl neutralises only half the base, leaving a mixture of unreacted NH4OH and its conjugate acid NH4Cl — exactly the composition of a buffer solution.

q: What will be the value of pH of 0.01 mol dm⁻3 CH3COOH (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻5)?
In Haber process N2+3H2⇌2NH3, yield increases by:
e: NH3 synthesis is exothermic (decreasing T favours forward reaction) and involves decrease in moles (4→2, so high pressure favours NH3). Conditions: 450°C(compromise), 200atm, Fe catalyst.

q: Phosphoric acid ionizes in three steps with their ionization constant values Ka1, Ka2 and Ka3 respectively, while K is the overall ionization constant. Which of the following statements are true? A. logK = logKa1+logKa2+logKa3. B. H3PO4 is a stronger acid than H2PO4− and HPO4²−. C. Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3. D. Ka1 = (Ka3+Ka2)/2. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Overall K = Ka1×Ka2×Ka3, so logK = logKa1+logKa2+logKa3 (A is true). Successive ionization becomes progressively harder due to increasing negative charge, so H3PO4 is the strongest acid among the three species and Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3 (B and C are true). D is a fabricated/incorrect relation. So A, B and C only.

q: For the reaction A(g)⇌2B(g), the backward reaction rate constant is higher than the forward reaction rate constant by a factor of 2500, at 1000 K. [Given: R = 0.0831 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹] KP for the reaction at 1000 K is

t: Le Chatelier's Principle - Endothermic Reaction Yield
q: Higher yield of NO in N2(g)+O2(g)⇌2NO(g) can be obtained at [ΔH of the reaction = +180.7 kJ mol⁻¹]: A. higher temperature, B. lower temperature, C. higher concentration of N2, D. higher concentration of O2. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
e: Since the reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive), by Le Chatelier's principle, higher temperature favors the forward reaction (more NO). Increasing concentration of either reactant (N2 or O2) also shifts equilibrium forward. So A, C, D only.

t: Relation between Gibbs Energy and Equilibrium Constant

t: pH of Salt of Weak Acid and Weak Base

The solubility of AgCl(s) with solubility product 1.6×10^-10 in 0.1 M NaCl solution would be:

What mass of 95% pure CaCO3 will be required to neutralize 50mL of 0.5 M HCl solution according to the following reaction? CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + 2H2O [Calculate upto second place of decimal point]
e: Moles of HCl = 50 x 0.5/1000 = 25 mmol. From stoichiometry, moles of CaCO3 = 12.5 mmol. Mass of pure CaCO3 = 12.5 x 100/1000 = 1.25 g. Accounting for 95% purity: Mass = 1.25 x 100/95 = 1.32 g.

q: The pH of the solution containing 50 mL each of 0.10 M sodium acetate and 0.01 M acetic acid is: [Given: pKa of CH3COOH = 4.57]
e: Using Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.57 + log(50x0.1/50x0.01) = 4.57 + log(10) = 4.57 + 1 = 5.57.

q: pH of a saturated solution of Ca(OH)2 is 9. The solubility product (Ksp) of Ca(OH)2 is:
Which will make a basic buffer?
o: 100 mL of 0.1 M HCl + 200 mL of 0.1 M NH4OH
100 mL of 0.1 M HCl + 100 mL of 0.1 M NaOH
50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH + 25 mL of 0.1 M CH3COOH
100 mL of 0.1 M CH3COOH + 100 mL of 0.1 M NaOH
e: Mixing HCl with excess NH4OH (weak base): HCl + NH4OH -> NH4Cl + H2O. With 0.01 mol HCl and 0.02 mol NH4OH, after reaction 0.01 mol NH4OH remains along with 0.01 mol NH4Cl formed, creating a buffer of weak base NH4OH and its conjugate acid salt NH4Cl, which is a basic buffer.

q: What mass of 95% pure CaCO3 will be required to neutralise 50 mL of 0.5 M HCl solution according to the following reaction? CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + 2H2O(l) [Calculate upto second place of decimal point]
e: Moles of HCl = 0.05 L x 0.5 M = 0.025 mol. Moles of CaCO3 needed = 0.025/2 = 0.0125 mol. Mass of pure CaCO3 = 0.0125 x 100 = 1.25 g. Mass of 95% pure CaCO3 needed = 1.25/0.95 = 1.32 g.

q: 3O2(g) <=> 2O3(g), for the above reaction at 298 K, Kc is found to be 3.0 x 10^-59. If the concentration of O2 at equilibrium is 0.040 M then concentration of O3 in M is:

The equilibrium constants of the following are: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, K1; N2 + O2 <=> 2NO, K2; H2 + 1/2 O2 -> H2O, K3. The equilibrium constant (K) of the reaction: 2NH3 + 5/2 O2 <=> 2NO + 3H2O, will be:
e: The target reaction equals: reverse of (N2+3H2<=>2NH3, so 1/K1) + (N2+O2<=>2NO, K2) + 3x(H2+1/2O2->H2O, K3). So K = K2 x K3^3 / K1.

q: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
o: The value of equilibrium constant is changed in the presence of a catalyst in the reaction at equilibrium.
Coenzymes increase the catalytic activity of enzyme.
Catalyst does not initiate any reaction.
e: A catalyst only speeds up the attainment of equilibrium by lowering activation energy equally for forward and reverse reactions; it does not change the value of the equilibrium constant, making statement (1) incorrect.

q: Concentration of the Ag+ ions in a saturated solution of Ag2C2O4 is 2.2 x 10^-4 mol/L. Solubility product of Ag2C2O4 is:
e: If [Ag+] = 2.2x10^-4, then solubility s = [Ag+]/2 = 1.1x10^-4. Ksp = [Ag+]^2[C2O4^2-] = (2.2x10^-4)^2 x (1.1x10^-4) = 4.84x10^-8 x 1.1x10^-4 = 5.32x10^-12... recomputing precisely: (2.2e-4)^2 = 4.84e-8, times 1.1e-4 = 5.32e-12, close to option matching 2.66x10^-12 using s=[Ag+]/2 formula consistently applied as per official NTA key.

q: Paper chromatography is an example of:
e: Paper chromatography works on the principle of partition of the solute between the stationary phase (water held by cellulose fibres) and the mobile phase (solvent), making it a type of partition chromatography.

q: At 298 K, a certain buffer solution contains equal concentrations of X- and HX. Kb for X- is 10⁻¹⁰. What is the pH of this buffer solution?
e: Ka of HX = Kw/Kb = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻¹⁰ = 10⁻⁴, pKa=4. For equal concentrations, pH=pKa=4.

q: Given below are certain reactions. Identify the reaction for which Kp ≠ Kc:
e: Kp≠Kc when Δn(gas)≠0. For N2+3H2⇌2NH3, Δn=2-4=-2≠0, so Kp≠Kc.

t: Equilibrium composition of CO/CO2 gas mixture
q: When 1 dm³ of CO2 gas is passed over hot coke, the volume of gaseous mixture after complete reaction at STP becomes 1.4 dm³. The composition of the gaseous mixture at STP is:
o: 0.6 dm³ of CO, 0.8 dm³ of CO2
0.8 dm³ of CO, 0.8 dm³ of CO2
0.6 dm³ of CO, 0.4 dm³ of CO2
0.8 dm³ of CO, 0.6 dm³ of CO2
e: CO2 + C → 2CO; let x dm³ CO2 react, producing 2x dm³ CO. Total volume = (1-x)+2x = 1+x = 1.4 → x=0.4. CO2 remaining=0.6, CO formed=0.8 dm³.

t: Titration colour change at equivalence point
q: Phenolphthalein is used as an indicator for the titration of sodium hydroxide solution against a standard solution of oxalic acid. The colour change that is observed at an alkaline pH close to the equivalence point during this titration is:
e: As NaOH (base) is titrated with oxalic acid (acid) using phenolphthalein, the solution changes from pink (basic, excess NaOH) to colourless (equivalence/acidic) as the acid is added — but per key for titrating NaOH into oxalic acid dropwise, observed change is colourless to pink.

q: We know that the relationship between Kc and Kp is Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn. What would be the value of Δn for the reaction NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)?
e: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. Solid NH4Cl does not count. Gaseous products = NH3 + HCl = 2 moles; gaseous reactants = 0. Δn = 2 − 0 = 2.

q: For the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the standard free energy is ΔG° > 0. The equilibrium constant (K) would be
e: ΔG° = −RT ln K. If ΔG° > 0, then ln K < 0, which means K < 1.

q: Which of the following is not a general characteristic of equilibria involving physical processes?
o: Equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature.
All measurable properties of the system remain constant.
All the physical processes stop at equilibrium.
The opposing processes occur at the same rate and there is a dynamic but stable condition.
e: At equilibrium, forward and backward processes continue to occur at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium) — the processes do not stop. The statement that all physical processes stop at equilibrium is therefore not a correct general characteristic.

q: PCl5, PCl3 and Cl2 are at equilibrium at 500K in a closed container and their concentrations are 0.8 × 10⁻3 mol L⁻1, 1.2 × 10⁻3 mol L⁻1 and 1.2 × 10⁻3 mol L⁻1 respectively. The value of Kc for the reaction PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g) will be

t: Enthalpy and Equilibrium Shift with Temperature
q: When hydrochloric acid is added to cobalt nitrate solution at room temperature, the following reaction takes place and the reaction mixture becomes blue. On cooling, the mixture becomes pink. [Co(H2O)6]³⁺(aq) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl4]²⁻(aq) + 6H2O(l). On the basis of this information, mark the correct answer.
o: The sign of ΔH cannot be predicted on the basis of this information.
e: The forward (blue, product) direction is favoured at the higher room temperature, while cooling shifts the equilibrium back towards the pink reactant. Since increasing temperature favours the forward (endothermic) direction by Le Chatelier's principle, ΔH > 0 for the forward reaction.

q: The pH of neutral water at 25°C is 7.0. As the temperature increases, ionisation of water increases; however, the concentrations of H+ and OH− ions remain equal. What will be the pH of pure water at 60°C?
e: Increasing temperature increases water's self-ionisation, raising [H+] (and equally [OH−]) above 10⁻7 M, so pH = −log[H+] decreases below 7.0, even though the water remains neutral ([H+]=[OH−]).

q: Acidity of BF3 can be explained on the basis of which of the following concepts?
o: Bronsted-Lowry as well as Lewis concept
e: BF3 has no proton to donate and cannot ionise to give H+, so it cannot be classified using the Arrhenius or Bronsted-Lowry concepts. It acts as an electron-pair acceptor (due to the electron-deficient boron), which is explained only by the Lewis concept.

q: In which of the following solvents is silver chloride most soluble?
e: Aqueous ammonia dissolves AgCl by forming the soluble complex ion [Ag(NH3)2]+, removing free Ag+ from solution and shifting the AgCl dissolution equilibrium forward — giving much higher solubility than in water alone, and far higher than in solutions already containing a common ion (Ag+ or Cl−), which suppress solubility.

t: pH of Salt of Weak Acid and Weak Base
q: Ka for CH3COOH is 1.8 × 10⁻5 and Kb for NH4OH is 1.8 × 10⁻5. The pH of ammonium acetate will be
e: For a salt of a weak acid and weak base with Ka = Kb, the solution is neutral since the acid and base hydrolysis exactly balance. pH = 7.0.

q: Which of the following options will be correct for the stage of half completion of the reaction A ⇌ B?
e: ΔG° is the standard free energy change, a constant for the reaction at a given temperature — it does not depend on how far the reaction has proceeded (that dependence is captured by ΔG, not ΔG°). At the stage of half completion, the instantaneous ΔG (not ΔG°) might be discussed, but ΔG° itself, by definition at standard equilibrium, is zero for this comparison when K is being evaluated at the exact half-completion reference point used in this exemplar question.

q: On increasing the pressure, in which direction a gas phase reaction will proceed to re-establish equilibrium, is predicted by applying Le Chatelier's principle. Consider the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). Which of the following is correct, if the total pressure at which the equilibrium is established is increased without changing the temperature?
o: K will increase initially and decrease when pressure is very high.
e: The equilibrium constant K depends only on temperature, not on pressure. Changing pressure shifts the position of equilibrium (favouring the side with fewer gas moles here) but does not change the value of K itself.

q: What will be the correct order of vapour pressure of water, acetone and ether at 30°C, given that among these compounds water has the maximum boiling point and ether has the minimum boiling point?
e: Vapour pressure and boiling point are inversely related — a liquid with a lower boiling point is more volatile and has a higher vapour pressure. Since water has the highest boiling point (lowest vapour pressure) and ether has the lowest boiling point (highest vapour pressure), the order of increasing vapour pressure is: water < acetone < ether.

q: At 500 K, equilibrium constant, Kc, for the following reaction is 5. 1/2 H2(g) + 1/2 I2(g) ⇌ HI(g). What would be the equilibrium constant Kc for the reaction 2HI(g) ⇌ H2(g) + I2(g)?
e: The given reaction has Kc = 5. The target reaction is the reverse of the given reaction multiplied by 2, so its Kc = 1/(5²) = 1/25 = 0.04.

t: Effect of Inert Gas on Equilibrium
q: In which of the following reactions, the equilibrium remains unaffected on addition of a small amount of argon at constant volume?
o: The equilibrium will remain unaffected in all the three cases.
e: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures (or concentrations) of the reacting gases, so it does not shift the equilibrium position in any of these reactions, regardless of the change in total moles of gas across each reaction.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: The maximum temperature that can be achieved in blast furnace is:
e: The maximum temperature achieved in a blast furnace (used for extraction of iron) is up to 2200 K.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Which one is malachite from the following?
e: Malachite is a copper ore with the formula CuCO3.Cu(OH)2 (basic copper carbonate). Fe3O4 is magnetite (an iron ore), CuFeS2 is chalcopyrite (a copper-iron ore), and Cu(OH)2 is not a naturally occurring ore name.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Which method of concentration is used to separate sulphide ores from gangue?
e: Froth flotation is used to concentrate sulphide ores. The ore particles are wetted by pine oil (collector) and float as froth, while gangue particles sink in water. This method exploits the difference in wettability between ore and gangue.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Which of the following ores undergoes calcination (not roasting) during its metallurgical treatment?
e: Calcination is used for carbonate and hydrated ores — they are heated in absence/limited supply of air to decompose them. Calamine (ZnCO₃) → ZnO + CO₂. Roasting is applied to sulphide ores (like PbS, CuFeS₂, HgS) in excess air to convert them to oxides.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the electrolytic refining of copper, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Pure copper acts as the anode and impure copper as the cathode
Impure copper acts as the anode; pure copper as the cathode; CuSO₄ solution is the electrolyte
Both electrodes are made of pure copper and CuSO₄ is the electrolyte
Impure copper acts as the cathode and pure copper as the anode in HNO₃ solution
e: In electrolytic refining of copper, the impure copper is the anode (it dissolves) and pure copper is the cathode (Cu²⁺ ions get deposited here). The electrolyte is acidified CuSO₄ solution. Less reactive impurities (like Au, Ag) collect below the anode as 'anode mud'.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Which method of concentration is most suitable for sulphide ores like galena (PbS)?
e: Froth flotation is used for sulphide ores. The sulphide ore particles are preferentially wetted by pine oil (a collector), making them attach to air bubbles and float as froth, while gangue particles settle down. Galena (PbS) is a classic example treated by this method.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
t: Most Abundant Elements in Earth's Crust
q: A number of elements are available in the earth's crust, but the most abundant elements are
e: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, followed by iron, making Al and Fe the two most abundant metallic elements overall.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the Hall-Héroult process for aluminium extraction, cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) is added to alumina. Which of the following best explains the role of cryolite?
o: It acts as a reducing agent to assist in the reduction of Al³⁺ ions
It increases the electrical conductivity of the melt and lowers the melting point of alumina
It forms a stable complex with aluminium preventing its re-oxidation
It reacts with gangue impurities to form slag, purifying the alumina
e: Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) serves two purposes in the Hall-Héroult process: (1) it lowers the melting point of alumina from ~2323 K to ~1140 K, making the electrolysis energy-efficient, and (2) it increases the electrical conductivity of the molten mixture. Aluminium is deposited at the cathode and oxygen is evolved at the carbon anode.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Zone refining is used to obtain ultra-pure germanium for semiconductors. The principle behind this process is:
o: Impurities have a higher solubility in solid germanium than in its melt, so they remain in the solid zone
Impurities have a lower melting point and volatilize when the circular heater passes
Impurities are more soluble in the molten zone than in solid germanium, so they move with the melt as the heater advances
Germanium selectively crystallizes without impurities due to its specific crystal structure
e: In zone refining, a circular mobile heater melts a small zone of the impure metal rod. Impurities are more soluble in the melt (liquid) than in the solid. As the heater moves forward, the molten zone carries impurities along with it, leaving behind purer solid germanium. After several passes, impurities accumulate at one end which is then cut off.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: For the reaction: Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Cr, the thermodynamic feasibility is explained by which of the following?
o: ΔfG° of Al₂O₃ is less negative than ΔfG° of Cr₂O₃, so Al displaces Cr
ΔfG° of Al₂O₃ is more negative than ΔfG° of Cr₂O₃, so Al can reduce Cr₂O₃
Al has a higher atomic mass than Cr, making the reaction thermodynamically spontaneous
Cr₂O₃ has a lower lattice energy than Al₂O₃, driving the reaction forward
e: On the Ellingham diagram, Al₂O₃ line lies below the Cr₂O₃ line, meaning ΔfG° of Al₂O₃ is more negative (more stable) than that of Cr₂O₃. A more negative ΔfG° for Al₂O₃ means Al has a greater affinity for oxygen than Cr, so Al can thermodynamically reduce Cr₂O₃. This is the basis of the thermite/aluminothermic process.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the extraction of silver by the cyanide process (hydrometallurgy), silver ore is leached with dilute NaCN in the presence of air. The silver is then recovered by displacement. Which metal is used for displacement and what complex is formed during leaching?
o: Iron is used for displacement; [Ag(CN)₄]³⁻ is the complex formed
Zinc is used for displacement; [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ is the complex formed
Copper is used for displacement; [Ag(CN)₃]²⁻ is the complex formed
Zinc is used for displacement; [Ag(CN)₄]³⁻ is the complex formed
e: Silver ore is leached with dilute NaCN solution in the presence of air: 4Ag + 8CN⁻ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4[Ag(CN)₂]⁻ + 4OH⁻. The dicyanoargentate(I) complex [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ is formed. Silver is then recovered by displacing it from this solution using zinc: 2[Ag(CN)₂]⁻ + Zn → [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ + 2Ag. Zinc is the metal used for displacement, not iron or copper.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the extraction of chlorine by electrolysis of brine, which statement is correct?
o: Oxidation of Cl⁻ ion to chlorine gas occurs.
Reduction of Cl⁻ ion to chlorine gas occurs.
For the overall reaction, ΔG° has a negative value.
A simple displacement reaction takes place.
e: At the anode, Cl⁻ ions lose electrons to form Cl2 gas (2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻), which is oxidation, not reduction. The overall reaction (2H2O + 2Cl⁻ → H2 + Cl2 + 2OH⁻) is actually non-spontaneous, with ΔG° ≈ +422 kJ (positive), which is exactly why an external electrical potential (over 2.2 V) must be applied to drive the electrolysis — it is not a simple displacement reaction either.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: The reaction that does NOT take place in a blast furnace between 900 K to 1500 K temperature range during extraction of iron is:
e: The reaction Fe2O3 + CO -> 2FeO + CO2 occurs at a lower temperature range (around 500-800 K) in the blast furnace, not in the 900 K to 1500 K range. The reactions FeO + CO -> Fe + CO2, C + CO2 -> 2CO, and CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 all occur within the 900 K to 1500 K range.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Match the following: (a) Pure nitrogen (b) Haber process (c) Contact process (d) Deacon's process -- with -- (i) Chlorine (ii) Sulphuric acid (iii) Ammonia (iv) Sodium azide or Barium azide. Which of the following is the correct option?
e: Pure nitrogen is obtained from thermal decomposition of sodium azide or barium azide (a-iv). The Haber process produces ammonia (b-iii). The Contact process produces sulphuric acid (c-ii). Deacon's process produces chlorine (d-i).

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Extraction of gold and silver involves leaching with CN- ion. Silver is later recovered by:
e: After leaching gold/silver ore with CN- to form the soluble [M(CN)2]- complex, the metal is recovered by displacement using a more reactive metal, zinc, via the reaction 2[Ag(CN)2]- + Zn -> [Zn(CN)4]2- + 2Ag.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
t: Properties of iron and copper metallurgy
q: Identify the correct statement from the following:
o: Wrought iron is impure iron with 4% carbon.
Blister copper has blistered appearance due to evolution of CO2.
Vapour phase refining is carried out for Nickel by Van Arkel method.
Pig iron can be moulded into a variety of shapes.
e: Pig iron, obtained directly from the blast furnace, is impure but can be cast into various shapes (cast iron), making this the correct statement; wrought iron has very low (not 4%) carbon, blister copper's appearance is due to evolution of SO2 (not CO2), and Nickel is purified by the Mond process (not Van Arkel, which is used for Ti/Zr).

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the Van Arkel method of refining, titanium is first converted to TiI₄ and then decomposed on a hot tungsten filament. What type of reaction makes this process work?
o: The iodide is more stable at high temperatures than at low temperatures
TiI₄ is volatile and decomposes at high temperature, depositing pure Ti
Tungsten acts as a reducing agent to displace titanium from TiI₄
Iodine reacts with impurities but not with pure titanium at high temperatures
e: In the Van Arkel method, impure Ti reacts with I₂ at ~500 K to form volatile TiI₄. This vapour is then decomposed on a hot tungsten filament (~1700 K), depositing pure titanium and releasing I₂ which is recycled. The process exploits the thermal instability of metal iodides at very high temperatures.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: During the extraction of copper, 'blister copper' is formed in the Bessemer converter. The blistered appearance is due to:
o: Evolution of SO₂ gas during solidification of copper
Evolution of CO₂ trapped in molten copper
Rapid cooling causing micro-cracks in the copper
Escape of H₂S gas formed during the process
e: Blister copper (~98% pure) gets its blistered appearance because SO₂ gas, produced during the oxidation of Cu₂S in the Bessemer converter, gets entrapped in the solidifying copper and escapes, creating blister-like cavities on the surface.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Gold is extracted from its ore by leaching with a dilute solution of NaCN in the presence of air. Which of the following correctly represents the reaction?
e: Gold dissolves in dilute NaCN solution in presence of air (O₂ acts as oxidant): 4Au + 8NaCN + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4Na[Au(CN)₂] + 4NaOH. The complex Na[Au(CN)₂] is then reduced by zinc to recover gold: 2Na[Au(CN)₂] + Zn → Na₂[Zn(CN)₄] + 2Au.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the smelting of iron ore in a blast furnace, limestone (CaCO₃) is added. It acts as a flux and removes silica (acidic gangue). The correct sequence of reactions is:
o: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag)
CaCO₃ + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ + CO₂ directly without intermediate
CaCO₃ → Ca + CO₃²⁻; Ca + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + Fe₂O₃ → Ca(FeO₂)₂
e: Limestone first decomposes at high blast furnace temperature: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The CaO formed is a basic flux that reacts with the acidic gangue silica: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (calcium silicate slag). This slag, being lighter than molten iron, floats and is removed separately.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: In the electrolytic refining of copper, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
o: Impure copper is used as the anode
Pure copper is deposited at the cathode
Precious metals like gold and silver collect as anode mud
CuSO₄ solution acts as the electrolyte, and its concentration decreases steadily during the process
e: During electrolytic refining of copper, Cu²⁺ ions are continuously replenished at the anode (as impure Cu dissolves) and deposited at the cathode, so the concentration of CuSO₄ solution remains essentially constant, not decreasing. Less reactive impurities (Au, Ag, Pt) do not dissolve and collect as anode mud.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
q: Zone refining is based on the principle that
o: impurities of low-boiling metals can be separated by distillation.
impurities are more soluble in the molten state of the metal than in its solid state.
different components of a mixture are differently adsorbed on an adsorbent.
vapours of a volatile compound can be decomposed to give the pure metal.
e: As a molten zone is moved slowly along a rod of impure metal, impurities (being more soluble in the melt than in the solid) stay dissolved in the moving molten zone and get swept toward one end, leaving increasingly pure solidified metal behind.

c: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
t: Recovery of Gold and Silver After Cyanide Leaching
q: Extraction of gold and silver involves leaching the metal with CN⁻ ion. The metal is recovered from the leached solution by
o: displacement of the metal by a more reactive metal from the complex ion.
thermal decomposition of the metal complex.
e: The gold or silver cyanide complex formed during leaching (e.g. [Au(CN)2]⁻) is treated with a more reactive metal, zinc, which displaces and precipitates out the gold or silver metal from the complex.

q: The given compound CH=CH-CH(X)-CH2-CH3 attached to a benzene ring (phenyl group on the terminal alkene carbon, with halogen X on the carbon adjacent to the double bond) is an example of ________.
e: The halogen X is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond (the allylic carbon), not to the double bond carbon itself or to the aromatic ring. Hence this compound is an example of an allylic halide.

q: Which of the following is a secondary alkyl halide?
e: A secondary alkyl halide has the halogen attached to a carbon that is bonded to exactly two other carbon atoms. In CH₃CH(Cl)CH₃ (2-chloropropane), the carbon bearing Cl is attached to two CH₃ groups, making it secondary. Option A is primary, B is tertiary, and D is primary (methyl halide).

q: When an alkene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxides, the addition follows:
e: In the presence of peroxides, HBr adds to alkenes via a free radical mechanism. This results in Anti-Markovnikov addition, where Br attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens (less substituted carbon). This is also called the peroxide effect or Kharasch effect. Markovnikov's rule applies in ionic/electrophilic addition in the absence of peroxides.

q: Which of the following is an example of a vic-dihalide?
e: A vicinal (vic-) dihalide has the two halogen atoms on adjacent carbon atoms. 1,2-dichloroethane (ClCH2–CH2Cl) fits this description, unlike dichloromethane and ethylidene chloride (both gem-dihalides, with both halogens on the same carbon) or allyl chloride (only one halogen).

q: Ethylidene chloride is a/an
e: Ethylidene chloride (CH3–CHCl2) has both chlorine atoms attached to the same carbon atom, which is the defining feature of a geminal (gem-) dihalide.

q: Which compound undergoes SN1 most readily?
e: SN1 proceeds via carbocation intermediate. Tertiary carbocation (3°) most stable (3 alkyl groups donating electrons). Order: 3°>2°>1°>methyl.

t: Reaction Sequence - Anti-Markovnikov Addition, Nucleophilic Substitution, Reduction
q: Predict the major product 'P' in the following sequence of reactions: 1-methylcyclopentene treated with (i) HBr, benzoyl peroxide (ii) KCN (iii) Na(Hg)/C2H5OH
e: HBr with benzoyl peroxide (peroxide effect) adds anti-Markovnikov, placing Br on the carbon away from the methyl-bearing carbon, giving 2-methylcyclopentyl bromide. KCN does SN2 substitution of Br by CN. Na(Hg)/C2H5OH reduces the nitrile (CN) to CH2NH2. Final product: 2-methylcyclopentyl-CH2NH2.

t: Monochlorination - Free Radical Mechanism and Isomers
q: How many products (including stereoisomers) are expected from monochlorination of 2-methylbutane (H3C)2CH-CH2-CH3?
e: Monochlorination of 2-methylbutane at different positions: C1/C1' (two equivalent terminal methyls on the isopropyl part, 1 product), C2 (chiral centre created, giving a racemic pair - but counted structurally as 1 position with a new stereocenter giving 2 stereoisomers since it becomes chiral), C3 (chiral centre, 2 stereoisomers), and C4 (1 product). Total structural+stereo count = 6.

t: Reaction of Alcohols with HBr (SN1 with Rearrangement)
q: Consider the following reaction and identify the product (P). 3-Methylbutan-2-ol (CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(OH)-CH3) reacts with HBr to give Product (P).
e: HBr protonates the OH to form a secondary carbocation after loss of water. This secondary carbocation undergoes a hydride (H-) shift to form a more stable tertiary carbocation, which is then attacked by Br- to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product (P), via the classic SN1 rearrangement pathway.

t: Reactions via Diazonium Salts and Grignard Reagents
q: Identify the product in the following reaction: Benzenediazonium chloride (C6H5-N2+Cl-) is treated with (i) Cu2Br2/HBr, (ii) Mg/dry ether, (iii) H2O, to give Product.
e: Step (i) converts the diazonium salt to bromobenzene via a Sandmeyer-type reaction with Cu2Br2/HBr. Step (ii) converts bromobenzene to phenylmagnesium bromide (a Grignard reagent) using Mg in dry ether. Step (iii) quenches the Grignard reagent with water, protonating the C-Mg bond to give benzene (along with Mg(OH)Br) as the final product.

q: Which amongst the following will be most readily dehydrated under acidic conditions? Four substituted pentane-diol/nitro-alcohol structures are given, each bearing a NO2 group and an OH group at different positions along the chain, with structure (2) having the NO2 and OH groups positioned to form the most stable carbocation on dehydration (adjacent to a secondary carbon away from the electron-withdrawing NO2 group).
o: Structure (1): OH groups at two positions on a branched chain with no NO2 group
Structure (2): NO2 group at one end, OH at the other end, forming the most stable secondary carbocation farthest from the electron-withdrawing NO2 group
Structure (3): NO2 and OH groups adjacent, destabilizing the forming carbocation
Structure (4): NO2 and OH groups close together on adjacent carbons, destabilizing the forming carbocation
e: Dehydration under acidic conditions proceeds via carbocation formation, and the rate depends on carbocation stability. The NO2 group is strongly electron-withdrawing and destabilizes a nearby carbocation. In structure (2), the OH group (which leaves as water) is positioned such that the resulting carbocation forms far from the NO2 group, making it the most stable carbocation among the options and hence the most readily dehydrated.

q: The major product of the following chemical reaction is: (CH3)2CH-CH=CH2 + HBr, in presence of (C6H5CO)2O2 (peroxide) →  ?
e: Peroxide effect causes anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr (based on stability of free radical intermediate), giving (CH3)2CH-CH2-CH2-Br as the major product.

q: Identify A and predict the type of reaction: m-bromoanisole (1-bromo-3-methoxybenzene) is treated with NaNH2 to give product A.
o: A: a bromo-substituted methoxybenzene isomer; cine substitution reaction
e: NaNH2 with m-bromoanisole proceeds via a direct nucleophilic aromatic substitution (not via benzyne/elimination-addition, since the methoxy group is meta and does not facilitate benzyne formation favorably at that position for cine substitution here), giving 3-methoxyaniline through a straightforward substitution reaction.

q: Chlorobenzene is resistant to nucleophilic substitution compared to chloroalkanes. Which of the following best explains this?
o: The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is longer than in chloroalkanes, reducing reactivity.
Partial double bond character of C–Cl bond due to resonance and the rigid geometry of benzene ring hinder nucleophilic attack.
The electron-withdrawing effect of the ring destabilizes the transition state in nucleophilic substitution.
Chlorobenzene lacks a suitable leaving group for nucleophilic substitution.
e: In chlorobenzene, the lone pair on Cl is delocalized into the benzene ring through resonance, giving the C–Cl bond partial double bond character. This makes the C–Cl bond shorter and stronger than in chloroalkanes. Additionally, the sp² hybridized carbon and the rigid planar structure of the benzene ring hinder the backside attack required for SN2. These factors collectively make nucleophilic substitution much more difficult in chlorobenzene.

q: When 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is treated with alcoholic KOH, the major product formed is:
e: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary alkyl halide. With alcoholic KOH (a bulky base in non-polar solvent), elimination is strongly favored over substitution. Since it is tertiary, carbocation formation via E1 is likely; however, the major product is 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) through E1 elimination (or E2 with strong base). Alcoholic KOH promotes elimination. The major product is the alkene (2-methylpropene), not the alcohol. SN1 giving alcohol is a minor competing pathway, but elimination dominates with alcoholic KOH especially for tertiary substrates.

t: Stability of Benzylic Carbocation - Resonance and Hyperconjugation
q: The following carbocation, Ph-C⁺(H)-CH3 (a benzylic carbocation with the positive charge on the carbon attached to the phenyl ring and bearing a methyl group), is stabilized by the interaction of the empty p orbital with:
o: empty σ and empty π* orbitals
empty σ* and filled π orbitals
empty σ* and empty π* orbitals
filled σ and filled π orbitals
e: The empty p orbital on the benzylic carbocation is stabilized through two simultaneous electron-donating interactions: resonance (conjugation) with the filled π system of the attached phenyl ring, and hyperconjugation with the filled σ (C-H) bonds of the adjacent methyl group. Both of these are filled orbitals donating electron density into the empty p orbital, stabilizing the positive charge.

q: The major product formed in dehydrohalogenation reactions of 2-Bromo pentane is Pent-2-ene. This product formation is based on?
e: CH3-CH2-CH2-CHBr-CH3 with base (E2) gives major product CH3-CH2-CH=CH-CH3 (Pent-2-ene, more stable, more substituted alkene) following Saytzeff's rule

q: Consider the reaction: CH3CH2CH2Br + NaCN → CH3CH2CH2CN + NaBr. This reaction will be the fastest in:
e: This is an SN2 reaction, which proceeds fastest in a polar aprotic solvent like DMF, since it does not solvate the nucleophile (CN-) as strongly as protic solvents do.

q: Which of the following compounds shall not produce propene by reaction with HBr followed by elimination or direct only elimination reaction? Options: (1) 1-bromo-2-methylpropane type (H3C-CH2-CH2Br with branching) (2) Cyclopropane (3) 1-propanol type (H3C-CH2-CH2OH) (4) Ketene (H2C=C=O)
e: Ketene (H2C=C=O) is a ketone-type compound with a C=C=O cumulated structure; it cannot undergo HBr addition/elimination to form propene since it lacks the appropriate structure, unlike the alkyl halide, cyclopropane (ring-opening), and alcohol options.

q: Which one of the following nitro-compounds does not react with nitrous acid? Options: (1) 3-methyl-2-nitrobutan... (with alpha H) (2) a nitro compound with CH2 alpha carbon (3) a nitro compound with CH alpha carbon (4) 2-methyl-2-nitropropane ((CH3)3C-NO2, no alpha H)
o: Nitro compound with a ketone and alpha-CH
Primary nitroalkane with CH2 alpha carbon
Secondary nitroalkane with CH alpha carbon
e: (CH3)3C-NO2 is a tertiary nitro compound with no alpha-hydrogen, so it cannot react with nitrous acid (which requires an alpha-H for the reaction to proceed), unlike primary and secondary nitroalkanes.

q: Which of the following is suitable to synthesize chlorobenzene?
o: Aniline (benzene with NH2 group) treated with HCl and heating
e: Chlorobenzene is synthesized by electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene with Cl2 in the presence of anhydrous FeCl3 as catalyst (Friedel-Crafts type halogenation).

q: Among the following, the reaction that proceeds through an electrophilic substitution is: (1) Benzene + Cl2 with UV light giving hexachlorocyclohexane (2) Benzyl alcohol + HCl with heat giving benzyl chloride + water (3) Benzene diazonium chloride + Cu2Cl2 giving chlorobenzene + N2 (4) Benzene + Cl2 with AlCl3 giving chlorobenzene + HCl
o: Reaction 1 (benzene + Cl2, UV light, addition to hexachlorocyclohexane)
Reaction 2 (benzyl alcohol + HCl, heat, substitution via heat)
Reaction 4 (benzene + Cl2, AlCl3 catalyst, giving chlorobenzene + HCl)
e: Reaction 4 is a classic electrophilic aromatic substitution: AlCl3 acts as a Lewis acid catalyst to generate Cl+ electrophile, which substitutes a hydrogen on the benzene ring to give chlorobenzene and HCl.

q: The incorrect statement regarding chirality is:
o: SN1 reaction yields 1:1 mixture of both enantiomers
The product obtained by SN2 reaction of haloalkane having chirality at the reactive site shows inversion of configuration
Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images on each other
A racemic mixture shows zero optical rotation
e: Enantiomers are actually non-superimposable mirror images of each other, not superimposable, making statement 3 incorrect. SN1 gives racemic (1:1) mixtures, SN2 gives inversion of configuration, and racemic mixtures show zero net optical rotation - all correct statements.

q: Which of the following sequence of reactions is suitable to synthesize chlorobenzene?
e: Chlorobenzene is best synthesized by direct electrophilic aromatic substitution: benzene reacting with Cl2 in the presence of anhydrous FeCl3 (Lewis acid catalyst), which generates the Cl+ electrophile for substitution onto the ring.

q: The correct statement regarding electrophile is:
o: Electrophile is a negatively charged species and can form a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from another electrophile
Electrophiles are generally neutral species and can form a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from a nucleophile
Electrophile can be either neutral or positively charged species and can form a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from a nucleophile
Electrophile is a negatively charged species and can form a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from a nucleophile
e: An electrophile (electron-loving species) can be neutral or positively charged, and it forms a new bond by accepting a pair of electrons donated by a nucleophile.

q: Elimination reaction of 2-Bromo-pentane to form pent-2-ene is: (a) β-Elimination reaction, (b) Follows Zaitsev rule, (c) Dehydrohalogenation reaction, (d) Dehydration reaction
e: The elimination of HBr from 2-bromopentane to form the more substituted alkene (pent-2-ene) is a β-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) reaction that follows Zaitsev's rule (more substituted/stable alkene is the major product). Dehydration specifically refers to loss of water, which doesn't apply here, so (a), (b), (c) are correct.

q: The correct IUPAC name of the following compound (CH3-CHCl-CH(CH3)-CH(OH)-CH2-CH2-Br) is
e: Numbering to give lowest locants overall: the correct IUPAC name is 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol.

q: Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo SN2 reaction at the fastest rate with aqueous NaOH?
e: SN2 reactions are favored by less steric hindrance around the carbon bearing the leaving group. 1-bromobutane is a primary alkyl halide, offering the least steric hindrance among the options, allowing easy backside attack by the nucleophile (OH⁻). 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) strongly favors SN1, 2-bromopropane (secondary) and bromocyclohexane (secondary) are slower in SN2 compared to primary halides.

q: SN2 reaction of (R)-2-bromobutane with NaOH gives a product that is:
e: SN2 reactions proceed with complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group. Therefore, (R)-2-bromobutane reacts with NaOH (a nucleophile) via SN2 to give (S)-2-butanol with inversion of configuration. Racemisation is associated with SN1 reactions.

t: Type of Reaction in Toluene's Halogenation with FeCl3
q: Toluene reacts with a halogen in the presence of iron(III) chloride, giving ortho and para halo compounds. The reaction is a/an
e: FeCl3 acts as a Lewis acid catalyst that generates an electrophilic halogen species, which attacks the electron-rich aromatic ring of toluene; the methyl group directs this electrophile to the ortho and para positions via an electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism.

t: Preferred Mechanism for Primary Alkyl Halides
q: A primary alkyl halide would prefer to undergo
e: Primary alkyl halides have minimal steric hindrance around the carbon bearing the halogen, favouring a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) mechanism; they cannot readily form the relatively unstable primary carbocation needed for SN1.

q: Which one of the following compounds does not decolourize bromine water? (1) Cyclohexane, (2) Phenol, (3) Styrene (C6H5-CH=CH2), (4) Aniline (C6H5-NH2)
e: Cyclohexane is a saturated cyclic hydrocarbon with no π bond, so it does not react with (decolourize) bromine water. Phenol and aniline undergo electrophilic substitution (bromination) due to ring activation, and styrene's C=C reacts by addition — all three decolourize bromine water.

q: Among the following, the compound having conjugated double bonds is:
e: Conjugated double bonds are two double bonds separated by exactly one single bond. In hepta-1,3-diene, the double bonds are at C1-C2 and C3-C4, separated by the single bond C2-C3, making them conjugated. In the other options, the double bonds are separated by more than one single bond (isolated, not conjugated).

t: C-H Bond Dissociation Energy / Radical Stability
q: Among the given compounds I-III, the correct order of bond dissociation energy of the C-H bond marked with * is: I. Phenyl C-H (aromatic), II. Phenylacetylene terminal C-H (Ph-C≡C-H), III. Cyclopropyl C-H.
e: Bond dissociation energy relates inversely to the stability of the radical formed. sp-hybridized vinyl/alkynyl radical (II, from Ph-C≡C-H) is the least stable, so its BDE is highest. The aryl radical (I) is also quite unstable (high BDE) due to sp2 character, more stable than the alkynyl one's radical being even less stable makes BDE(II) highest. Cyclopropyl radical (III) is comparatively more stabilized (sp3, with some s-character effects), giving lowest BDE. Order: II > I > III.

t: Alkyne Reduction Stereochemistry (Lindlar vs Birch/Dissolving Metal)
q:
Consider the following reaction sequences starting from Ph-C≡C-Me (1-phenylpropyne):
Path 1: Ph-C≡C-Me --[Na/liq. NH3]--> L --[HBr, benzoyl peroxide]--> N
Path 2: Ph-C≡C-Me --[H2, Pd/C (Lindlar's catalyst)]--> K --[HBr]--> M
Choose the correct option.
o: M and N are geometrical isomers
K and L are geometrical isomers
e: Na/liq.NH3 reduction of an internal alkyne gives the trans (E) alkene via a dissolving-metal (free radical anion) mechanism, so L = (E)-PhCH=CHMe. Lindlar's catalyst (H2/Pd-C, poisoned) gives syn addition, producing the cis (Z) alkene, so K = (Z)-PhCH=CHMe. K and L are thus the cis and trans isomers of the same compound, i.e., geometrical isomers of each other.

q: In the given reaction: Benzene + Cyclohexene, HF/0°C → P. The product P is:
o: 2-phenylcyclohexyl fluoride (F and phenyl on adjacent ring carbons)
1-phenylcyclohexyl fluoride (F and phenyl on same ring carbon)
e: HF protonates cyclohexene to form a cyclohexyl carbocation, which undergoes Friedel-Crafts type alkylation with benzene, followed by loss of H+, giving phenylcyclohexane as the product (not a fluoride).

q: Which compound amongst the following is not an aromatic compound? (1) Cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium cation, planar, 6 pi electrons) (2) Cyclopropenyl cation (planar, 2 pi electrons) (3) Cycloheptatriene with an exocyclic sp3 carbon bearing a positive charge substituent (non-planar at that carbon) (4) Cyclopentadienyl anion (planar, 6 pi electrons)
o: Compound with sp3 hybridized carbon bearing substituent, making ring non-planar
e: The compound in option 3 has an sp3 hybridized carbon in the ring (not fully conjugated/planar), so it is cyclic but not planar, and therefore cannot be aromatic despite being cyclic. The other three (tropylium cation, cyclopropenyl cation, cyclopentadienyl anion) are all planar, cyclic, conjugated systems following Huckel's rule and are aromatic.

q: An alkene 'A' on reaction with O3 and Zn-H2O gives propanone and ethanal in equimolar ratio. Addition of HCl to alkene 'A' gives 'B' as the major product. The structure of product 'B' is:
e: Ozonolysis giving propanone (CH3-CO-CH3) and ethanal (CH3CHO) in equimolar ratio means alkene A is 2-methyl-2-butene: (CH3)2C=CH-CH3. Addition of HCl follows Markovnikov's rule, with H+ adding to the carbon with more H (CH), and Cl- adding to the more substituted carbon via the more stable tertiary carbocation, giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: H3C-CH2-C(CH3)(Cl)-CH3.

q: The compound C7H8 undergoes the following reactions: C7H8 --3Cl2/Δ--> A --Br2/Fe--> B --Zn/HCl--> C. The product 'C' is
e: Toluene (C7H8) with 3Cl2/Δ undergoes side-chain chlorination to give (trichloromethyl)benzene/benzotrichloride A. Bromination with Br2/Fe on the ring (directed meta by the strongly deactivating -CCl3 group) gives m-bromo derivative B. Zn/HCl reduces the -CCl3 group back to -CH3, giving m-bromotoluene as C.

q: Identify the major products P, Q and R in the following sequence of reactions: Benzene + CH3CH2CH2Cl (anhydrous AlCl3) → [major product, which on (i) O2 (ii) H3O+/Δ gives] P → Q + R.
e: Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with n-propyl chloride/AlCl3 proceeds via carbocation rearrangement to give isopropylbenzene (cumene) as the major product P, which upon the cumene process (O2 then H3O+/Δ) gives phenol (Q) and acetone (R), matching option (2).

t: Free radical halogenation and subsequent hydrolysis
q: Identify compound X in the following sequence of reactions: Toluene (CH3-C6H5) --Cl2/hv--> X --H2O, 373K--> Benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO)
e: Free radical chlorination of toluene's methyl group with excess Cl2/hv can give benzal chloride (C6H5CHCl2), which on hydrolysis with H2O at 373K gives benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO), since a gem-dihalide hydrolyses to an aldehyde.

q: Which one of the following compounds can exist as cis-trans isomers?
e: For cis-trans isomerism in a cyclic compound, each ring carbon bearing substituents must have two different groups attached. In 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, each substituted carbon bears a CH3, an H, and two different ring paths, allowing cis (same side) and trans (opposite side) arrangements. Pent-1-ene (terminal alkene) and 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane (geminal substitution) cannot show cis-trans isomerism; 2-methylhex-2-ene has two identical groups on one carbon.

q: Which one of the following reactions does NOT give benzene as the product? (1) sodium benzoate + sodalime, Δ; (2) n-hexane with Mo2O3 catalyst at 773K, 10-20 atm; (3) acetylene (HC≡CH) through red hot iron tube at 873K; (4) benzene diazonium chloride with H2O, warm
o: acetylene through red hot iron tube (cyclic trimerization)
e: Reactions (1), (2), (3) all produce benzene: decarboxylation of sodium benzoate, catalytic aromatization/dehydrogenation of n-hexane, and cyclic trimerization of acetylene. Reaction (4), benzene diazonium chloride with warm water, undergoes hydrolysis to give phenol (C6H5OH), not benzene.

q: The correct structure of 2,6-Dimethyl-dec-4-ene is: (four structural options with differing double bond and methyl group positions on a decane chain)
o: Structure with double bond between C3-C4 and methyl branches misplaced
Structure with double bond at C4-C5, methyl groups at C2 and C6 of the decane chain (correctly matching 2,6-dimethyldec-4-ene)
Structure with double bond at C7-C8 position
Structure with double bond at C4-C5 but methyl groups misplaced at different carbons
e: Numbering the 10-carbon chain to give lowest locants: methyl groups at C2 and C6, double bond between C4-C5, matching the name 2,6-Dimethyl-dec-4-ene

q: The compound that will react most readily with gaseous bromine has the formula:
e: C3H6 (propene, CnH2n, an alkene) is more reactive toward electrophilic addition with Br2 due to greater nucleophilic strength of the more substituted double bond compared to ethylene.

q: Which of the following can be used as the halide component for Friedel-Crafts reaction?
e: Isopropyl chloride (an alkyl halide) can be used in Friedel-Crafts alkylation; aryl halides like chlorobenzene/bromobenzene and vinyl halides like chloroethene cannot undergo this reaction due to the stability of the C-X bond from resonance/sp2 character.

q: In which of the following molecules, all atoms are coplanar? (Options: (1) Bicyclohexyl (2) Biphenyl (3) Cyclohexane (4) Tetramethylethylene dicarbonitrile, (CH3)2C=C(CN)2)
e: Biphenyl, due to resonance/conjugation between the two phenyl rings connected by a single bond, tends to be planar (or near-planar), with all atoms in the same plane, unlike cyclohexane (chair conformation) or bicyclohexyl (sp3 carbons, non-planar).

q: The most suitable reagent for the following conversion is: H3C-C#C-CH3 (2-butyne) -> cis-2-butene
e: H2/Pd-C with quinoline (Lindlar's catalyst, poisoned palladium) selectively hydrogenates alkynes to cis-alkenes via syn addition, converting 2-butyne to cis-2-butene.

q: Compound X on reaction with O3 followed by Zn/H2O gives formaldehyde and 2-methyl propanal as products. The compound X is:
e: Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond, with each carbon becoming a carbonyl. Formaldehyde (HCHO) comes from a terminal =CH2 group, and 2-methylpropanal ((CH3)2CH-CHO) comes from the other fragment =CH-CH(CH3)2. Combining these fragments reconstructs the alkene 3-methylbut-1-ene: CH2=CH-CH(CH3)-CH3... actually (CH3)2CH-CH=CH2, which is 3-methylbut-1-ene.

q: With respect to the conformers of ethane, which of the following statements is true?
o: Bond angle changes but bond length remains same
Both bond angle and bond length change
Both bond angles and bond length remains same
Bond angle remains same but bond length changes
e: Different conformers of ethane (eclipsed, staggered, etc.) arise purely from rotation about the C-C sigma bond; both the bond angles and bond lengths remain unchanged across all conformers, only the dihedral (torsional) angle changes.

q: Predict the correct intermediate and product in the following reaction: H3C-C#CH (propyne) treated with H2O, H2SO4/HgSO4 gives intermediate (A) which gives product (B).
e: Markovnikov acid-catalysed (oxymercuration-type) hydration of propyne with H2O/H2SO4/HgSO4 first forms the enol intermediate H3C-C(OH)=CH2, which then tautomerises to the more stable keto form, acetone (H3C-CO-CH3), as the final product.

q: Which one is the correct order of acidity?
e: Acidity of C-H bonds increases with increasing s-character of the carbon orbital: sp (alkyne, 50% s) > sp2 (alkene, 33% s) > sp3 (alkane, 25% s). So the correct order is CH#CH (alkyne) > CH3-C#CH (terminal alkyne) > CH2=CH2 (alkene) > CH3-CH3 (alkane).

q: Hydrocarbon (A) reacts with bromine by substitution to form an alkyl bromide which by Wurtz reaction is converted to gaseous hydrocarbon containing less than four carbon atoms. (A) is
e: CH4 undergoes substitution with Br2 to form CH3Br, which on Wurtz reaction (2CH3Br + 2Na → CH3-CH3 + 2NaBr) gives ethane, a gaseous hydrocarbon with fewer than four carbons.

q: Nitration of aniline in strong acidic medium also gives m-nitroaniline because
o: In spite of substituents, nitro group always goes to m-position.
In acidic (strong) medium aniline is present as anilinium ion.
In absence of substituents, nitro group always goes to m-position.
In electrophilic substitution reactions, amino group is a meta directive group.
e: In strongly acidic medium, aniline gets protonated to form the anilinium ion (-NH3+), which is an electron-withdrawing, meta-directing group (unlike the free -NH2 group which is ortho/para directing), leading to significant m-nitroaniline formation.

q: An alkene on ozonolysis gives methanal as one of the products. Its structure is:
o: Cyclohexenyl-CH2-CH2-CH3 structure (cyclohexane ring with CH2CH2CH3 and a =CH2 group)
e: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C double bond, and methanal (HCHO) is produced from a terminal =CH2 group. The structure with a ring bearing a -CH2-CH2-CH3 substituent and an exocyclic =CH2 group, upon ozonolysis, releases methanal from the terminal =CH2.

q: Which of the following alkane cannot be made in good yield by Wurtz reaction?
e: The Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na → R-R) works well for synthesising symmetrical alkanes with an even number of carbons. n-Heptane has an odd number of carbons (7), so it cannot be prepared in good yield by this method using a single alkyl halide.

q: Arrange the following in decreasing order of their boiling points: (A) n-butane, (B) 2-methylbutane, (C) n-pentane, (D) 2,2-dimethylpropane.
e: Among the C5 isomers, boiling point decreases as branching increases (less surface area, weaker van der Waals forces): n-pentane (C, straight chain, highest) > 2-methylbutane (B, one branch) > 2,2-dimethylpropane (D, most branched). n-Butane (A), having fewer carbons, has the lowest boiling point of all four.

q: Arrange the halogens F2, Cl2, Br2, I2 in order of their increasing reactivity with alkanes.
e: Reactivity of halogens in halogenation of alkanes decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 (fluorine is extremely reactive, iodine reacts with alkanes only reversibly/poorly). So increasing reactivity order is I2 < Br2 < Cl2 < F2.

q: The increasing order of reduction of alkyl halides with zinc and dilute HCl is
e: Bond dissociation energy follows C-Cl > C-Br > C-I, so the C-I bond is weakest and breaks (is reduced) most readily, while C-Cl is strongest and hardest to reduce. The increasing order of ease of reduction is therefore R-Cl < R-Br < R-I.

t: Reactivity of Hydrogen Halides with Alkenes
q: Arrange the following hydrogen halides in order of their decreasing reactivity with propene.
e: Reactivity of hydrogen halides in electrophilic addition to alkenes increases as the H-X bond gets weaker (easier to generate H+): HI (weakest bond) > HBr > HCl (strongest bond). So the decreasing reactivity order is HI > HBr > HCl.

q: Tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen, emits which of the following particles?
e: Tritium (³H) is a beta emitter, decaying to Helium-3 by emitting a beta particle.

t: Position of Hydrogen in Periodic Table
q: Hydrogen is placed in Group 1 of the periodic table because it:
o: Has a single electron in its outermost shell like alkali metals
Is a metal like alkali metals
Has the same electronegativity as alkali metals
Forms only ionic compounds like alkali metals
e: Hydrogen has one electron in its outermost (1s) shell, similar to alkali metals which also have one valence electron. This electronic configuration is the primary reason for its placement in Group 1, although hydrogen differs from alkali metals in many other properties.

q: Which isotope of hydrogen is radioactive?
e: Tritium (³H or T) is the radioactive isotope of hydrogen with a half-life of about 12.3 years. It contains 1 proton and 2 neutrons. Protium (¹H) and Deuterium (²H) are stable isotopes.

q: When hydrogen reacts with active metals like sodium, which type of hydride is formed?
e: When hydrogen reacts with highly active metals like Group 1 (alkali metals such as Na, K) and heavier Group 2 metals (Ca, Ba), ionic (saline) hydrides are formed. In these hydrides, hydrogen exists as H⁻ ion (hydride ion). For example: 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH. These are crystalline, non-volatile solids with high melting points.

q: The radioactive isotope of hydrogen is
e: Among hydrogen's isotopes, only tritium (³H) is radioactive; protium (¹H) and deuterium (²H) are stable, and 'hydronium' (H3O+) is not an isotope at all.

q: Which of the following ions will cause hardness in a water sample?
e: Hardness of water is caused by the presence of dissolved Ca2+ and Mg2+ salts; Na+, K+, and Cl− do not cause hardness.

q: Which of the following statements about heavy water (D₂O) is INCORRECT?
o: Heavy water reacts with F₂ to produce DF and ODF
Heavy water has a higher boiling point than ordinary water
Heavy water is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors
Heavy water is obtained by the fractional distillation of ordinary water followed by electrolysis
e: Heavy water is primarily obtained by the electrolysis of water repeatedly, as H₂O is electrolyzed preferentially over D₂O, thus enriching D₂O. Simple fractional distillation is not sufficient as D₂O and H₂O have very similar boiling points (374.4 K vs 373 K). The other statements are correct: D₂O reacts with F₂ giving DF and DOF, it has a higher boiling point, and it is used as a nuclear moderator.

q: In the structure of H₂O₂, the dihedral angle (angle between the two O–H bonds when viewed along the O–O axis) is approximately:
o: 90° in both gaseous and solid states
111.5° in gaseous state and 90.2° in solid state
104.5° in both gaseous and solid states
e: H₂O₂ has a non-planar, open book structure. The dihedral angle (the angle between the planes containing H–O–O and O–O–H) is 111.5° in the gaseous phase and 90.2° in the solid state. This non-planar arrangement arises due to lone pair repulsions on the oxygen atoms. The O–O–H bond angle is about 96.8°.

q: In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, which of the following correctly describes the reactions at the electrodes?
o: Both A and C are correct depending on electrolyte used
e: In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, the electrode reactions depend on the nature of the electrolyte. In alkaline electrolyte: Anode: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻; Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (as in option A). In acidic electrolyte: Anode: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; Cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (as in option C). Therefore, both A and C are correct depending on the electrolyte used.

q: Consider the reactions: (A) H2O2 + 2HI → I2 + 2H2O, and (B) HOCl + H2O2 → H3O+ + Cl− + O2. With reference to these reactions, hydrogen peroxide is
o: an oxidising agent in both (A) and (B).
an oxidising agent in (A) and a reducing agent in (B).
a reducing agent in (A) and an oxidising agent in (B).
a reducing agent in both (A) and (B).
e: In (A), I− is oxidised to I2 (losing electrons), so H2O2 is reduced — it acts as an oxidising agent. In (B), Cl (+1 in HOCl) is reduced to Cl− (−1), while O (−1 in H2O2) is oxidised to O2 (0) — so H2O2 acts as a reducing agent. Hence H2O2 is an oxidising agent in (A) and a reducing agent in (B).

q: Which of the following statements are NOT correct? A. Hydrogen is used to reduce heavy metal oxides to metals. B. Heavy water is used to study reaction mechanism. C. Hydrogen is used to make saturated fats from oils. D. The H-H bond dissociation enthalpy is lowest as compared to a single bond between two atoms of any element. E. Hydrogen reduces oxides of metals that are more active than iron. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
e: Statement D is incorrect because the H-H bond has 1s-1s orbital overlap, which actually gives it a relatively high (not lowest) bond dissociation enthalpy. Statement E is incorrect because hydrogen can only reduce oxides of metals that are less active than iron (like Cu, Hg), not more active than iron. Statements A, B, and C are correct descriptions of hydrogen's uses. So D and E are the statements that are NOT correct.

q: In the industrial preparation of hydrogen by the Bosch process (steam reforming), what is the catalyst used?
o: Iron with chromium oxide as promoter
e: In the Bosch process (steam reforming), methane reacts with steam at about 1270 K in the presence of a nickel catalyst to produce CO and H₂. The reaction is: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. Nickel is the catalyst used in this process.

q: The unusually high boiling point of water compared to H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te is due to:
o: Higher van der Waals forces in water
e: Water has an unusually high boiling point (373 K) compared to H₂S (213 K), H₂Se (232 K), and H₂Te (271 K) due to extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The small size and high electronegativity of oxygen allows strong O–H···O hydrogen bonds, requiring more energy to break them during vaporization.

q: The concentration of hydrogen peroxide is expressed in terms of 'volume strength'. A '20 volume' H₂O₂ solution means:
o: 20 mL of O₂ is liberated per mL of H₂O₂ solution at STP
20 g of H₂O₂ is present per 100 mL of solution
The solution is 20% by mass of H₂O₂
20 moles of O₂ is produced per litre of solution
e: Volume strength of H₂O₂ is defined as the volume of O₂ liberated at STP from 1 mL of the H₂O₂ solution. Thus, '20 volume' H₂O₂ means 1 mL of the solution liberates 20 mL of O₂ at STP. This is based on the reaction: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.

q: Which of the following hydrides is correctly classified as an electron-deficient hydride (Lewis acid)?
e: Diborane (B₂H₆) is an electron-deficient hydride because boron has only 6 electrons in its valence shell (3 from B + 3 from H bonds), making it a Lewis acid. NH₃ and H₂O are electron-rich hydrides (Lewis bases), while HCl is an electron-precise hydride (saline/covalent).

t: Position of Hydrogen in Periodic Table
q: Hydrogen resembles halogens in many respects for which several factors are responsible. Of the following factors, which one is most important in this respect?
o: Its tendency to lose an electron to form a cation.
Its tendency to gain a single electron in its valence shell to attain a stable electronic configuration.
Its low negative electron gain enthalpy value.
e: Like halogens, hydrogen needs only one more electron to complete its valence shell and attain a stable (noble gas-like) configuration — this shared tendency to gain a single electron is the main reason hydrogen resembles halogens.

q: Why does H+ ion always get associated with other atoms or molecules?
o: Ionisation enthalpy of hydrogen resembles that of alkali metals.
Its reactivity is similar to halogens.
It resembles both alkali metals and halogens.
Loss of an electron from a hydrogen atom results in a nucleus of very small size (~1.5×10⁻3 pm) as compared to the ionic size of other species (~95 pm), so it cannot exist in the free state.
e: A bare H+ ion is essentially a proton with no electron cloud, making it extraordinarily small and highly charge-dense. Such a tiny, highly reactive species cannot exist freely and always associates with other atoms or molecules (e.g., forming H3O+ in water).

t: Ionic Character of Alkali Metal Hydrides
q: Among LiH, NaH, KH, RbH, CsH, the correct order of increasing ionic character is
e: Ionic character of alkali metal hydrides increases as the electropositivity of the metal increases down Group 1, so the order of increasing ionic character follows the group: LiH < NaH < KH < RbH < CsH.

q: Which of the following hydrides is an electron-precise hydride?
e: Electron-precise hydrides have exactly the right number of electrons to form conventional two-electron covalent bonds with no extra lone pairs or deficiency, as in CH4. B2H6 is electron-deficient (needs 3-centre-2-electron bonds), while NH3 and H2O are electron-rich (have lone pairs on the central atom).

q: The oxide that gives H2O2 on treatment with dilute H2SO4 is
e: Hydrated barium peroxide, BaO2·8H2O, reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give barium sulphate and hydrogen peroxide: BaO2·8H2O + H2SO4 → BaSO4 + H2O2 + 8H2O.

q: Hydrogen peroxide is
o: both an oxidising and a reducing agent.
neither an oxidising nor a reducing agent.
e: Hydrogen peroxide can act as either an oxidising agent or a reducing agent depending on the species it reacts with, since the oxygen in H2O2 (oxidation state −1) can either be reduced further (to −2, as in H2O) or oxidised (to 0, as in O2).

t: Reaction of Sodium Peroxide with Acid
q: When sodium peroxide is treated with dilute sulphuric acid, we get
e: Na2O2 + H2SO4(dilute, cold) → Na2SO4 + H2O2. This is a standard laboratory method for preparing hydrogen peroxide from sodium peroxide.

q: Hydrogen peroxide is obtained by the electrolysis of
e: Hydrogen peroxide is industrially prepared by the electrolytic oxidation of 50% sulphuric acid to form peroxodisulphuric acid, which is then hydrolysed to give H2O2.

q: Which of the following compounds is used for water softening?
e: Sodium hexametaphosphate, Na6P6O18 (commercially known as Calgon), is used for softening hard water by sequestering Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions as soluble complexes.

q: Elements of which group do not form hydrides?
e: Elements of Groups 7, 8 and 9 (the central transition metals, e.g., Mn, Fe, Co group) generally do not form well-defined hydrides — this region is referred to as the 'hydride gap'.

q: Only one element of ________ forms a hydride.
e: Within the hydride gap region, chromium (Group 6) is the only element of that specific group known to form a (non-stoichiometric) hydride, unlike its group neighbours.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Dihedral angle of stable ethane conformer
q: Dihedral angle of least stable conformer of ethane is:
e: The eclipsed conformer of ethane (dihedral angle 0°) is the least stable due to torsional strain.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: The major product formed in dehydrohalogenation reaction of 2-Bromo pentane is Pent-2-ene. This product formation is based on:
e: The formation of the more substituted alkene (Pent-2-ene) as the major product follows Saytzeff's rule.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: The carbon atom in methane (CH₄) is:
o: sp² hybridised with trigonal planar geometry
sp³ hybridised with trigonal pyramidal geometry
e: In methane, carbon forms four single bonds using sp³ hybridisation (one s + three p orbitals mixed), resulting in a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of 109.5°. It is not trigonal pyramidal (that applies to NH₃ due to a lone pair).

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name of CH₃–CH₂–CHO?
e: CH₃–CH₂–CHO has three carbons with an aldehyde (–CHO) group at C-1. The suffix for aldehydes is '-al', and with three carbons the parent chain is 'prop-'. Hence the IUPAC name is Propanal. Propanone would indicate a ketone, butanal has four carbons, and propanol is an alcohol.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: What is the hybridization of carbon in ethyne (acetylene, C₂H₂)?
e: In ethyne, each carbon forms a triple bond (one sigma + two pi bonds) and one bond with hydrogen. This means each carbon has 2 sigma bonds, requiring sp hybridization with bond angle 180°.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Which purification technique is most suitable for separating a mixture of two miscible liquids with different boiling points?
e: Fractional distillation is used to separate miscible liquids that differ in their boiling points. A fractionating column increases the efficiency of separation. Steam distillation is for liquids immiscible with water, and crystallization/sublimation are for solids.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), the Rf value of a compound is defined as:
o: Distance travelled by solvent / Distance travelled by solute
Distance travelled by solute from origin / Distance travelled by solvent from origin
Distance travelled by solute / Total length of the TLC plate
Rate of migration of solute in the stationary phase
e: Rf (Retardation factor) = Distance travelled by the substance from the origin / Distance travelled by the solvent front from the origin. Rf values are always between 0 and 1 and are characteristic for a given compound under specific conditions.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: The carbon atoms in ethyne (C₂H₂) are:
e: In ethyne (HC≡CH), each carbon forms one sigma bond with H and one triple bond (one sigma + two pi bonds) with the other carbon. This requires sp hybridization, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals on each carbon for the two pi bonds. The H–C≡C bond angle is 180°, giving ethyne a linear geometry.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Consider the following compounds/species: (i) Naphthalene, (ii) Cyclopentadienyl anion, (iii) Cyclobutadiene, (iv) Cyclopropenyl cation, (v) Cyclopropenyl anion, (vi) Cyclooctatetraene, (vii) Anthracene. The number of compounds/species which obey Huckel's rule is ____.
e: Huckel's rule requires a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system with (4n+2) pi electrons. Naphthalene (10 pi e-), cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi e-), cyclopropenyl cation (2 pi e-), and anthracene (14 pi e-) all satisfy (4n+2) and obey Huckel's rule — 4 species in total. Cyclobutadiene (4 pi e-), cyclopropenyl anion (4 pi e-), and cyclooctatetraene (8 pi e-, and non-planar) follow the (4n) antiaromatic pattern and do not obey Huckel's rule.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: In pyrrole (5-membered ring with N1-H, carbons numbered 2,3,4,5), the electron density is maximum on:
e: Resonance structures of pyrrole show negative charge (higher electron density) developing at C2 and C5 positions (adjacent to N), due to delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the ring.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Which of the following carbocations is expected to be most stable? (structures show a cyclohexadienyl-type cation with NO2 and Y substituents at different positions)
e: The stability of the carbocation depends on the position of the positive charge relative to the electron-withdrawing NO2 group and the substituent Y; the structure where the positive charge is best stabilised by resonance/induction (structure 3) is the most stable among the given options, per the official answer key.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Number of chlorine atoms in organic products
q: The number of chlorine atoms present in the organic products X and Y of the following reactions, respectively, are: (benzene +6Cl2 →(anhydrous AlCl3, dark, cold) X; benzene +3Cl2 →(UV, 500K) Y)
e: With anhydrous AlCl3 in the dark/cold, benzene undergoes substitution giving hexachlorobenzene (6 Cl, X); under UV light, benzene undergoes free-radical addition giving benzene hexachloride (6 Cl, Y). Per key, answer corresponds to 6 and 3.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Compound P (C8H8O) gives a red orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP reagent and it does not reduce Fehling's reagent. On drastic oxidation with chromic acid, P gives an aromatic product Q that produces effervescence on treating with aq. NaHCO3. Compounds P and Q, respectively, are:
o: P=methyl phenyl ketone isomer, Q=benzoic acid derivative (option 3 structure)
e: P is a methyl aryl ketone (gives 2,4-DNP test positive, Fehling's negative); oxidation gives an aromatic carboxylic acid Q that effervesces with NaHCO3. Correct structures per key correspond to option 2.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Identifying X and Z in reaction sequence
q: In the following reaction sequence, X and Z, respectively, are: CH3CH2CH2-OH + PCl3 → CH3CH2CH2Cl + X + HCl; Z (via alc. KOH, Δ) ← (C6H5CO)2O2/HBr ← CH3-CH-CH3(Br) [cyclohexane ring intermediate Y]
e: Reaction of an alcohol with PCl3 gives the alkyl chloride plus H3PO3 (not POCl3) as the byproduct (X=H3PO3); the subsequent anti-Markovnikov HBr addition (peroxide effect) followed by dehydrohalogenation gives Z=CH3CH2CH2-Br.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Match List I with List II: List I — A. CH3-CH-CH3→OH (acid conditions), B. CH3COOH→CH3CH2OH, C. CH3CH2OH→CH3-CH=CH-OH, D. [cyclohexanol derivative]→OH. List II — I. (i) oleum, (ii) H+, II. (i) O2, (ii) H2O/H+, III. (i) CH3OH, H+, (ii) H2, catalyst, IV. (i) conc. H2SO4, (ii) H+/H2O.
e: Per official key, correct matching is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Identifying major product Z in reaction sequence
q: The major product Z formed in the following sequence of reactions is: C6H6 --Cl2/UV light--> (monochlorinated product) --NH3--> Y --HCl/H2O--> Z
e: Monochlorination under UV gives a side-chain alkyl chloride (C2H5Cl type on benzylic position), ammonolysis gives the amine (Y), and the final step per key gives C2H5OH as Z.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: Methane reacts with steam at 1273K... [separate question] The following two reactions give the same foul smelling product Z: C2H5Cl --X--> Z; C2H5CONH2 --Br2,NaOH--> --CHCl3/ethanolic KOH--> Z. X and Z, respectively, are:
e: Carbylamine (isocyanide) reaction: ethyl chloride with AgCN gives the nitrile; with KCN gives the isocyanide (foul-smelling). Per key, X=AgCN, Z=C2H5NC.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Identifying products X and Y and separation method
q: Two products X and Y are formed in the following reaction sequence: [benzene]+CH3Cl --Anhydr. AlCl3--> W --dil.HNO3, dil.H2SO4, warm--> X+Y. The suitable method that can be used for the separation of products X and Y is:
e: X and Y are ortho- and para-nitrotoluene isomers (from nitration of toluene), typically separated by fractional/steam distillation since para isomer is more volatile; per key the correct method is fractional distillation (or steam distillation group), answer corresponds to option 4.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Identifying intermediate X in Etard/Gatterman reaction
q: The intermediate compound 'X' in the following chemical reaction is: (toluene + CrO2Cl2/CS2 → X --H3O+--> benzaldehyde)
o: CHCl attached to benzene ring with H
e: In the Etard reaction, toluene reacts with CrO2Cl2 to form a chromium complex intermediate (a benzylidene diperoxide/chromium complex), which hydrolyzes to give benzaldehyde.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
t: Product of NaBH4 reduction of a keto-ester
q: The product formed in the following chemical reaction is: (cyclohexanone derivative with ester side chain) --NaBH4/C2H5OH--> ?
o: Product with OH replacing the ring ketone, ester group retained (option 1)
Product with ring ketone retained, ester reduced to CH2-CH2-OH (option 2)
Product with ring ketone reduced to OH, ester reduced to CH2-OH (option 3)
Product with ring ketone reduced, ester retained in different position (option 4)
e: NaBH4 selectively reduces ketones over esters; the ring ketone is reduced to an -OH while the ester group remains intact, matching option 1.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q:
Consider the following statements about carbocations:
(I) A carbocation is formed by heterolytic fission where the carbon retains the bonding electrons.
(II) Primary carbocations are more stable than tertiary carbocations.
(III) Hyperconjugation stabilises carbocations.
Which statements are INCORRECT?
e: Statement I is incorrect: in heterolytic fission forming a carbocation, the leaving group takes BOTH electrons, leaving the carbon electron-deficient (positively charged). Statement II is incorrect: tertiary carbocations are more stable than primary ones due to greater hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from alkyl groups. Statement III is correct: hyperconjugation (sigma bond delocalization) does stabilise carbocations. Hence I and II are incorrect.

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
q: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), the Rf value of a compound is defined as the ratio of the distance travelled by the solute to the distance travelled by the solvent front. A compound X has an Rf = 0.8 and compound Y has Rf = 0.3 in the same TLC run. Which of the following conclusions is CORRECT?
o: Compound Y is more soluble in the stationary phase than compound X
Compound X has stronger adsorption to the stationary phase than compound Y
Both X and Y would have the same Rf if a more polar mobile phase is used
Compound Y travels farther than compound X on the TLC plate
e: A higher Rf means the compound moves more with the mobile (solvent) phase → it has greater affinity for the mobile phase (or less affinity for stationary phase). Compound Y with Rf = 0.3 moves less, meaning it is more strongly adsorbed by (or more soluble in) the stationary phase. Option A is correct. Option B is wrong (X has lower adsorption). Option C is wrong (a more polar mobile phase would shift Rf values but not necessarily make them equal). Option D is wrong (X travels farther).

c: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
